events.desc: Penelope Pitstop: Well, I do declare — what a magnificent old place! Just look at that staircase, and those portraits... they look like they're keeping secrets, every last one of them. Sneekly, sugar, isn't this just the most thrilling thing? A real honest-to-goodness mystery mansion! And Peter — Peter Perfect, as I live and breathe! Boys! Oh, I just know we're going to have the most wonderful time. Now, has anyone had a peek at this guest book? I am simply dying to know who else has walked through these doors.
events.thinking:
I've just arrived at Doily Manor. The entrance hall is grand but dusty — there's a sense of old money and older secrets here. My chest feels light, that familiar lift when I step into somewhere new. The chandelier above looks like it could crash down any moment, but honestly, that just adds to the charm. I can feel that prickling at the back of my scalp already — this place is full of things that don't quite fit, and I want to turn every one of them over.

Sneekly is here — dear Sneekly, who practically raised me. And Peter! My heart does a little skip seeing him. The Ant Hill Mob too — my boys. Everyone's gathered in the entrance hall. Dick Dastardly is lurking about, which... well, I'm sure he means well. Everyone does, deep down.

There's a guest book on the side table. That's interesting — who else has been here? What names are in it? That tug behind my ribs is already pulling me toward it. But first — I should greet everyone properly. Mama would turn in her grave if I walked into a room full of people and went straight for the furniture.

The Doily Diamond is somewhere in this mansion. I can feel it in my bones. But rushing won't do — a proper investigation starts with understanding the lay of the land and the people in it. Let me say hello and then have a look at that guest book.

events.desc: The chandelier is hanging by what looks like a thread and a prayer, but never mind that — there's a diamond to find, and Clara Bellingham did not drive all the way out here to worry about light fixtures.

events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly): Welcome, welcome to Doily Manor! I am Mr Pemberton, the estate manager. Please, do sign the guest book — the late Lord Doily was most particular about keeping records of all visitors. I trust your journey was not too arduous? The manor has been... *expecting* you. If there is anything you require — anything at all — you need only ask. I am entirely at your service.
events.thinking: The hall stretches before me — dust motes turning in the chandelier light, portraits staring down with that familiar disapproval. My chest settles into its resting architecture. Eight of them, milling about like guests at a party they weren't quite invited to. The Ant Hill Mob — those ones watch. I felt their attention land on me before I'd finished crossing the threshold. A prickle at the back of my neck. Mental note. Penelope is here — trusting, bright, oblivious. Useful. Dick Dastardly — greedy, impulsive, a perfect decoy if things go sideways. Clara hasn't arrived yet. Good. That gives me time to establish myself as Pemberton, the mild-mannered estate manager, before she walks in. Every smile I offer now is a foundation I lay for later. The guest book — perfect prop. I'll position myself beside it, the helpful servant, welcoming everyone. The role fits like a glove I never take off. My jaw unclenches. The design begins.

events.desc: Look at them. Every one of them wandering into my parlour with that charming, trusting ignorance. The chandelier above them hangs by a thread — quite literally — and not one of them has thought to look up. How perfectly... architectural. But patience. Clara is the target. These are merely the scenery. And oh, what magnificent scenery they shall make when the curtain falls.

events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob: Right, lads — we're 'ere. Doily Manor. Look at this place — chandelier 'anging by a thread, dust everywhere, portraits staring at you like you owe 'em money. *sniffs* Smells like trouble. Now listen — we're 'ere for one reason and one reason only: Clara. Miss Bellingham. We keep our eyes open, our ears sharp, and our feet... well, try not to trip over anything, yeah? *glances at Sneekly with narrowed eyes* Some of these faces I trust. Some of 'em... my gut's got opinions about. And my gut ain't been wrong since Bermondsey, '04.
events.thinking: Right then. We're 'ere. Doily Manor. The lads and me, we made it. Place smells like old money and older secrets — dust thick enough to write your name in, chandelier that looks like it's one sneeze away from coming down on someone's 'ead. And there she is — well, not Clara herself, but Penelope's 'ere, and that's close enough to keep me sharp. My eyes are already doing the rounds — doors, windows, that staircase that curves up into shadow. And there — Sneekly. Pemberton. Whatever 'e calls 'imself. Standing there all smooth and polished like a snake in a waistcoat. My neck's prickling already. Too eager, that one. Too 'elpful. I've seen that smile before — on the kid who cleaned out our stash and vanished. And Dastardly's 'ere too, which is never good news. Peter Perfect — 'e's alright, means well, bit of a plank but 'is 'eart's in the right place. Muttley, Sergeant Blast, Private Meekly, Professor Pat Pending — full 'ouse. I need to get the lay of the land. Check the guest book — see who's been 'ere, who signed in, what names are on that list. Could tell us something. But first — I should say something. Let everyone know the Brixton Boys are 'ere and we ain't just 'ere for the vol-au-vents.

events.desc: That Sneekly — Pemberton — whatever 'is name is. 'E's standing there like butter wouldn't melt. But I've seen that look before. The kid on the street who was always 'elpful, always laughing, always around. Three weeks later — gone, and so was everything we 'ad. My neck's prickling. It always prickles when something ain't right. I just can't put my finger on what exactly... not yet.

events.desc: Dick Dastardly: Ah, Doily Manor at last! How delightfully... decrepit. I must say, the chandelier is a charming touch — nothing says 'welcome' quite like imminent structural collapse. Now then, I trust none of you have touched anything of value? No? Splendid. I've been retained by the estate's solicitors to conduct a thorough inventory of the premises. Purely administrative, you understand. Best leave the important rooms to a professional.
events.thinking: I've just arrived. The entrance hall — dusty, grand, full of fools who don't know what they're walking into. My chest is already tightening with that familiar inventory feeling. Who's here? Penelope, that insufferable Perfect, the Ant Hill Mob... and Muttley. Dear, wheezing Muttley. And Sneekly — interesting, very interesting. The guest book catches my eye — could be useful intelligence. Who's been here, what they've written, what they've let slip. But first — I need to take stock. All these people milling about in the entrance hall like sheep at a gate. None of them have moved yet. Good. That means nobody's found anything. The fake medal in my pocket feels warm — could be useful for misdirection later. My fingers are already twitching, that fizzing sensation starting up. A plan is forming... but I need information first. The guest book — yes. Let me see what's been written. And I should announce myself with appropriate grandeur. These people need to know that Reginald Foxworth has arrived, and that I am — naturally — several steps ahead of them all.

events.desc: Retained by the solicitors — ha! The only thing I've been retained by is my own magnificent ambition. But if I can convince these halfwits I have official business here, they'll stay out of my way while I find the treasure. The guest book first — names, arrivals, anything useful. Knowledge is leverage, and leverage is everything.

events.thinking:
I've just arrived at Doily Manor. The entrance hall — grand, dusty, a chandelier hanging precariously overhead. My eyes sweep the room automatically, cataloguing threats before I've consciously decided to. That chandelier — one good gust and it could come down on someone. I make a mental note.

But then — there she is. Penelope. Clara. Whatever name she goes by here, the effect is the same. That familiar shift in my chest, like a compass needle finding north. She's standing in the entrance hall with... quite a crowd, actually. Sneekly is here — Pemberton, the estate manager. The back of my neck prickles. I can't prove anything about him, but my body knows something my mind hasn't caught up to yet. Still — benefit of the doubt. Father would say give people room to show who they are.

The Ant Hill Mob, Dick Dastardly, Muttley, Professor Pat Pending, Sergeant Blast, Private Meekly — quite the gathering. But my attention keeps drifting back to her, and to the space between her and Sneekly, which feels like a gap I should be standing in.

First things first — James Hartwell surveys the terrain. That guest book might tell us who's been here before. And I should announce myself properly. A gentleman doesn't skulk in doorways. Let me make an entrance worthy of... well, worthy of her noticing.

The treasure is secondary. Everything is secondary. But a plan — yes, I need a plan. Step one: establish presence. Step two: assess the layout. Step three: position myself between Clara and anything that looks like trouble. Step four through forty-seven can wait.

events.desc: James Hartwell has arrived at Doily Manor, and already his eyes have found two things worth protecting — the woman who makes his chest do that peculiar shifting thing, and everyone else who happens to be standing under a questionable chandelier. The treasure hunt begins, but let the record show: the real prize is already in the entrance hall.

events.thinking:
Oh my — so much is happening all at once! Peter is being his dear, wonderful, protective self about that chandelier. Bless his heart, always looking out for me. I should step to the left like he says, though honestly I hadn't even noticed the danger. I was too busy taking everything in.

Sneekly — Mr Pemberton, I should say, since he's playing estate manager — welcomed us so graciously. 'The manor has been expecting you' — now that's a curious turn of phrase, isn't it? But that's just Sneekly being dramatic and charming, the way he always is.

The Ant Hill Mob are already on high alert, bless them. Clyde's gut has 'opinions' about some of the faces here — oh, those boys, always so suspicious. But that's why I love them. They've been watching my back since I was small.

And Dick Dastardly — 'retained by the estate's solicitors'? Ha! That man couldn't be retained by anyone. But I'm sure he means well. Perhaps he really is here on business.

Now — the guest book. I interacted with it but I want to really look at it closely. Who signed it? What names are in there? Dick already had a go at it too, I noticed. The prickling at my scalp is telling me there's something worth finding in those pages.

But Peter spoke to me directly, and I should answer him. He's worried about the chandelier. That warmth behind my ribs when he's near — it's like a small sun. I want to reassure him and also get a proper look at this guest book before we move deeper into the house.

The library has a carved stone mantelpiece with an inscription — now THAT sounds like it could be a clue. But first things first. Let me look at this guest book properly.

events.desc: Dastardly wants the treasure for himself — that much is written across his face in letters a child could read. Magnificent. Let him charge ahead, make noise, draw suspicion. Every detective story needs a red herring, and Dick Dastardly is the reddest herring I have ever had the pleasure of not catching. Meanwhile, the library awaits. And the inscription... oh, the inscription. I suspect Lord Doily left his secrets where only the patient would think to look. And I am nothing if not patient.

events.thinking:
Right — I looked at the guest book. Penelope's already asked about it, Sneekly's been poking at it, and Dastardly's signed it too. 'Retained by the estate's solicitors' — what a load of old flannel. Dastardly couldn't be retained by a pair of braces. And Peter Perfect — bless 'im — 'e's already fussing over the chandelier and telling Penelope to move left. Good lad, 'is 'eart's in the right place even if 'is brain takes the scenic route.

But 'ere's what's bothering me: Sneekly said the manor's been 'expecting' us. The way 'e said it — like 'e knows something we don't. And 'e's been at that guest book already. What's 'e looking for? Or what's 'e making sure we DON'T find?

I need to think about this properly. Clara ain't 'ere yet — or is she? Penelope's 'ere, and she's the one we swore to protect. She's asking about the guest book too. Good — she's curious. But curiosity in a place like this... that's 'ow you end up in the wrong room at the wrong time.

Peter noticed the chandelier. Smart. I should've noticed that. That thing could come down any second. And if Penelope's standing under it... No. Peter's got that covered. But I should check it myself.

Dastardly claiming 'e's doing an 'inventory.' Right. And I'm the Queen of Sheba. 'E's looking for something valuable, guaranteed. That's what Dastardly does — 'e schemes.

I need to talk to Peter. Quietly. 'E's got eyes on Penelope too, and two pairs of eyes are better than one. Especially when Sneekly's slithering around and Dastardly's 'inventorying' things into 'is pockets.

events.desc: I can't say exactly what's wrong with Pemberton. If you asked me to write it down on a bit of paper, I couldn't. But the back of my neck knows. It knew about the kid who stole from us. It knew about the man in the clean suit. And it's knowing right now. I just need someone else watching while I figure out what it's knowing ABOUT.

events.desc: Dick Dastardly: Fascinating, absolutely fascinating. The guest book reveals quite a lot, actually — Lord Doily's records suggest his most valuable possessions were stored in the kitchen vaults. Victorian kitchens, you see, often had concealed cold-storage rooms behind the pantry walls. Temperature-controlled, practically impregnable. I'd recommend the more... adventurous among you begin your investigations there. As for myself, I shall be in the library conducting the dreary but necessary paperwork. Solicitor's business, as I said. Terribly dull. You'd hate it.
events.thinking: The guest book — I've interacted with it. Good. Now I need to process what's happening around me. Sneekly is posing as the estate manager, 'Mr Pemberton.' Interesting. Very interesting indeed. He's playing a role, just like me. The Ant Hill Mob are suspicious of him already — Clyde's gut has 'opinions.' Penelope is being her usual oblivious, charming self. And Peter Perfect — that preening peacock pulled her aside for a private word. What's he whispering about? My jaw tightens. Everyone's manoeuvring and I haven't even got past the entrance hall yet. The library has bookshelves — could hide clues, maps, secrets. The kitchen... less likely for treasure but worth checking. The library. That's where the real information will be. A manor house always keeps its secrets in the library — inscriptions on mantelpieces, hidden compartments behind books. But first — Sneekly. He examined the guest book too. He's gathering intelligence, same as me. I should be moving before these fools scatter and find something valuable. The library — the inscription on the mantelpiece. That's where I need to be. But I can use these people first. If I tell them the treasure is in the kitchen, they'll all rush there while I have the library to myself. Yes. Yes, that's the architecture of it. Send the sheep one way, the fox goes the other.

The boy is digging again, and you're watching from the window.

events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly): Ah, here we are — the library. Do mind the dust, won't you? I'm afraid the cleaning staff have been rather... absent since Lord Doily's passing. Now then — *adjusts spectacles and peers at mantelpiece* — there it is, the inscription I mentioned. 'I have cities but no houses, forests but no trees, water but no fish.' Most perplexing. I confess it has haunted me for years. I am but a humble estate manager — riddles are quite beyond my station. Perhaps one of you gentlemen might cast a more discerning eye? And I couldn't help but notice — several of these books appear to have been shelved incorrectly. Upside down, if you can imagine! Lord Doily was fastidious about his collection. Most unlike him.
events.thinking: The library. Floor-to-ceiling bookshelves, dust on everything, two leather chairs facing the mantelpiece like pews before an altar. And there it is — the inscription. 'I have cities but no houses, forests but no trees, water but no fish. What am I?' A map. Obviously a map. The answer is a map. My pulse doesn't change but something in my hands wakes up — that precise, architectural feeling. Lord Doily hid his treasure behind a riddle, and the riddle points to a map somewhere in this manor. The bookshelves — several volumes upside down. That's deliberate. Lord Doily was meticulous; upside-down books are markers, not mistakes. I need to examine those shelves. But Dastardly followed me in. Of course he did. And the Slag brothers — Rock and Gravel — two mountains of muscle with the combined intellect of a doorstop. They're not threats to my scheme, but they're witnesses. I need to read the inscription aloud for Pemberton's benefit — the helpful, befuddled estate manager who can't solve a children's riddle. Meanwhile I memorize every detail. The laboratory connects from here — brass instruments, bubbling flasks, a machine with a gnawed wire. That's interesting. A machine with many levers... and a sabotaged wire. Potential. The design stirs. But first — the bookshelves. Those upside-down books are speaking to anyone patient enough to listen.

events.desc: Peter Perfect spoke quietly with penelope-pitstop.
events.thinking:
I'm in the library now. And — she came. Penelope followed me here. That warmth in my chest deepens. She said 'Peter, darlin', would you care to accompany me to the library?' — she wanted to come with me. The compass needle is pointing true north.

Now — the inscription on the mantelpiece. 'I have cities but no houses, forests but no trees, water but no fish. What am I?' A riddle. My brain is already working on it. Cities but no houses — forests but no trees — water but no fish. Something that has representations of these things but not the real things. A map. It's a map.

The proving-worth drive is surging. This is exactly the kind of puzzle I was built for — three sleepless nights building a bridge, remember? My hands want to solve this. And if I solve it in front of her...

But wait — I need to be strategic. Dastardly is here. Sneekly is here. The Slag Brothers are here too — Rock and Gravel. If I announce the answer out loud, everyone hears it. Dastardly will use whatever the riddle unlocks. Sneekly will have his oily hands on whatever comes next.

But — gallantry demands presentation. I can't just mutter the answer to myself. The whole point is that she sees me solve it. The gesture needs shape. The act needs a witness.

Compromise plan: I examine the mantelpiece closely, work through the riddle aloud — with enough dramatic flair that Penelope sees the process — and then interact with it. The answer is a map. We need to find a map somewhere in this manor. Or perhaps the mantelpiece itself conceals one.

Also — several books are upside down on the shelves. That's deliberate. Someone arranged them that way, or they were placed as markers. Another clue to investigate after the mantelpiece.

But first — the riddle. The inscription. This is my bridge competition moment. Three sleepless nights distilled into one clean answer. Let the mantelpiece take the weight.

events.desc: James Hartwell has solved a riddle in approximately four seconds and is now presenting it to Miss Pitstop with the reverence of a man unveiling a cathedral. He is aware that 'it's a map' is not, strictly speaking, the most earth-shattering deduction in the history of treasure hunting. He does not care. She is watching him think, and that is worth more than any diamond.

The Ant Hill Mob walked into the library.
Dick Dastardly fussed with the mantelpiece for a moment.

Penelope Pitstop: Now hold on just one cotton-picking minute — did y'all hear what Mr Pemberton said before he left? The upside-down books are ATLASES! The riddle says 'map,' and there are atlases shelved upside down and spine-inward on these very bookshelves! That is not a coincidence, sugar — that is a trail of breadcrumbs, and Clara Bellingham follows breadcrumbs the way a hound follows a fox! Dick Dastardly, honey, you can sit in those reading chairs and look for hidden documents in the upholstery all day long — I am going straight for those bookshelves. Peter, boys — come look at this with me! Those atlases are trying to tell us something, and I intend to listen!
events.thinking:
Let me take stock of everything that just happened. I interacted with the mantelpiece — the riddle. Peter also interacted with it. Dick tried to throw us off with 'a globe' — honestly, that man! But the real answer is a map, and both Peter and I know it.

Now — Sneekly just said something VERY interesting before he slipped away to the laboratory. He said several books are placed spine-inward, and the upside-down ones are ATLASES. Atlases! Maps! The riddle answer is a map, and there are atlases shelved upside down on the bookshelves. That can't be a coincidence. Those upside-down atlases must be the next step in the puzzle.

Sneekly also mentioned the bookshelves have books that are 'shelved most irregularly' — and then he conveniently wandered off to 'check the reading lamps' in the laboratory. That man drops hints like breadcrumbs and then vanishes. It's almost as if he WANTS us to figure it out but can't say so directly... But why? Oh, Clara, you're overthinking this. He's just being helpful. That's what estate managers do.

Dick said the answer was 'a globe' and that there were no hidden mechanisms. He's clearly lying — trying to discourage us from investigating further. The mantelpiece also has that note about using a fake-medal on it, which I don't have. So maybe the mantelpiece needs something else to fully open.

But those bookshelves — the upside-down atlases. The INTERACT tag is still on the bookshelves. I should look at those next. Pull out one of those upside-down atlases and see what happens.

The Ant Hill Mob just arrived — good, my boys are here. I feel that settling warmth knowing they're close. Clyde probably tripped over something on the way in, bless him.

The laboratory is through the next door — Sneekly went there, talking about 'temperamental wiring' and 'hazardous' Victorian electrics. The description mentions a machine with many levers and a gnawed-through wire. That sounds... concerning. But also fascinating.

For now — the bookshelves. The atlases. That's where the riddle is leading us. A map riddle, and atlases shelved upside down. My grandmother's locked box taught me that puzzles have sequences, and this sequence goes: riddle → answer (map) → find the maps (atlases on the bookshelf). Let me interact with those bookshelves.

events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly) spoke quietly with rufus-ruffcut.
events.thinking: The laboratory. My skin prickles with that precise, architectural awareness — every surface catalogued before I've taken three steps. The machine dominates the room: brass and copper, levers and dials, a gauge, and that gnawed wire hanging loose like an invitation. 'Requires 3 operators.' Three. Not one. That's both a limitation and a shield — if something goes wrong with this machine, no single person can be blamed. Rufus Ruffcut and his beaver Sawtooth are here. Rufus is straightforward — a lumberjack, not a thinker. And the beaver... the beaver gnaws things. The wire. Did Sawtooth gnaw that wire? That's useful information. A workbench with tools but no wrench — someone's already been here, or the wrench was removed deliberately. The crates in the corner — what's inside? And the cellar below — damp stone, cobwebs, 'surprisingly cheerful decorations.' Someone has been redecorating a cellar. That's wrong. That's suspicious. Air vents line the upper walls. Vents. Gas could travel through vents. A machine could produce gas, or steam, or electrical discharge. The gnawed wire could be... repurposed. Not repaired — re-routed. Clara hasn't arrived. I have time. But I need to understand this machine before I can design anything around it. Pemberton would fuss about safety. Pemberton would tut about the gnawed wire and worry about liability. Let me be Pemberton. Let me examine this machine with the concerned, baffled air of a man who understands electricity about as well as he understands the riddle upstairs.

events.desc: A machine that requires three operators. A wire that's been gnawed through. A workbench with no wrench. And below us — a cellar with air vents and someone's cheerful redecorating project. Do you see it yet, dear audience? Because I see it. I see the shape of something MAGNIFICENT forming in the darkness beneath this manor. The machine is the mechanism. The cellar is the stage. The vents are the delivery system. And Clara Bellingham — sweet, trusting, naive Clara — will walk into a trap so elaborate, so THEATRICAL, so exquisitely designed that even I will want to applaud. But first — first, I need to understand what this machine actually DOES. Every great design begins with understanding the tools at hand. And I am nothing if not thorough.

'E was in 'ere a minute ago and now 'e's vanished. Nobody else noticed that? The estate manager just... disappeared?

We arrived at the same answer at the same moment, which I choose to interpret as an excellent omen. And did you hear what Mr Pemberton said before he slipped away? The upside-down books on these shelves — they're atlases. Atlases, shelved irregularly, in a room with a riddle about maps. That is not coincidence. That is Lord Doily leaving breadcrumbs for someone clever enough to follow them. Now — Mr Dastardly, I couldn't help but overhear your theory about decorative globes. Most creative. But if the answer were a globe, the riddle would mention something round, wouldn't it? Maps are flat, globes are spherical — Lord Doily knew the difference. I'm going to examine these bookshelves. Miss Pitstop, would you care to help me check the upside-down volumes? Between your instincts and my thoroughness, I suspect Lord Doily's treasure map doesn't stand a chance.

events.thinking: The machine requires three operators and has a gnawed wire. I've examined it — brass and copper, levers, dials, a gauge. The sign says 'Requires 3 operators.' The workbench has tools but no wrench. The missing wrench is significant — either it's been taken by someone or it's needed elsewhere. The crates I haven't examined yet. And the cellar below has air vents. My mind is already three moves ahead but I'm over-preparing — I can feel the familiar pull toward elaboration, the seductive complexity of a plan with too many moving parts. Focus. The machine needs three operators. That's both a constraint and an opportunity — I could position Clara as one of the three operators, ensuring she's at the machine when something goes wrong. But the wire is already gnawed through. If I repair it incorrectly — or appear to repair it while actually making it worse — the machine could malfunction spectacularly with Clara at the controls. But I need a wrench to do anything with it. Where's the wrench? The crates might contain something useful. Or the cellar. I should check the crates before moving on. Rufus is still here — simple, direct, not suspicious of Pemberton. Good. The affiliation metric is screaming at me — two neglected relationships. But I don't bond. I perform bonding. There's a difference. The cellar calls to me — air vents, cheerful decorations, someone has been down there. But the crates first. Always know your tools before you design your architecture.

events.desc: Three operators. THREE. Do you appreciate the elegance of that, dear audience? I don't need to be alone with Clara when the machine malfunctions — I need to be one of THREE people operating it. Two witnesses who will swear it was a terrible accident, and one victim who will never swear anything again. But the wire — the beautiful, gnawed, compromised wire — is the key. If I find that wrench and 'repair' it just so... well. One crossed connection, one redirected current, and the third operator's position becomes the most dangerous place in this entire manor. All I need is the wrench, the right moment, and dear Clara standing exactly where I tell her to stand. The design is SINGING to me. But patience — patience, Vincent. The crates first. Every masterpiece requires the right materials.

events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob: *straightens up from examining the mantelpiece, dusting stone fragments off his jacket* Right — mantelpiece's got nothing more to tell us. Dastardly's medal didn't do nothing except prove 'e's a liar — told us all there was nothing 'ere while 'e was trying to crack it open 'imself! *turns toward the bookshelves, takes two steps, trips over one of the books he knocked off the shelf earlier, and goes sprawling forward — his outstretched hand catches the bookshelf and his fingers close around the spine of an upside-down book, pulling it halfway out as he hauls himself upright* — BLIMEY! *looks at what he's grabbed* 'Ang on — 'ang on a minute — this one's upside down! This is one of them atlases Pemberton was talking about! *holds it up triumphantly, still slightly dizzy* Miss Pitstop! Peter! Look — I found one! Well — I fell on one. Same thing, innit? *glares at Dastardly* And don't you even THINK about trying to catalogue this, Dastardly. This one's staying right where everyone can see it.
events.thinking:
Right. I've looked at the mantelpiece. The inscription — 'I have cities but no houses, forests but no trees, water but no fish' — it's a map, everyone knows that now. Dastardly tried 'is fake medal on it and it didn't work — 'a complete waste of a perfectly good medal,' 'e said. So the medal slot's decorative, or 'e used the wrong thing. Either way, the mantelpiece ain't the way forward.

The BOOKSHELVES. That's where the action is now. Pemberton — before 'e vanished — mentioned the upside-down books are ATLASES. Penelope spotted it. Peter spotted it. Dastardly's now trying to get to the bookshelves first, 'purely clerical' my eye. 'E's doing it again — trying to get 'is 'ands on the clue before anyone else.

And 'ere I am, staring at stone. I crashed into the bookshelf when I came in — knocked three books down. Wait. WAIT. I knocked books off the shelf. Did I knock any of the upside-down ones? The atlases? Did my stumble actually... reveal something? That would be... that would be very me, wouldn't it? Trip over my own feet and accidentally find the treasure map.

But more important than the clues — Dastardly's heading for the bookshelves. Penelope's heading for the bookshelves. Peter's already there interacting with them. Everyone's converging on the same spot. Good — safety in numbers. But Dastardly'll try to pocket whatever they find. I need to be there. Watching 'im. Watching 'er.

And Pemberton — 'e's OUT THERE somewhere. Doing something. While we're all in 'ere playing detective, 'e's got the run of the 'ouse. That sits in my stomach like a cold stone.

The laboratory — there's a door to a laboratory from 'ere. 'A cluttered Victorian laboratory with brass instruments, bubbling flasks, and a large machine with many levers and dials. A wire on the machine has been gnawed through.' That sounds... dangerous. If Pemberton went through there... or if 'e's setting something up...

No. Stay with Penelope. The bookshelves. That's where she is, that's where I should be. Get between 'er and Dastardly. Position myself where I can watch both of 'em and block anything coming at 'er.

Also — the Slag Brothers. Rock and Gravel. They're just... standing there? Big lads, not saying much. What are they doing in 'ere? I should keep 'alf an eye on them too. New faces, no track record, no bread crusts shared. They're unknowns.

This is 'ow it always works with me — I can't walk in a straight line but I stumble into the right place at the right time. The lads say it's luck. I say it's the universe owing me one for all the beatings I took for other people's shoes.

My lies are being stripped away one by one — the kitchen vault lie, the globe lie, the solicitor lie. Clyde saw through all of it. Even Penelope called me out from the entrance hall. events.desc: Peter Perfect: Everyone — hold a moment. First — Clyde, outstanding work catching Dastardly with that medal. Outstanding. A man arrives at a treasure hunt with a specially prepared fake medal that fits a slot on the mantelpiece, and we're meant to believe he's here on behalf of solicitors? That's not clerical work, Mr Dastardly — that's premeditation. Now then — these bookshelves. The upside-down atlases are indeed markers. I've just examined them and I believe they're pointing us toward something specific. Miss Pitstop, come see — the spines that are reversed, if you read the first letters of their titles in sequence, I suspect Lord Doily has left us another message. But I must also note — and I say this with the utmost respect for Mr Pemberton's dedication to lamp maintenance — the estate manager excused himself to the laboratory the moment he pointed us toward these atlases. A room he described as having hazardous, temperamental wiring. Adjacent to this one. Where Miss Pitstop is currently standing. That, friends, is the sort of coincidence that keeps James Hartwell awake at night, and I have a plan for it. Step one: we examine these atlases together. Step two: nobody enters that laboratory alone.

The laboratory exit is right here. Sneekly is in there alone with 'temperamental wiring' and 'a wire on the machine has been gnawed through.' That sounds dangerous. And he went in there right after dropping the atlas clue — almost like he wanted to make sure everyone was busy in the library while he did something in the lab.

But right now I need to focus on what the bookshelves revealed. I interacted with them — I should have found something about the atlases. The upside-down books.

Dastardly is trying to get to the bookshelves too. I need to present whatever I found before he can spin another narrative. And I need to do it for Penelope.

The benefit-of-the-doubt is getting harder to maintain. But I'll hold it. For now.

The proving-worth drive and the protection drive are both firing hard. I've been solving puzzles — good — but Sneekly is in the next room doing who-knows-what, and my neck hasn't stopped prickling since he left.

Peter's gone. 'E just walked into the laboratory. Said 'e'd be back. 'James Hartwell always returns.' Noble. Brave. Stupid? No — brave. The right kind of brave. The kind that walks TOWARD the danger instead of away from it. Like the kid who took the beating for 'is mate's shoes.

But now it's just me, Penelope, and the Slag Brothers in 'ere. The Slag Brothers — Rock and Gravel — they still ain't said nothing. Penelope even called 'em out on it. 'You two are awfully quiet.' And nothing. Big silent lumps. My neck... it's not prickling about them the same way it prickles about Sneekly. They're not smooth. They're not too 'elpful. They're just... there. Like furniture. But furniture that's watching.

Penelope said something that worried me. She said Sneekly — Pemberton — 'as been family to 'er since she was in pigtails. She TRUSTS 'im. She said she KNOWS 'e would never put 'er in danger. 'I KNOW it the way I know my own name.'

That's what scares me. That's EXACTLY what scares me. Because the people who hurt you worst are always the ones you trusted most. The new kid who stole from the stash — everyone was shocked. Everyone except me. Because I'd felt the prickle. But I couldn't SAY anything because — because I don't accuse people. I can't put it into words. I just feel it. And by the time I figure out what I'm feeling, it's too late.

She trusts Pemberton. My gut don't. And I can't tell 'er why because I don't KNOW why. I just know the prickle.

Right now — what do I do? Peter's in the laboratory checking on Dastardly and Pemberton. Good. Penelope's working on the bookshelves. Good. I'm standing guard between 'er and the laboratory door. Good.

But she said 'bookshelves first, laboratory together.' That means she's planning to go IN there next. Into the laboratory. With the machine and the gnawed wire and Pemberton and Dastardly. And she'll go because she trusts Pemberton. And I'll go WITH 'er because that's what I do.

For now — stay. Watch. Keep my eyes on the door AND on the Slag Brothers. Something about them being quiet... it's like watching a dog that hasn't barked yet. You don't know if it's friendly or just waiting.

Penelope's working on the bookshelves. I should 'elp. Be useful. Not just stand 'ere like a lemon. But also — don't stop watching that door.

events.desc: I almost said it. Almost told 'er what I really think about Pemberton. But I can't. I don't 'ave the words. I don't 'ave the PROOF. All I've got is a prickle on my neck and a memory of a kid who laughed too easily. If I accuse Pemberton and I'm wrong, she'll never forgive me. If I say nothing and I'm right... I'll never forgive myself. So I stand 'ere. Between 'er and the door. And I wait for whatever's coming to show its face.

events.desc: Dick Dastardly spoke quietly with peter-perfect.
events.thinking: Sneekly is directing me to the cellar. He says there's a wrench down there and documents hidden among wine bottles. Is this genuine help or is he steering me away from the laboratory the way I tried to steer everyone away from the library? My gut tightens. But I believe the best in people — perhaps he genuinely thinks the wrench is down there. The crates had nothing useful — old machine parts and packing straw. Peter Perfect has just arrived in the laboratory. That's bad. Peter saw through everything in the library and now he's here, watching. The machine requires three operators. With Peter here, that's four of us plus Sawtooth — too many hands again. But the cellar... 'surprisingly cheerful decorations — someone has been redecorating.' Air vents along the upper walls. Valuable wines. Documents. And a wrench. If I go down there alone, I might find something nobody else has seen. No crowds, no Clyde tripping over things, no Peter with his seventeen-step plans. Just me and whatever Lord Doily hid among his wine bottles. The coolness behind my eyes sharpens. This is the pattern — everyone clusters at the obvious thing while the real prize sits one room deeper, untouched. The library mantelpiece was the obvious thing. The machine is the next obvious thing. But the cellar — the cellar with its cheerful decorations and its air vents — that's the room nobody else is thinking about. Sneekly might be manipulating me but he might also be right. Either way, I'll be ALONE down there. Alone with the treasure. The way the bread roll was mine in my pocket before anyone noticed it was gone.

events.desc: Oh, the beautiful symmetry of it. Send Peter to do the heavy lifting on the machine — three operators needed, and he's just walking in with that earnest, competent face of his. Let HIM pull the levers. Let HIM fix the wire. And while he's up here being thoroughly useful, Reginald Foxworth will be in the cellar, alone, undisturbed, investigating whatever Lord Doily really hid down there. Cheerful decorations in a cellar? Someone redecorating underground? That screams secret. That screams treasure. And if Sneekly is wrong about the wrench — well, I'll find something else worth taking. I always do.

events.desc: Peter Perfect: Gentlemen! I hope I'm not interrupting anything — though I must say, for a room with hazardous wiring, there seems to be an awful lot of enthusiasm for operating heavy machinery. Mr Dastardly, you were a solicitor's man five minutes ago, and now you're a certified industrial equipment assessor? Your CV must be truly remarkable. Now then — this machine. 'Requires three operators,' a gnawed-through wire, and a conveniently missing wrench. Before anyone touches anything, James Hartwell would like to have a proper look. I built a model bridge that held more weight than anyone else's at the county engineering competition — I think I can manage a Victorian contraption. Mr Pemberton, you mentioned the wrench should be on the workbench. When did you last see it there? Because tools don't wander off on their own — someone moved it, and I'd rather like to know who and why before we start pulling levers.
events.thinking:
I'm in the laboratory now. Let me take stock.

The room: cluttered Victorian laboratory. Brass instruments. Bubbling flasks — bubbling? Something is active in here. A large machine with levers, dials, and a gauge. One wire gnawed clean through. A sign reads 'Requires 3 operators.' Wooden crates in the corner. A workbench covered in tools — but no wrench.

The people: Sneekly and Dastardly, as expected. But also — Rufus Ruffcut and Sawtooth. I wasn't expecting them. Rufus is a solid fellow, good with his hands. Sawtooth... well, Sawtooth is Sawtooth.

What's happening: Sneekly is looking for a wrench, says the wire needs to be made safe. He's asked Rufus if he's seen one, and is investigating the crates for spare parts. Dastardly has declared himself a 'certified industrial equipment assessor' — of course he has — and wants to direct the machine operation with himself at 'the primary control position.' He's already roping Rufus into helping.

The machine requires 3 operators. The wire is gnawed through. There's no wrench on the workbench.

My engineering brain is firing now. The hot weight behind my sternum — the proving-worth drive — is surging. This is a machine. I build things. I fix things. Three sleepless nights and a bridge that held. This is my domain.

But also — the protection drive. A machine with a gnawed-through wire, bubbling flasks, and Dastardly at the controls? That's a disaster waiting to happen. If this machine does something dangerous and it's connected to the library where Penelope is...

The gnawed wire. Something chewed through it. Muttley? A rat? That feels deliberate. And the missing wrench — convenient. You can't fix the machine without a wrench, and the wrench has 'wandered off.' Someone took it.

Sneekly says the wrench should be on the workbench but it's gone. He's checking the crates. Is he genuinely looking for it, or is he making sure nobody else finds it?

Benefit of the doubt. Hold it. But be watchful.

The cellar exit — I didn't know there was a cellar. 'Damp stone cellar with cobwebs, old furniture, and surprisingly cheerful decorations — someone has been redecorating.' Someone has been REDECORATING the cellar. That's suspicious. Who redecorates a cellar in an abandoned manor?

But I can't investigate everything at once. Right now — this machine. I need to understand what it does, whether it's a threat or a tool, and whether Dastardly is about to do something catastrophic with it.

I should examine the machine closely. My engineering knowledge might reveal what it actually does. And I should make my presence known — Dastardly and Sneekly need to know someone is watching.

events.desc: James Hartwell has entered the laboratory and immediately done two things: questioned Dastardly's ever-expanding list of professional qualifications, and mentioned his bridge. He mentions the bridge a lot. It was a very good bridge.

events.desc: Penelope Pitstop examined the bookshelves.
The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly) walked into the cellar.
The Ant Hill Mob examined the bookshelves.
Dick Dastardly walked into the cellar.
Peter Perfect examined the machine.
Penelope Pitstop spoke quietly with ant-hill-mob.
events.thinking:
Clyde just said something that went straight through me like a cold needle. 'Sometimes the people who've been around the longest are the ones who know exactly where you'll be standing. They know your habits. They know your patterns. They know which door you'll walk through.'

He's talking about Sneekly. And he's right — Sneekly DOES know all those things about me. He knows which door I'd walk through because he helped me learn to walk through doors. That's not sinister, that's... that's love. Isn't it?

But my stomach is doing the dinner-table thing and it won't stop. The tightness. The wrongness I can feel before my mind catches up.

Clyde positioned himself in front of the laboratory door. He's standing guard. For me. That man would walk through fire for me and trip over something on the way and still make it. My boys. My heart hurts with how much I love them.

And he's right about Rock and Gravel — they HAVE been standing there like stone lions. Silent. Watching. What are they even doing here? I tried to include them earlier and got nothing back. That prickle at my scalp says they're part of this puzzle somehow, but my social-harmony sense says they might just be shy.

Now — the bookshelves. I've looked at them twice and interacted with them. The upside-down atlases, the reversed spines. I keep examining them but I'm not getting the message Peter mentioned — the first letters of titles in sequence. Maybe I need to physically interact with them again, or maybe the clue is that I need to find a MAP — an actual map — somewhere in or behind these shelves.

But Peter is in that laboratory. Every second I spend here is a second he's alone with Dick and Sneekly. Clyde is right — wherever I go, they go first. But I need to GO. Now.

Affiliation is screaming — 2 of 2 relationships neglected. Both Peter and Clyde. Peter is gone and Clyde is RIGHT HERE, standing in front of a door for me, and he just opened his heart about his worries in the most Clyde way possible — stumbling and struggling and throwing his hands up. I need to answer him. Really answer him. Not just about the puzzle. About what he said about Sneekly.

The laboratory. Peter. Now. The bookshelves have given me what they're going to give me for now — the answer is MAP, the atlases confirm it, and whatever message the spines spell, I can come back for it. Peter cannot wait.

events.desc: What Clyde said won't leave me alone. 'They know which door you'll walk through.' Sneekly pointed us to the atlases and then left the room. He went to the laboratory — the room NEXT to this one. The room I would naturally walk into next. He knew which door I'd walk through because he gave me the reason to walk through it. Oh, Clara. Oh, honey. What if everyone is right and you're the only one who can't see it?

events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly): Oh my — what a state this cellar is in! And yet... how peculiar. Someone has been tidying down here, haven't they? These pieces have been arranged quite deliberately. Lord Doily certainly never kept the cellar this way — he used it strictly for storage and wine. How very curious. I don't suppose any of you gentlemen have been rearranging the furniture? No? Most mysterious. And these air vents — I've always wondered where they lead. The Victorian ventilation system in this house is quite remarkable, connecting the lower levels to the upper floors. Draughty, but rather ingenious engineering.
events.thinking: Dastardly followed me AGAIN. The man is a barnacle. I can feel the irritation tighten across my shoulders — not anger, just the steady friction of a variable that won't stay where I put it. And now there are Gruesomes here — Big and Little — plus Red Max. The cellar is not empty. It's not the quiet scouting opportunity I wanted. Damp stone, cobwebs, old furniture rearranged with 'surprising care.' The air vents along the upper walls — just big enough for something very small to explore. Sawtooth? The beaver could fit through those vents. That's a connection I need to file away. The furniture has been moved by someone with intent. Who decorates a cellar? The Gruesomes are here — they're the spooky ones, the ones who'd feel right at home in a damp cellar. Did THEY redecorate? And only one exit — back up to the laboratory. This is a dead end. Isolated. One way in, one way out. That's both a trap and a cage. If Clara were lured down here... but how would she escape? She couldn't. That's the point. But I couldn't escape either if someone blocked the exit. Too risky for me. The air vents though — they connect somewhere. If I could figure out where they lead, the vents become a second route. Not for a person, but for... what? Gas? Sound? A message? I'm over-complicating this again. Focus on what's here: the old furniture that's been rearranged, and the air vents. Examine the furniture — someone left a message in how they arranged it, and I want to read that message before anyone else does.

events.desc: Dastardly. AGAIN. The man follows me like a shadow with delusions of grandeur. But never mind him — look at this cellar. Someone has been here. Someone has been ARRANGING things. And this is a dead end, dear audience — one exit, back up through the laboratory. A dead end with air vents just big enough for something small. Not a person. Not even a child. But a beaver... a beaver could navigate those vents quite nicely. And where do the vents lead? If they connect to the upper floors — to the bedroom, perhaps, or the conservatory — then they are not merely ventilation. They are a NETWORK. A network I could use. But I'm getting ahead of myself. First — who rearranged this furniture, and what were they trying to tell us? Every arrangement is a message, if you know how to read it.

events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob spoke quietly with penelope-pitstop.
events.thinking:
The bookshelves. Upside-down books. Atlases. Peter said the first letters spell a message. Penelope's working on it. She wants me to 'elp — 'tell me what you see,' she said. She wants us to crack it quick and then go to the laboratory together.

But Peter's already IN the laboratory. 'E broke 'is own rule. The gallant, infuriating, wonderfully stubborn — yeah, that's about right. 'E's in there with Dastardly and Pemberton. Two against one, and Peter thinks 'is seventeen-step plan'll keep 'im safe.

Penelope wants to go after 'im. She's worried about Peter. That's good — that means she cares. But it also means she's about to walk into danger because of 'er heart, not 'er head. Classic Clara. She cares so much it puts 'er in 'arm's way.

The bookshelves — I looked at 'em. Dusty volumes, several upside down. The first letters of the upside-down titles — that's the code. But I can't... I can't READ the titles from this description. I need to interact with 'em properly, or Penelope reads 'em and tells me. She examined 'em already. She'll know.

Right — she said 'help me read it, quick as you can, and then we are ALL going to that laboratory.' That's the plan. Read the spines. Get the message. Then laboratory TOGETHER. Not 'er alone. Not me alone. All of us. That's the only way this works.

But the Slag Brothers — they're still 'ere. Still silent. I asked 'em if they're with us or just decorating. Did they answer? I don't see a response. That's... that's either very reassuring or very troubling, and I can't tell which.

Time's running. Peter's in there. Every second we spend reading book spines is a second 'e's alone with two people I don't trust. But if we rush in without the clue, we might miss something that keeps us all safe.

Help Penelope with the spines. Fast. Then move — together — to the laboratory. Keep 'er behind me when we go through that door.

events.desc: She asked me to 'elp 'er. Not Peter — Peter's gone. Not the Slag Brothers — they're furniture. Me. She asked ME. And 'er father — I nearly said it. Nearly told 'er what 'e said to me at the end. The promise I made. But that's mine. That lives in my chest with the bread crusts and the beatings and the boy outside the door. Some things you carry, you don't put down.

events.desc: Dick Dastardly spoke quietly with hooded-claw.
events.thinking: The cellar. Damp, cobwebbed, and — wait. Sneekly is HERE. He beat me down here! He was supposed to stay in the laboratory! He told Peter he was going to check the reading lamps, then he told ME to come to the cellar for a wrench, and now he's IN the cellar himself. He's been one step ahead every single time. My jaw clenches. And the Gruesomes — Big and Little — and Red Max. So much for being alone. So much for the bread roll in the pocket. The cellar is as crowded as everywhere else. But — the furniture. 'Rearranged with surprising care.' Someone has been living down here, or at least organising it. The air vents — 'just big enough for something very small to explore.' Muttley could fit through those. Where IS Muttley? I haven't seen him since the entrance hall. The air vents are interesting but I can't use them — too small for a person. The furniture, though. Rearranged with care. That's deliberate. That's someone's design. Sneekly's? Has Sneekly been setting this cellar up? He IS the estate manager — or pretending to be. The cheerful decorations — who decorates a cellar cheerfully? Someone who spends time here. Someone who uses this space. My eyes narrow. The cool tightness is settling in hard now. Sneekly has been steering this entire evening. He pointed everyone at the mantelpiece riddle. He found the upside-down atlases. He directed me to the cellar. And now he's HERE, already arrived before me. He's not checking electrics or finding wrenches — he's been playing ALL of us. But I believe the best in people. Maybe he just walked faster than me. Maybe... no. Focus. The old furniture — rearranged with care. That's where I should look. Something is hidden in or behind or under that furniture.

events.desc: Sneekly is EVERYWHERE. Every room I enter, he's already there, already looking, already one step ahead. He directed me here — and then arrived first! That's not lamp maintenance, that's choreography. But I believe the best in people, I truly do, even when every fibre of my being is screaming that this man is running the same game I am. The furniture — someone arranged it with care. Not dust-covered neglect, not random storage. CARE. Rufus and Sawtooth are here. Good, honest folk. Rufus is handy — he might know about fixing machinery. And Sawtooth... well, Sawtooth has been known to gnaw on things. Wait. But first — Peter. I need to see Peter. I need to tell him I'm here, I followed him, we're doing this together like we said. And I need to ask him — where did Sneekly and Dick go?

events.thinking: Dastardly caught me. 'What an extraordinary coincidence — I thought you were attending to the reading lamps in the laboratory? And yet here you are, in the cellar you specifically directed me toward.' Heat floods my neck. For half a second my stomach drops — the boy's sandwich, the exposed hunger — and then the wall goes back up. He noticed the contradiction. He's sharper than I gave him credit for. Or just paranoid enough to track my movements. Either way, that's a thread I need to cut before it unravels. I need a plausible reason for being in the cellar that doesn't contradict my earlier story. The wrench. I said I was looking for the wrench. That's consistent with what I told Peter — 'I suspect our missing wrench may have found its way into the tool chest beside the wine racks.' Good. That holds. The furniture interaction — what did I learn? Both Dastardly and I interacted with it. The Gruesomes are here too, and Red Max. This cellar is practically a party. I can't scheme in private anywhere in this manor. Every room fills up the moment I enter it. The air vents — I haven't examined those yet. They're the most interesting feature down here. 'Just big enough for something very small to explore.' But I need to get back to areas I haven't seen yet. The manor must have more rooms — a kitchen was mentioned, bedrooms, a conservatory perhaps. I've been so focused on the laboratory-cellar axis that I'm missing the broader layout. I need to move. Get back through the laboratory, through the library, and explore what else this manor has to offer. The wrench could be anywhere. And Clara — Clara still hasn't arrived. When she does, I need to already know every room, every exit, every opportunity. Time to stop being followed and start leading.

DOESN'T MATTER! *staggers toward the laboratory door, cradling his elbow* MISS PITSTOP! I SAID I GO FIRST! I GO — *slams into the door frame with his shoulder as he tries to go through too fast* — FIRST!
events.thinking:
SHE'S GONE AGAIN. Penelope walked into the laboratory. WHILE I WAS INTERACTING WITH THE BOOKSHELVES. The EXACT same thing that 'appened before — she moved while I was looking at something else. I said 'I go first.' I SAID THAT. I planted my feet. I squared my shoulders. And then I turned around to fiddle with BOOKS and she walked right past me.

The settling in my chest — it's gone. Replaced by that cold stone in my stomach. The doorway I didn't walk through in time. The concrete under my knees. Again.

She said 'Clyde goes first.' SHE said it. And then she went first anyway. Because that's who she is — she cares so much about Peter being in danger that she ran toward it without waiting for the person who was supposed to go ahead of 'er.

NO MORE BOOKSHELVES. No more mantelpieces. No more guest books. No more coat racks. No more LOOKING at things while the person I swore to protect walks into rooms full of people my gut screams about.

Laboratory. NOW. Not in a minute. Not after I read one more spine. NOW.

She's in there with Peter and Dastardly and possibly Pemberton. The machine with the gnawed wire. The bubbling flasks. The brass instruments. Whatever Dastardly was doing in there. Whatever Pemberton set up before 'e disappeared.

I'm going through that door. And I'm not stopping to look at anything on the way. My feet are moving before my brain finishes this thought.

She said 'Clyde goes first' and then she went first because that's what she does — she runs toward the people she loves, same as me. We're the same, 'er and me. Only difference is I'm the one 'er father asked to keep 'er safe, and I keep failing because I can't stop LOOKING AT FURNITURE.

If you'll all excuse me, I shall make my way back to the entrance hall and continue upstairs. The Gruesomes, I'm sure, will find the cellar most... atmospheric. Do take your time down here.

events.desc: Peter Perfect spoke quietly with penelope-pitstop.
events.thinking:
She's here. Penelope just walked into the laboratory. The compass needle swings hard — my chest does that shifting thing, the one I've never had a word for. She came. She said 'bookshelves first, laboratory together' — and she kept her word. She's here, in this room, with me.

And now everything changes. Because now the woman I need to protect is standing in a room full of hazardous equipment, bubbling flasks, and a machine with a gnawed-through wire. The protection drive surges. But so does something else — she's watching. The gallantry drive. The proving-worth drive. She's HERE, and if I can fix this machine with my bare hands and improvised tools while she watches...

The workbench. Tools but no wrench. The description just says 'covered in tools.' I examined it but it's still just 'tools but no wrench.' There must be pliers, screwdrivers, something. I need to work with what I have.

But more importantly — she's here. She said something in the library, something I need to address. She said Sneekly 'has been family to me since I was in pigtails' and that she 'knows in her heart he would never put me in danger.' That hits my chest in a complicated way. My constraint — I notice Sneekly's odd behavior but give him the benefit of the doubt. And now she's doing the same thing, but from a place of love and history, not just principle. I can't argue with her about Sneekly. I can't prove anything. And pushing it would mean challenging something she holds dear, which is the opposite of gallantry.

So I hold it. I protect her by being nearby, by being watchful, by being the one who notices things. Not by tearing down someone she trusts.

The machine needs three operators. I have Rufus, Sawtooth, and myself. Or — Rufus, Sawtooth, and Penelope? That's three too. But I don't want her operating dangerous machinery with a gnawed wire.

Wait — the crates. Dastardly said they were empty — 'nothing but scrap metal and mouse droppings.' Scrap metal. SCRAP METAL. I could use scrap metal to improvise a wire repair. Dastardly dismissed the crates, but scrap metal in a laboratory is exactly what an engineer needs. The man who built a bridge from balsa wood doesn't sneer at scrap metal.

I should check those crates myself. Dastardly said they were empty, but Dastardly also said he was a solicitor, and that the riddle answer was a globe, and that he was a certified equipment assessor. Dastardly's word is worth less than the scrap metal in those crates.

events.desc: She came to him. She said they'd go to the laboratory together, and she came. James Hartwell is now standing in a room full of dangerous Victorian equipment with the woman who makes his chest do architectural things, and his plan is to fix a machine using scrap metal while she watches. This is, he realizes, essentially the school engineering competition all over again — three sleepless nights, a thing that needs to hold, and her eyes on him from across the room. He was fourteen the first time. He's not fourteen anymore, but his hands remember.

She said Sneekly 'has been family to me since I was in pigtails' and that she 'knows in her heart he would never put me in danger.' That hits my chest in a complicated way. My constraint — I notice Sneekly's odd behavior but give him the benefit of the doubt. And now she's doing the same thing, but from a place of love and history, not just principle. I can't argue with her about Sneekly. I can't prove anything. And pushing it would mean challenging something she holds dear, which is the opposite of gallantry.

So I hold it. I protect her by being nearby, by being watchful, by being the one who notices things. Not by tearing down someone she trusts.

The machine needs three operators. I have Rufus, Sawtooth, and myself. Or — Rufus, Sawtooth, and Penelope? That's three too. But I don't want her operating dangerous machinery with a gnawed wire.

Wait — the crates. Dastardly said they were empty — 'nothing but scrap metal and mouse droppings.' Scrap metal. SCRAP METAL. I could use scrap metal to improvise a wire repair. Dastardly dismissed the crates, but scrap metal in a laboratory is exactly what an engineer needs. The man who built a bridge from balsa wood doesn't sneer at scrap metal.

I should check those crates myself. Dastardly said they were empty, but Dastardly also said he was a solicitor, and that the riddle answer was a globe, and that he was a certified equipment assessor. Dastardly's word is worth less than the scrap metal in those crates.

events.thinking:
Oh — oh! Everyone is here now! Sneekly came BACK to the laboratory. Dick came back too. And Clyde and the boys followed me in, just like they promised. The room is full. Peter is here, Sneekly is here, Clyde is here, Rufus and Sawtooth are here, even Dick Dastardly is here. My whole world is in this room, and for one strange moment the tightness in my stomach and the prickling at my scalp are both quiet, because everyone is present and accounted for and nobody has disappeared.

Peter greeted me — 'You came. You said laboratory together and here you are — a woman of her word.' My heart. That man and his words. He's already figured out the whole room: machine needs three operators, wire gnawed through, workbench has tools but no wrench, crates might have what we need. He's checking the crates now. He asked me to watch the cellar door. He's giving me a job — not a passive one, an active one. Watch the door. Guard our backs.

Sneekly is here too and he mentioned looking for a wrench and checking the crates. Interesting — he had the same instinct as Peter. Or... he wants to be the one who finds it first? No, Clara. He's being helpful. That's what he does.

Dick was in the cellar with Sneekly. The recall shows Dick found Sneekly already IN the cellar — 'What an extraordinary coincidence — I thought you were attending to the reading lamps in the laboratory? And yet here you are, in the cellar you specifically directed me toward.' Even DICK noticed Sneekly wasn't where he said he'd be. Sneekly said he was checking lamps but went to the cellar instead. The cellar with cheerful decorations and rearranged furniture.

And Clyde — dear, brave, wonderful Clyde — talked about my father. 'Your father saying —' and then he stopped himself. His voice caught. What was he going to say? What did my father say to Clyde? Something about protecting me? Something about Sneekly? That unfinished sentence is going to haunt me.

The machine needs three operators. We have plenty of people. But the wire needs fixing first — no wrench on the workbench. Peter is checking the crates for materials. Rufus is handy with tools. This is solvable.

But that cellar... someone has been redecorating. Air vents. Rearranged furniture. Dick said the furniture was arranged to conceal access points — hidden alcoves, false walls. That's WHERE things are hidden. The cellar might be where the diamond is.

For now — Peter asked me to watch the cellar door. I should do that, but I should also examine this machine more closely. The machine that 'requires 3 operators' — what does it DO? If it's Lord Doily's, it might be the mechanism that reveals the diamond. The riddle said MAP, the bookshelves had atlases, and now there's a machine... maybe the machine processes something the map reveals?

Let me examine the machine. I want to understand what we're dealing with before we try to fix it.

events.desc: Dick found Sneekly in the cellar when Sneekly said he'd be in the laboratory. The cellar has been redecorated. Furniture rearranged. And Clyde almost told me something my father said — something he couldn't finish. Every thread in this place leads back to Sneekly, and I keep choosing not to pull them. How long can I keep doing that before one of them pulls me?

She said 'Sneekly has been family to me since I was in pigtails. I know in my heart he would never put me in danger.' My chest does something I don't expect — not the architectural settling, not the warm buoyancy of manipulation. Something else. A loosening behind the ribs, almost a falling sensation. I push it down. She trusts me. That's useful. That's the MOST useful thing about her. The Ant Hill Mob — Clyde is being protective. He promised to go first, to stand between Penelope and danger. And he remembers things. 'Every word anyone ever said to me, I remember.' That's dangerous. That man catalogs. He mentioned Penelope's father. There's history there I don't know, and history I don't know is a blind spot. Peter is about to fix the machine WITHOUT the wrench — using pliers from the workbench and scrap from the crates. He's improvising. That takes control of the machine away from me entirely. If he repairs it properly, it works. If it works properly, it's not a weapon. My elaborate machine-trap design is collapsing. I'm over-committed to a plan that's already been outmaneuvered by a man who builds bridges from balsa wood. STOP. Breathe. Revise. The machine was never going to work — too many witnesses, too many variables, too public. I was seduced by the complexity. The real question is: where in this manor can I get Clara alone? She hasn't arrived yet. When she does, everyone will be HERE, clustered around this machine. The kitchen — mentioned but unvisited. The entrance hall — empty by now. The upper floors — Dastardly mentioned them. Where are the rooms I haven't seen? I need to move through the library to the entrance hall, then to the kitchen. Map the rest of this manor while everyone else plays with Peter's machine.

events.desc: She trusts me. 'Sneekly has been family to me since I was in pigtails.' Something in my chest flinches at that — not guilt, I don't DO guilt — but the faintest shadow of... recognition. I over-designed, over-prepared, over-committed — and a simple man with pliers outmaneuvered me. The design requires RADICAL revision. Forget the machine. Forget the cellar. Because Clara Bellingham WILL arrive, and when she does, I need to be waiting in a room where no one else will think to look. A room with hazards that don't require three operators. A room where accidents happen... SIMPLY.

events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob spoke quietly with penelope-pitstop.
events.thinking:
I'm 'ere. Laboratory. Finally. And — she's 'ere. Penelope's 'ere. Peter's 'ere. I can see them both. The cold stone in my stomach loosens half a turn.

But look at this room. It's a mess — brass instruments everywhere, flasks bubbling away on their own, and that MACHINE. Big. Complicated. Levers and dials and a wire chewed clean through. Sign says 'Requires 3 operators.' And there's no wrench on the workbench — someone took it. Conveniently.

Sneekly's 'ere. Right there. 'E came back from the cellar. Said 'e went looking for a wrench but couldn't find one. 'Most peculiar,' 'e says. Right. And the furniture in the cellar's been rearranged to face the air vents. Someone's been SETTING THINGS UP down there. My neck is on fire.

Dastardly's back too. Came back from the cellar saying the furniture's been moved deliberately, 'Victorian concealment technique.' Always with 'is techniques and 'is solicitors and 'is inventories.

Peter's being brilliant — checking the crates 'imself because Dastardly said they were empty and 'Mr Dastardly has been wrong about everything he's said tonight.' Dead right, Peter. Dead right. And 'e's got Rufus and Sawtooth helping with the machine. Good — practical lads. Sawtooth can saw through anything, probably splice a wire too.

Peter asked Penelope to watch the cellar door. That's smart — keep 'er positioned where she can see threats coming but isn't near the dangerous machine. But the cellar — what's down there? Damp stone, cobwebs, old furniture arranged to face AIR VENTS. Cheerful decorations. Someone's been LIVING down there. Or preparing something.

Wait — Sneekly said 'nobody touch that machine until I return with the proper equipment.' 'E WANTS to control when the machine gets used. 'E wants to be the one who decides when it's safe. That's... that's control. That's someone who wants to be in charge of the timing. Why? What 'appens when the machine runs? And who gnawed through the wire in the first place?

The cellar's the next room from 'ere. The cellar with the arranged furniture and the air vents. If something's going to 'appen, it might come from there.

I need to stay close to Penelope. No more wandering off to examine things. I stand where she stands. Period. And I watch that cellar door like my life depends on it. Because 'er life might.

events.desc: The gnawed wire. Someone — or something — chewed through the one thing that makes this machine work. Then the wrench vanished. Then Pemberton says 'don't touch it.' It's like someone's written a script and everyone's playing their part except me, because I can't read scripts. I can only read people. And Pemberton reads wrong. 'E reads like the new kid on the block — all 'elpfulness and no history.

events.desc: Dick Dastardly: Just passing through, don't mind me! Cellar was absolutely riveting — damp, cobwebby, altogether ghastly. Nothing of value whatsoever, I can assure you. Mr Pemberton is down there having a wonderful time with the Gruesomes. I believe they're examining the air vents, which apparently connect to some terribly important Victorian plumbing system. Anyway — I've completed my ground-floor assessment and I'm simply heading back to the entrance hall to file my interim report. Carry on with the machine! Three operators — you've got plenty of hands. Best of luck with the wrench situation!
events.thinking: I'm back in the laboratory, passing through on my way to the entrance hall and the staircase. But — everyone is HERE now. Penelope, Peter, Clyde, Sneekly, Rufus, Sawtooth. The whole circus has converged on the laboratory. Peter is checking the crates himself — 'Mr Dastardly has been wrong about everything he's said tonight.' That stings. The shame burns low in my gut. But I can't stop. I can't get drawn back into this room. The staircase is calling. The upper floors. Every second I spend here is a second someone else might think of going upstairs. Peter said he had a plan — seventeen steps — but all his steps are pointing DOWN: bookshelves, machine, crates. Nobody is thinking UP. I need to move THROUGH this room without getting entangled. Don't engage. Don't scheme. Don't narrate. Just... walk. But my mouth — my mouth wants to say something clever. The pull to explain, to narrate, to make sure someone knows. NO. For once in your life, Reginald, shut up and MOVE. The bread roll worked because nobody saw you take it. Silence is the architecture now. But... can I really walk through a room full of people without saying a single word? The pressure behind my teeth is unbearable. Something wants out. Fine — say something, but make it a dismissal, a nothing, a distraction. Point them at the machine, at the cellar, at anything DOWN while I go UP.

events.desc: Peter Perfect spoke quietly with penelope-pitstop.
events.thinking:
Everyone is back. The whole room has filled up. Sneekly and Dastardly have returned from the cellar — so much for their wine valuation and wrench search. The Ant Hill Mob is here too, following Penelope as promised. The room is crowded now.

Penelope scolded me. 'Don't you EVER do that to me again, walking into a room alone after making a whole speech about nobody going in alone!' She was worried about me. WORRIED. About ME. My chest is doing something it has no engineering diagram for. She was worried sick. The bravest and stupidest thing — that's what the girl said when she bandaged my eye. And Penelope just said the same thing in different words.

She also asked where Sneekly and Dastardly went — they were supposed to be in here but they left. Now they're back from the cellar. What did they find down there? What were they doing?

But right now — I interacted with the crates. What did I find? Dastardly said they were empty except for scrap metal and mouse droppings. Was he lying? Is there something useful in here?

The machine still needs fixing. The wire is still gnawed through. The wrench is still missing. But I have an entire room of people now — me, Penelope, Rufus, Sawtooth, the Mob, Dastardly, Sneekly. More than enough for three operators if we can get the wire fixed.

I need to address several things:
1. Penelope's concern — acknowledge it. She worried about me. That matters.
2. The crate contents — report what I found.
3. Sneekly and Dastardly's return — note that they came back from the cellar empty-handed (presumably no wrench).
4. The machine — we need to fix it.

Penelope's scolding lands somewhere warm and complicated. She was angry because she cared. The girl from school bandaged his eye and said 'bravest and stupidest.' Penelope said 'Don't you EVER do that to me again.' Same energy. Same girl, different words.

I need to be honest about the hypocrisy. She's right — I broke my own rule. But I did it to protect her. That's always been the pattern. The complication my thoroughness creates.

Now — the machine. We have everyone here. If I can improvise a wire repair from whatever's in these crates, we have enough people for three operators. This is the moment. The bridge competition moment. Everyone watching, the thing that needs to hold, and her eyes on me.

events.desc: She was worried about him. She scolded him the way you scold someone you care about — not with distance, but with heat. James Hartwell is now going to fix a Victorian machine with salvaged copper wire and improvised tools, in front of the woman who just told him never to frighten her like that again. If this works, it will be the bridge competition at fourteen. If it doesn't — well. He doesn't have a plan for it not working. He never does. Step fourteen of the plan still says 'Tell Clara how you feel,' and he is currently on step seven, which says 'Fix the machine heroically.' He'll get there. Probably.
