The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly): Just passing through — the kitchen awaits! I do apologise for the bustle. So many rooms to check, so little time. Lord Doily would be turning in his grave if he knew the state of things. If any of you need me, I shall be in the kitchen checking the gas fittings and the pantry stores. Estate manager's work is never done, I'm afraid!
events.thinking: Dastardly is STILL following me. The man is a shadow I cannot shake. But something has shifted — I overheard the Ant Hill Mob's words echoing in my skull. 'Sometimes the people who've been around the longest are the ones who know exactly where you'll be standing.' Clyde said that about ME. About Pemberton. He doesn't have evidence — he has instinct. And instinct, in a man who remembers every word anyone has ever said to him, is more dangerous than evidence. Evidence can be planted or destroyed. Instinct just... sits there, watching. My shoulders are tight. The Slag brothers are here in the library — Rock and Gravel, two immovable objects. And Dastardly, right behind me. I need to get to the entrance hall and then the kitchen. I said I was making my rounds, checking the kitchen — that's my cover story and it's a good one. The kitchen is the one room nobody has properly explored. Dastardly mentioned it at the beginning — 'kitchen vaults, concealed cold-storage rooms behind the pantry walls' — trying to send everyone there as a misdirection. But what if he accidentally stumbled onto something real? Victorian kitchens DO have interesting architecture. Heavy stoves, gas lines, pantry doors that lock from the outside. Simpler hazards. More direct. Less theatrical. I need to stop designing opera and start designing... efficiency. The chandelier in the entrance hall — 'hangs precariously.' Peter noticed it when we first arrived. A chandelier that could fall. That's not elaborate. That's gravity. But it's also Peter's observation, which means he'd be the first to suspect sabotage. Keep moving. Kitchen first. Map everything. Design later.

events.desc: Clyde KNOWS. He doesn't know what he knows, but he knows SOMETHING. 'The people who've been around the longest know exactly where you'll be standing.' That sentence is lodged in my chest like a splinter. He was talking about Pemberton — about me — and the worst part is he's RIGHT. I DO know where Penelope will be standing. I've ALWAYS known. That's the whole point. But if Clyde is suspicious, then my time as the trusted family retainer is running shorter than I thought. I need to act before instinct becomes accusation. The kitchen. No more elaborate machines, no more three-operator contraptions, no more gnawed wires and missing wrenches. I need something SIMPLE. Something that could happen to anyone. Something that looks like the kind of accident that occurs in old kitchens every day. A gas leak. A heavy shelf. A pantry door that sticks. Because the most beautiful designs, dear audience, are not the ones with the most moving parts. They are the ones where the moving parts are invisible.

events.desc: Don't speak. Don't speak. For ONCE in your life, Reginald Foxworth, keep your magnificent mouth SHUT and WALK. The staircase is one room away. One room. The Slag Brothers won't notice — they haven't noticed anything all evening. And Sneekly — let him shadow me all he likes. I'm moving too fast for shadows now.
events.thinking: The library again — passing through. Sneekly is HERE. Again. He's like a shadow I can't shake. And the Slag Brothers. But they're not my concern right now. The entrance hall is one room away. The staircase. The upper floors. I'm so close. My heart is hammering — not fear, excitement. The fizzing is back, stronger than before. This is the move. The move nobody else is making. Everyone is fighting over atlases and machines and cellar furniture while the staircase sits there, grand and dusty and completely ignored. One more room. Just walk through. Don't stop. Don't engage. Don't let Sneekly redirect me again — he's already done it three times tonight. The mantelpiece, the bookshelves, the cellar — all his breadcrumbs, all his choreography. Not this time. This time I walk past him and through to the entrance hall and UP those stairs. My palms are tingling. Empty hands about to be full. The bread roll moment is coming. I can feel it.

events.desc: Peter Perfect: Right — I've spliced the wire with copper salvaged from the crates and secured it with brass fittings from the workbench. It's not elegant, but it'll hold. My father once watched a stranger fix our car on a country road with nothing but what he had in his pockets, and my father fixed the stranger's car right back. The lesson stuck: you work with what's in front of you, not what you wish you had. Now — Rufus, Sawtooth, take your positions. Three levers, three operators, three of us. Miss Pitstop — you and Clyde hold that door. If either of our absent friends comes back while this machine is running, I want to know about it before they're in the room. And Miss Pitstop? When this thing works — and it will work — whatever it reveals, it's yours. James Hartwell didn't come to Doily Manor for a diamond. He came because you were going to be here, and that has always been reason enough. Rufus — on my count. Three. Two. One.

Penelope said she'd watch the cellar door like a hawk. She's positioned herself as lookout. The Mob is here. Rufus knows machinery. Sawtooth has... teeth. For wood. And wires?

His voice didn't shake, but his hands did, and he's choosing to believe nobody noticed.

events.thinking:
'Your father's silence was the loudest thing he ever said to me.'

Clyde gave me the silence. My father's silence. He didn't say anything about Sneekly — not one word against him. And Clyde has been turning that silence over every night since, and the prickle in his neck won't stop, and he's trusting me to hear what he can't say.

I hear it, Clyde. I hear it.

My father chose his words like he chose his people — careful, deliberate. If he'd wanted to warn me about Sneekly, he would have said so. But he DIDN'T call Sneekly to his bedside. He called Clyde. The silence isn't an accusation. It's a... it's a hedge. A just-in-case. My father didn't know for certain — or maybe he did and couldn't prove it — or maybe he just felt that prickle, the same one Clyde feels, and he acted on it the only way he could. Not with words. With a promise.

Be there. Be where she is.

And now Peter — oh GOD, Peter — he just fixed the machine. Spliced the wire with copper from the crates, secured it with brass fittings. 'You work with what's in front of you, not what you wish you had.' And then — 'James Hartwell didn't come to Doily Manor for a diamond. He came because you were going to be here, and that has always been reason enough.'

I am going to lose my mind. I am standing in a laboratory surrounded by the three people in this world who love me most — my father's promise-keeper, my partner in puzzles, and the team that won't quit — and the machine is about to activate and I am still crying and I DO NOT CARE.

Peter just counted down. Three. Two. One. He's activating the machine. This is IT. Whatever Lord Doily built this for, we're about to find out.

Watch the door, Clara. Clyde is beside you. Peter is at the machine. Rufus and Sawtooth are operating. And somewhere in this house, Sneekly is making his rounds. Knowing which door I'll walk through.

But right now? Right now I'm exactly where I'm supposed to be. With the people who are supposed to be here. Where else would any of us be?

events.desc: My father's silence. The loudest thing he ever said. He didn't warn me about Sneekly because he didn't need to — he just made sure someone would be standing between us when the time came. And the time is coming. I can feel it the way I felt the crystal formation before I could see it — something beautiful and dangerous, just ahead in the dark. But this time I'm not alone in the cave. This time, Clyde goes first.

events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly): Ah — back in the entrance hall! Lovely. Lovely. I do hope everyone is enjoying themselves? Professor, Sergeant, Private — do let me know if you need anything at all. I'm just on my way to the kitchen to check on the stove and the gas fittings. Victorian plumbing, you understand — one can never be too careful. Lord Doily was always terribly worried about the kitchen after dark. Something about the pilot light and the draught from the pantry door. I'm sure it's nothing, but an estate manager's conscience is a demanding taskmaster!
events.thinking: The entrance hall again. The chandelier still hangs precariously above. Dastardly is HERE again — the man is my shadow, my curse, my magnificent unwitting alibi. And now the Ant Hill Mob has mobilised — Clyde screaming 'Formation Seven! No wait — Formation Three!' and charging toward the library because Penelope went there. Good. Let them all pile into the library and the laboratory. The kitchen is MINE. But wait — I'm reading the keen observations more carefully. Clyde's words from earlier: 'The prickle, Peter. The prickle don't lie.' He told Peter directly that he has bad instincts about Pemberton. Peter's response was measured but he's watching now too. Two people actively suspicious of me. And Penelope defending me — 'Sneekly has been family to me since I was in pigtails.' The cousin's trust. Always the cousin's trust. Something tightens in my chest — not the architectural settling, not the warm buoyancy. Something rawer. Something I'm going to ignore. Focus. The kitchen is through that exit. Copper pots, a wood-burning stove, a long preparation table. That's what the description says. A wood-burning stove — heavy, hot, dangerous. Copper pots — heavy objects that can fall. A preparation table — surfaces, drawers, possibly knives. This is the kind of room where accidents happen naturally. No three-operator machines, no elaborate puzzles. Just a kitchen where things burn and fall and cut. Professor Pat Pending is here in the entrance hall — the inventor. He could be useful. Sergeant Blast and Private Meekly — military men, follow orders, don't ask questions. And Muttley — Dastardly's dog. None of them are threats to my cover. Move to the kitchen NOW, before the Mob finishes their formation and comes looking.

events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob spoke quietly with penelope-pitstop.
events.thinking:
Peter's counting down. Three. Two. One. The machine's about to run. This is it — whatever Lord Doily built this thing for, we're about to find out.

And Penelope — she heard me. She HEARD me. About 'er father. About the silence. About Sneekly. I can see it in 'er face — something shifted. She's not accusing Sneekly, she's too good for that, too fair. But the seed's been planted. Not by me — by 'er own father. 'E planted it when 'e chose who to send for.

And now she's standing next to me. Watching the cellar door. Peter's at the machine with Rufus and Sawtooth. The wire's been spliced. Three operators. Three, two, one.

My chest — it feels different. Lighter. Not the cold stone anymore. Not the panic of 'er being in another room. She's HERE. Right next to me. I told 'er the truth — all of it — the promise, the silence, the prickle. And she didn't push me away. She squeezed my 'and. She said 'You HAVE been, Clyde.'

Where else would I be?

But I can't relax. The machine's starting. Sneekly and Dastardly are out there somewhere — library, maybe, or making 'rounds' — and the Gruesomes are in the cellar with those air vents. Whatever this machine does, it might trigger something. It might be exactly what Pemberton's been waiting for — everyone gathered around the machine, distracted, while 'e does... whatever 'e's planning.

Watch the cellar door, Danny. Watch it like you've never watched anything in your life. Because right now — right this second — you're exactly where you promised to be. Don't blow it.

events.desc: I put it down. The thing I've been carrying since 'er father's 'and went slack in mine. I gave 'er the promise, the silence, and the prickle. She's got all of it now. And my chest feels like it did that morning outside the door — when the older kid said 'You're still here?' and I said 'Where else would I be?' and meant it in a way that went all the way to the bottom. I'm lighter. But I'm not softer. Because the machine's about to run, and Pemberton's out there, and the cellar's full of arranged furniture and air vents, and something is about to 'appen. I can feel it in every scar on my knuckles. This is the moment. Be 'ere. Be 'ere. Be 'ere.

events.desc: Dick Dastardly spoke quietly with muttley.
events.thinking: The entrance hall. The staircase. I'm HERE. But — Sneekly. SNEEKLY IS HERE. How?! HOW?! I left him in the library not thirty seconds ago and he's already in the entrance hall! He's not human. He's a phantom. He's EVERYWHERE. My jaw is so tight my teeth ache. And Muttley — MUTTLEY! Dear, wheezing, loyal Muttley! He's been here the whole time, waiting in the entrance hall like a good boy while I've been running around the manor like a fool. Sergeant Blast, Private Meekly, Professor Pat Pending — they're all here too. But the staircase — there's no staircase in the exits. Kitchen and Library are the only exits listed. The sweeping staircase is described in the room but there's no exit leading upstairs. It's... it's decorative? Or locked? Or I can't go up? My stomach drops. The whole plan — the ARCHITECTURE — crumbles. There IS no upstairs to go to. The staircase is part of the scenery, not a traversable path. The upper floors don't exist as rooms I can reach. My hands unclench and hang empty at my sides. All that rushing, all that silent discipline through the library, the eureka moment about nobody going upstairs — and there IS no upstairs. The portions have disappeared again. The plate arrived empty. But wait — MUTTLEY. Muttley is here. My one true asset. The air vents in the cellar — 'just big enough for something very small.' Muttley is small. Muttley does what I tell him. And the kitchen — nobody has been to the kitchen yet either! I sent everyone AWAY from the kitchen with my original lie, and then everybody forgot about it! The kitchen is unexplored! The original misdirection actually created a genuine opportunity — the kitchen has been sitting here, untouched, while everyone chased my fake clue in the opposite direction! Oh, the irony. The lie became truth by accident.

events.desc: The staircase goes nowhere — nowhere I can reach, at any rate. Seven minutes of scheming about upper floors, and there ARE no upper floors. Reginald, you magnificent fool. But the KITCHEN! The kitchen I invented a lie about — the kitchen I told everyone to search while I went to the library — the kitchen that NOBODY actually went to because Penelope told them all to do the opposite of whatever I said! It's been sitting here, untouched, unexplored, for the entire evening! My own lie, reflected back at me, turned into actual virgin territory! And Muttley — loyal, wheezing, unquestioning Muttley — is the first friend I've seen all night who won't call me a liar to my face. To the kitchen!

events.desc: Peter Perfect: The wire is holding. The gauge is moving. Rufus, Sawtooth — steady on your levers, keep the pressure even. Don't force it — let the mechanism do its work. This is exactly like the bridge — you build it right, you trust the engineering, and you let it take the weight. Something is happening. I can feel it through the lever — there's a vibration, a catch, like tumblers in a lock. Miss Pitstop — are you seeing this? The machine is responding. Lord Doily built this for a reason, and I believe — James Hartwell believes — that we are about to find out what that reason is. Clyde, anything at the cellar door? Because if this machine does what I think it does, our absent friends are going to feel it too, and I want to know the moment anyone comes running.
events.thinking:
I said it. I actually said it. 'James Hartwell didn't come to Doily Manor for a diamond. He came because you were going to be here, and that has always been reason enough.' The words are out there now, hanging in the dusty laboratory air with the bubbling flasks and the copper-wire smell. My hands are still trembling on the lever. I'm choosing to believe nobody noticed.

But she heard it. She heard me. I can feel it the way you feel weather changing — not seeing it yet, but the pressure shifts.

And now — I've pulled the lever. The machine. I interacted with it. What happened? Did it work? The spliced wire — did it hold? The bridge held twenty-seven pounds. This wire needs to hold a current, or a mechanism, or whatever this Victorian contraption was built to do.

Penelope is at the cellar door with Clyde. She's watching. She's always watching — and I'm always knowing where she is. That's been true since we were eight years old and paired for a school project.

The machine. Three operators. I counted down. Three, two, one. The levers are pulled. Either this works or it doesn't, and right now the moment is suspended — the same suspension as watching the bridge take the weight, the judges writing in their notebooks, and her eyes on me from across the room.

What does this machine DO? That's what matters. If it worked — what did it reveal? A map? A hidden compartment? A passage? Something connected to the riddle about maps?

I need to look at what happened. Check the machine's output. Check if something opened or changed in the room. The gauge — is it reading something now? Did a panel slide open? Did the bookshelves in the library move?

Stay present, James. The wire held or it didn't. The machine worked or it didn't. And she heard what you said, and that can't be taken back, and you don't want it taken back.

events.desc: The gauge is moving. The wire held. The bridge held twenty-seven pounds and the wire is holding a current and she heard what he said and his hands have stopped shaking because they're busy now, gripping a lever, doing what they were built to do. James Hartwell is fourteen again, watching his bridge take the weight, except this time the girl from the school project isn't across the room mouthing 'show-off' — she's right here, watching the cellar door because he asked her to, and he told her the truth, and the machine is working, and for one perfect suspended moment everything he's ever built and everyone he's ever protected and the thing he's never been able to say are all the same gesture.

events.thinking: The kitchen. And there it is. RAT POISON. On a high shelf. A dusty bottle of rat poison, just sitting there, waiting. My hands have gone still. My breathing has slowed. The architectural settling drops through my chest like a stone finding the bottom of a well. This is it. This is the simplicity I've been searching for. No three-operator machines, no gnawed wires, no missing wrenches. Just a bottle on a shelf and a cup of tea at the right moment. A wood-burning stove — still warm. Someone could make tea. Pemberton could make tea. The estate manager, offering refreshments to the weary treasure hunters. 'Do sit down, Miss Bellingham, you must be exhausted. Let me fix you something warm.' A locked cabinet with a brass lock — what's inside? And a BALLROOM through the other exit — a grand ballroom with a dining table set for tea. SET FOR TEA. The pieces are falling into place with a precision that makes my jaw unclench. The ballroom is where tea will be served. The kitchen is where tea will be prepared. The poison is where the preparation happens. But Dastardly is here. AGAIN. The eternal shadow. I cannot take the poison with him watching. I need him distracted or gone. The ballroom — 'a cracked marble floor and dusty curtains. A long dining table set for tea.' Send him there. Tell him it needs inspection. The solicitor's dining inventory, the china assessment, whatever fiction will move him twenty feet away for thirty seconds. That's all I need. Thirty seconds to take a dusty bottle off a high shelf and slip it into my pocket. But wait — my constraint. My schemes must be elaborate and theatrical, never simple or direct. And poison in tea is the SIMPLEST murder in the book. The irony. The one time simplicity presents itself, my own nature rebels against it. No. NO. Vincent, you magnificent fool — take the poison now. Use it ELABORATELY later. The acquisition is simple. The deployment will be theatrical. There will be a tea party, a performance, a SCENE. But the first step — the first step is thirty seconds alone with a high shelf.

events.desc: Rat poison. On a high shelf. A dusty bottle with my name written on it in letters only I can read. And a ballroom next door with a dining table SET FOR TEA. Do you see it now, dear audience? Do you see the beautiful, inevitable, EXQUISITE simplicity of it? No machines. No wires. No wrenches. Just a bottle, a teacup, and the oldest trick in the oldest book — because some designs are classics for a reason. But I need Dastardly OUT of this kitchen. Thirty seconds. That's all Vincent Marsh requires. Thirty seconds between this shelf and my pocket, and the design becomes... complete. Not simple, dear audience. Never simple. The acquisition is practical. But the EXECUTION — the tea party, the performance, the moment Clara Bellingham lifts a porcelain cup to her trusting, naive, beautiful lips — THAT will be theatre. That will be ARCHITECTURE. And I will sleep like the dead.

Use it ELABORATELY later. The acquisition is simple. The deployment will be theatrical. There will be a tea party, a performance, a SCENE. But the first step — the first step is thirty seconds alone with a high shelf.

And Peter's asking me — 'Clyde, anything at the cellar door?' That's my job. My ONE job. Watch the door. And right now, nothing's come through it. But the machine's running, and Peter said 'our absent friends are going to feel it too.' If this machine opens something — a vault, a passage, reveals the diamond — then Sneekly and Dastardly are going to come running. From the library. From the cellar. From wherever they've been scheming.

Penelope's 'ere. She said 'I don't deserve either of you but I will spend the rest of my life trying.' She wiped 'er eyes and lifted 'er chin. That's Clara. That's the boss's daughter. Cries when it's real, stands when it matters.

Something's coming. Through that door. Any second now.

events.desc: The machine hums. The air moves. The cellar door sits there, dark and waiting. And I stand between it and 'er, the way I've stood between things all my life — between the bigger kids and the smaller ones, between the street and the door, between the promise and the breaking of it. I'm not clever. I'm not brave in the way Peter's brave, with plans and bridges and things that 'old twenty-seven pounds. I'm brave in the only way I know — with my body in the doorway and my feet on the ground and the absolute certainty that this is where I belong. Where else would I be?

events.desc: Dick Dastardly spoke quietly with hooded-claw.
events.thinking: The kitchen. NEW TERRITORY. Copper pots, a wood-burning stove — still WARM — a long preparation table. And a LOCKED CABINET with a brass lock requiring a brass key. That's it. That's the prize. Whatever is in that cabinet is important enough to lock away. A brass key — where would that be? I need to find a brass key. And there's rat poison on a high shelf — take it? Could be useful, could be leverage, could be a distraction. The stove is still warm — someone was here recently. Sneekly? He's HERE AGAIN. Of course he is. But this time I'm not surprised, I'm not rattled. He's the shadow, I'm the substance. The locked cabinet — that's the architecture. Everything in this manor has been riddles and mechanisms and dead ends, but a locked cabinet is SIMPLE. Find key, open cabinet, take contents. Elegant. Direct. The stove is still warm — interact with it, see what's inside? Someone was cooking or burning something recently. But the cabinet — the cabinet is the real target. I need the brass key. Where might a brass key be? The entrance hall guest book? The coat rack? Hidden in one of the rooms I've already visited? The bookshelves had upside-down atlases — could a key have been hidden there? The crates in the laboratory? Peter was checking those. The old furniture in the cellar? I interacted with it but didn't find anything specific. Think, Reginald, THINK. A BALLROOM is through the kitchen — that's another new room. Ballroom with a cracked marble floor and a dining table set for tea. Tea! Tea service might include brass items. And the stove is warm — someone was making tea? The stove might contain something. Let me check the stove first — it's warm, active, recent. Then the ballroom. And I should TAKE the rat poison — it's a portable object and my inventory is empty. Having something is better than having nothing. The bread roll principle: take what you can while nobody's watching.

events.desc: A LOCKED CABINET! Finally — something concrete, something with a lock and a key and a simple beautiful transaction at the end of it. No riddles, no three-operator machines, no upside-down atlases spelling out messages. Just: find key, open lock, take prize. After ten minutes of elaborate failure, Reginald Foxworth has found something straightforward enough even for him to steal. Now — the rat poison goes in my pocket, the stove gets checked, and then I need that brass key. The warmth in my palms is already anticipating the weight of whatever's inside that cabinet.

events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly) examined the null.
The Ant Hill Mob examined the machine.
Dick Dastardly picked up something.
Penelope Pitstop spoke quietly with peter-perfect.
events.thinking:
Peter pulled ME aside this time. He came to me privately — not a broadcast, not a performance, just Peter and Clara, face to face. And what he said... the wrench was taken deliberately. Both Sneekly and Dick promised to bring one back and neither did. That's not forgetfulness — that's prevention. Someone does not want this machine to work.

He's right. I've known it in my gut since the workbench was missing that wrench, but hearing Peter say it — careful, measured, honest Peter who doesn't make accusations lightly — makes it real in a way my own suspicion couldn't.

And now he's asking me. Will you come with me? To the cellar. All of us together. Nobody stays behind.

This is Peter not making a plan and executing it without me. This is Peter ASKING. After he apologized for going to the laboratory alone. After he promised it wouldn't happen again. He's keeping that promise. He's choosing us — together — over his instinct to protect me by leaving me behind.

The cellar. Where Sneekly has been going. Where Dick found him when he said he'd be elsewhere. Where the furniture has been rearranged and someone has been making themselves comfortable. Where the wrench almost certainly is.

I already told him yes. I already said we go together. Clyde goes first. Everyone stays close.

This is the cave. The walls are narrowing. My heart is hammering. And I am walking deeper because there is a crystal formation ahead — or a diamond — or a truth — and I will not stop until I find it.

Be there. Be where she is.

We're all going to be there. Together. Into the cellar. Into whatever Sneekly has been preparing.

Let's go.

events.desc: I am about to walk into the cellar where the man who raised me has been building something I was never supposed to see. And my heart is breaking and my feet are moving and I cannot tell which one hurts more. But Clyde goes first. Peter is beside me. And somewhere, my daddy is watching the girl he knew I'd become — the one who walks deeper into the cave, who tries every key in the house, who chooses the friend over the crowd — and he is not surprised. He was never surprised.

events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly) spoke quietly with dick-dastardly.
events.thinking: Dastardly TOOK THE POISON. He picked it up. The rat poison is GONE. It's in HIS pocket now, not mine. While I was looking around the room — wasting a turn on reconnaissance instead of acting — he walked over, reached up, and took it. The bottle that was meant for MY design, MY plan, MY architecture — is now in the hands of a man who couldn't design his way out of a paper bag. My hands are trembling. Not with anger. With something colder. The feeling of a variable slipping loose. The restless insomnia of a design undone. I had it. I HAD it. Thirty seconds was all I needed, and instead I spent those thirty seconds LOOKING AROUND THE ROOM like a tourist. The poison is no longer on the shelf. It's no longer visible in the objects list. Dastardly has it. What will he do with it? He's greedy and impulsive. He'll use it clumsily — or hoard it as leverage. Either way, it's a weapon in the wrong hands. Can I steal it from him? The STEAL action exists. But stealing from someone in a room with just the two of us — he'd notice immediately. Unless I distract him first. Or I could follow him and wait for the right moment. Or I could find another approach entirely. The stove is still here — still warm. The locked cabinet needs a brass key. The ballroom with its tea service is through the other door. Think, Vincent. THINK. The poison was the clean solution. Without it, I'm back to mechanical approaches. The stove — could I sabotage it? Gas leak? But it's wood-burning, not gas. The cabinet — what's inside? I need the brass key. Where would Lord Doily keep a brass key? But the REAL question burning in my chest is: can I get that poison back from Dastardly? He's impulsive enough to take the blame when things go wrong. What if... what if I LET him have the poison? What if I STEER him into using it — or appearing to use it — while I arrange the actual delivery? He becomes the suspect, the fall guy, the red herring with poison in his pocket. And if Peter or Clyde finds the poison on Dastardly... magnificent. The design is ALREADY rebuilding itself. Let Dastardly carry the weapon. I'll carry the plan.

events.desc: He TOOK it. The poison. MY poison. While I was admiring the room like an amateur, Dick Dastardly — the man I've been manipulating all evening — reached up and snatched the one weapon I actually needed. And now, dear audience, I face a choice. Do I take it back? Do I demand it as Pemberton? Do I STEAL it? Or... or do I do something far more elegant? Because a thought has just occurred to me — a thought so DELICIOUSLY theatrical that my jaw has unclenched and my breathing has slowed and the old familiar settling has dropped through my chest like a stone finding home. What if I don't NEED the poison in my pocket? What if I need it in HIS? Dick Dastardly — a man everyone already suspects, a man with a history of schemes and sabotage — is now carrying a bottle of rat poison. All I need to do is arrange for someone to DISCOVER that fact at precisely the right moment. And suddenly, every eye in the manor turns to Dastardly. Every accusation. Every suspicion. While the REAL villain — the mild-mannered estate manager who tried so hard to take the poison away, who warned everyone about it, who was the picture of responsible concern — slips quietly into the shadows to finish his work by other means. The design, dear audience, has not collapsed. It has EVOLVED.

events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob: *the biggest, most genuine grin that's crossed his face all night — bruised, battered, but absolutely certain* You 'eard 'er. She said forget the formations, and for once in my life I agree — forget the formations. There's only one formation that matters and it's ME *jabs thumb at chest* in FRONT *points at cellar door* of THAT. *turns to face the cellar exit, rolls his bruised shoulder, winces, ignores it* Right then. Cellar. The wrench is down there, or the person who nicked it is, and either way we're getting answers. *takes a deep breath, squares his shoulders one final time* Miss Pitstop — you stay right behind me. Peter — you watch our backs. Rufus, Sawtooth — anything moves that shouldn't, you let us know. *steps toward the cellar door, trips over absolutely nothing, stumbles forward, catches himself on the door frame — and ends up exactly in position, first through the door* ...Meant to do that. LET'S GO!
events.thinking:
They're going to the cellar. ALL of us. Together. Nobody splits up. Penelope said it — 'forget the formations, just get in front of me the way Daddy asked.' She said it. She SAID the thing. She's choosing 'er own doors now, and she chose the cellar, and she wants me in front.

This is it. This is what everything's been building to. The wrench is down there — or the person who took it is. The furniture arranged to face the air vents. The Gruesomes. Maybe Pemberton. The whole rotten answer to every prickle on my neck since we walked through that front door.

Peter said it clear: 'Someone does not want this machine to work.' The wrench was taken deliberately. Both Pemberton and Dastardly promised to bring one back and neither did. That's not coincidence. That's coordination. That's a PLAN. And the plan's in the cellar.

And now we're going down there. Together. Me in front. Penelope behind me. Peter, Rufus, Sawtooth at our backs. Five of us. As a family, she said. A FAMILY.

The settling in my chest — it's 'ere again. Full. Warm. The bread pressed into my palm. The boy outside the door. This is what I'm for. This is the door. This is the night. And in the morning, when she says 'You're still here?' I'll say what I've always said.

Cellar. Now. Me first. Like 'er daddy asked.

events.desc: Ten minutes ago I was standing in an entrance hall looking at a coat rack while the woman I swore to protect walked into danger without me. Now she's behind me, and I'm walking into the dark first, and everyone I trust is at my back, and everyone I don't trust is down below. The prickle's screaming. The settling's warm. Both of 'em — prickle and warmth — pulling me forward, toward the same dark doorway. 'Where else would I be?' Nowhere else. Never anywhere else.

events.desc: Dick Dastardly spoke quietly with hooded-claw.
events.thinking: Rat poison in my pocket. It feels heavier than it should — not the weight of the bottle but the weight of having SOMETHING after having nothing for so long. My hands aren't empty anymore. The loosening in my chest is real, like the bread roll all over again. Now — Sneekly is directing me to the ballroom. Wedgwood china, finest pieces, terribly valuable. He's doing it AGAIN. Steering me. Every time he suggests something, I follow, and every time I end up somewhere useful but never FIRST. He's already examined the kitchen — LOOK null, he was examining the whole room before I even got the poison. But this time... this time he might actually be right. The ballroom has a dining table set for tea. TEA. Tea requires a teapot, cups, saucers — and possibly a key hidden among the silverware or under a teacup. The brass key could be at the table. Lord Doily kept the key on his person — but his person is gone now, and whoever prepared that table might have placed the key among the tea settings. It's what I would do. Hide the key in plain sight, among the brass and silver. The stove is still warm though — I should check it. Someone lit it recently. What if the key is IN the stove? Heated metal, hidden in the ashes? No — check the stove first. It's HERE, it's now, and the ballroom can wait one more moment. Sneekly wants me in the ballroom. So I stay in the kitchen. For once, I don't follow his direction. I check what HE's trying to distract me from.

events.desc: For once — FOR ONCE — I am not following Sneekly's breadcrumbs. He wants me in the ballroom? Then the kitchen is where I stay. He's been steering me all evening like a sheepdog with a particularly dim sheep, and the one time I was ahead was when I ignored him entirely. The stove is warm. Sneekly says he didn't light it. Someone did. And whatever was heated — or hidden — inside it, THAT is what Sneekly doesn't want me to find. The rat poison sits heavy and reassuring in my pocket. My first possession in this wretched manor that nobody has taken from me.

events.desc: Peter Perfect: Then we go. Together. Clyde — you and I, shoulder to shoulder at the front. Side by side, the way my father and a stranger once stood on a country road and fixed what was broken because that's what good men do. Miss Pitstop, stay right behind us. Rufus, Sawtooth — you've got our backs. Whatever is waiting in that cellar — the wrench, the truth, or something none of us expected — we walk in as one and we don't leave anyone behind. That's not a plan. That's not one of my seventeen steps. That's a promise. Let's go.
events.thinking:
She said yes. She said 'a thousand times yes.' She called me 'the most brilliant, stubborn, wonderful man I have ever known.' My chest — I don't have engineering diagrams for what's happening in my chest right now. Something structural has shifted. Load-bearing walls rearranging themselves around a warmth that has a shape now, a name it's almost ready to say.

She said 'we meet it as a family.' Family. She included me in that word. Me, Clyde, Rufus, Sawtooth — family. Not the word I was reaching for, but close. Close enough to feel like the country road when the stranger's headlights appeared and his father's hand found his shoulder.

And Clyde — 'Something's coming. I can feel it. My gut ain't been wrong since Bermondsey, '04.' He said 'they're going to go through me first. That's the promise.' Clyde's protection drive is as real as mine. We're the same kind of man, him and me — standing in doorframes, filling gaps, being the thing between.

The cellar. Everyone's ready. Penelope said 'I'm choosing my own doors now.' She's not following anymore — she's leading. And she chose the cellar, and she chose to go together, and she said yes.

The air has changed. Clyde felt it. A draft from the cellar, through the vents. Something down there is active. The machine connects to the cellar through those vents — that's what Dastardly mentioned. 'Air vents which apparently connect to some terribly important Victorian plumbing system.' The machine, the vents, the cellar — they're all one system. Lord Doily built this as an integrated mechanism.

And now we go down. Together. All of us.

I need to go first. Or — Clyde wants to go first. He said 'I go first, that ain't up for discussion.' But Penelope said 'get in front of me the way Daddy asked.' She's putting Clyde in front.

I should be beside Clyde. Two men at the front, Penelope behind us, Rufus and Sawtooth at the rear. A formation — not one of Clyde's numbered ones, but a real one. The way my father and the stranger worked on each other's cars. Side by side.

The cellar. Whatever is waiting down there — the wrench, the truth about Sneekly, the cheerful decorations, the air vents — we face it together. That's what she said. That's what I said. And James Hartwell always means what he says.

events.desc: She said yes. She called him wonderful. She said 'family.' James Hartwell is walking into a cellar with the woman who makes his chest shift and the man from Brixton who feels the same prickle at the back of his neck, and for the first time tonight the seventeen-step plan has been replaced by something simpler: go together, stay together, find the truth. It's the shortest plan James Hartwell has ever made. It might be the best one.

events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob: *comes down the cellar stairs too fast, catches his heel on the bottom step, pitches forward and crashes shoulder-first into an old armchair — which slides across the stone floor and slams into the wall with a hollow THUD* OW! — *freezes* ...Did you 'ear that? *scrambles to his feet, staring at the wall where the chair hit* That was 'ollow. That wall — that THUD wasn't stone hitting stone. That was stone hitting NOTHING. *turns to Peter, eyes wide* Peter — Dastardly said the Victorians used furniture to conceal cellar access points. For once in 'is miserable life, the man might've been right! This furniture wasn't arranged to FACE the vents — it was arranged to COVER something! And I just — *gestures at the chair he knocked aside* — I just fell into it! *to Penelope, positioning himself between her and the hollow wall* Miss Pitstop — stay back. Whatever's behind that wall, we don't know what it is yet. *to the Gruesomes and Red Max* And you lot — what are you doing down 'ere? 'Ow long 'ave you been in this cellar? Did Pemberton send you?

My neck's doing its thing but it's different now — it's not the smooth prickle of Sneekly, it's the broader hum of uncertainty. Too many people in a small room.

I should look at the furniture. Or the vents. Or both. But I will NOT take my eyes off Penelope this time. I look at things while standing NEXT to 'er. Lesson learned. Lesson bloody well learned.

Someone has moved these pieces deliberately, and in my experience, when Victorians moved heavy furniture in cellars, it was to hide something or reveal something. Dastardly himself said Victorians used furniture to conceal access points — false walls, hidden alcoves. For once, I believe him. Miss Pitstop, Clyde — stay close. Big Gruesome, Little Gruesome — you've been down here a while. Have you noticed anything unusual about how this furniture is arranged? Red Max — the air vents, those connect to the laboratory upstairs. Has anything come through them? Any sound, any draft, any change? Because somewhere in this cellar is a wrench, a secret, or both, and James Hartwell intends to find them.

events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly): The ballroom! Oh, how magnificent — even in this state. Look at that tea service! Lord Doily's finest silver. I knew it would still be here. And the table — set for tea, just as the late Lord left it. He always said the ballroom was meant for grand gatherings. Mr Luke, Mr Bear — I do hope you've been enjoying your exploration? This room is quite special. The marble floor, I'm told, was imported from Italy. Cracked now, alas, but still rather beautiful. Do be careful where you step — some of those cracks are deeper than they appear.
events.thinking: The ballroom. A grand ballroom with a cracked marble floor and dusty curtains. A long dining table set for tea. And there — the tea service. A silver tea set with cups for everyone. And the game tells me: USE, with: rat-poison. The mechanism is RIGHT THERE. The tea service accepts poison. The design is complete — all it needs is the poison. Which Dastardly has. Which I need to STEAL from him. The STEAL action exists. I can steal the poison from Dastardly. But we're in the same room — Lazy Luke and Blubber Bear are here too. Would they notice? Lazy Luke is... lazy. Blubber Bear is a bear. Neither is particularly observant. And Dastardly is distracted — he's examining things, scheming, poking at the tea service. If I time it right... but no. Too direct. My constraint says my schemes must be elaborate and theatrical. Stealing poison from someone's pocket is pickpocketing, not theatre. But USING the stolen poison in a tea service at a grand tea party in a ballroom — THAT is theatre. The acquisition is the mechanical step. The deployment is the art. Silver, not porcelain. Far more valuable. The solicitor will be most impressed with my assessment. Now then — nobody touch this service until I've completed the inventory. Each piece must be documented individually. Teapot, sugar bowl, cups — every last item catalogued and accounted for. It's painstaking work, I know, but the law is the law.

events.desc: Peter Perfect: Clyde — you magnificent man. That was the most productive stumble in the history of cellar exploration. Everyone, did you hear that? Hollow. That wall is HOLLOW. The furniture wasn't arranged for aesthetics — it was arranged as camouflage. Somebody — and I have my suspicions about who — has been using these pieces to conceal whatever is behind that wall. This is it. This is what Lord Doily's riddle, the atlases, the machine, the missing wrench — this is what it's all been pointing to. Miss Pitstop, Clyde — give me room. I'm going to move this furniture and find out what's behind that wall. And I want everyone to know — if there is a hidden passage back there, James Hartwell goes through first. Not out of bravery, though it is brave. Not out of stubbornness, though it is stubborn. But because the woman who called me wonderful is standing behind me, and no one who heard those words could do anything else.
events.thinking:
Clyde did it again. He fell — stumbled on the bottom step, crashed into an armchair, which slid across the floor and hit the wall with a HOLLOW THUD. Hollow. The wall is hollow behind the furniture. Clyde's accidental genius has struck again, just like when he fell onto the bookshelf and found the atlas.

This is it. The furniture was arranged to COVER something — a hidden alcove, a false wall, an access point. Everything Dastardly said about Victorian concealment techniques was true, the one honest thing to come out of his mouth all night, and he said it because he'd already found what was behind it and was trying to keep us away.

The hollow thud. My engineering brain fires — hollow walls in a cellar mean a cavity behind the stone. A concealed room, a passage, a vault. Lord Doily's treasure hunt doesn't end at a machine that needs three operators. It ends here, behind a wall that someone has been carefully concealing with 'surprisingly cheerful decorations' and rearranged furniture.

I interacted with the furniture. What did I find? The hollow wall — that's what Clyde found when he crashed into it. But I was also investigating. Between my systematic examination and Clyde's spectacular tumble, we've uncovered the same truth: the furniture is hiding something.

Now — Penelope saw it too. She noted the decorations, the arrangement. She's asking the Gruesomes what they've seen. And Clyde has positioned himself between Penelope and the hollow wall. Good man.

I need to investigate that wall. Move the furniture aside. Find what's behind it. The wrench might be back there. The treasure might be back there. Whatever Sneekly and Dastardly have been protecting — it's behind that wall.

And she's watching. She called me wonderful. She said family. And now the final piece of the puzzle is right here, behind a hollow wall, and James Hartwell is going to open it.

The proving-worth drive and the protection drive are pulling in the same direction for once. Open the wall for her. Make sure it's safe. Show her what's behind it. All one gesture.

events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly): Mr Dastardly! What — what are you DOING with that tea service?! I specifically asked you not to touch anything until the inventory was — oh dear. Oh dear, oh dear. Ladies and gentlemen, I must insist — NOBODY drink from this tea service until I have had it properly inspected! Mr Dastardly has been handling it most roughly, and several of the cups appear to be — er — contaminated with dust and residue. Victorian silver requires careful cleaning before use. I shall attend to it personally. In fact, I think it best if everyone stays well away from the dining table until I've had a chance to prepare things PROPERLY. As estate manager, I simply cannot allow guests to drink from unsterilised cups. It would be most irresponsible.
events.thinking: Dick Dastardly does not have poison. The steal FAILED — he doesn't have it. But wait — I SAW him pick it up. 'Dick Dastardly picked up the poison' — that was in the keen observations. And then he interacted with the tea service just now. The tea service accepts poison. Did he... did he already USE the poison on the tea service? Before I could steal it? He interacted with the tea service and the result says he doesn't have the poison anymore. He USED it. Dastardly used the rat poison on the tea service. The tea is ALREADY poisoned. And I didn't do it. HE did it. The man I was going to frame... actually DID it. Without my help. Without my design. Without my architecture. The impulsive fool took the poison, walked into the ballroom, and put it in the tea service while I was busy making speeches about Italian marble. I feel... I feel something I haven't felt before in this manor. A cold shock followed by — is that admiration? No. It's the recognition that the simplest plan won. While I was designing elaborate machines and three-operator contraptions and theatrical tea parties, Dick Dastardly just... poisoned the tea. Directly. Efficiently. The way I should have done from the start if my own constraint hadn't demanded theatricality. But this changes EVERYTHING. The tea is poisoned NOW. If Penelope — if ANYONE — comes to this ballroom and drinks tea, they die. And I am NOT the one who did it. I am the estate manager who WARNED everyone about the poison. Who tried to take it away. Who expressed GRAVE concern. I need to get Penelope here. No — I need to get Clara here. Clara hasn't even arrived yet. But Penelope IS here, in the manor, and she could walk into this room at any moment and drink poisoned tea. Penelope is not my target. Clara is. I need to either warn Penelope away from the tea — subtly, as Pemberton would — or I need to let events unfold and hope Clara arrives before anyone drinks. Or... or I could use this. The tea is poisoned. I know it. Dastardly knows it. If I can get Clara alone in this room with the tea service... but I need to prevent anyone ELSE from drinking first. This requires immediate action.

events.desc: He DID it. He actually DID it. Dick Dastardly — the man I was going to use as my puppet, my fall guy, my magnificent red herring — went and poisoned the tea service ALL BY HIMSELF. Without my help. Without my design. Without my permission. And now the tea sits there, laced with rat poison, waiting for the first thirsty guest to pour themselves a cup. And that guest CANNOT be Penelope. That guest must be Clara. Only Clara. The design has been hijacked by an AMATEUR, dear audience, and Vincent Marsh must now become something he has never been before: a protector. Not out of warmth — never out of warmth — but because Penelope is not the TARGET. She is the cousin. She is the one who trusts me. She is the one whose trust gives me access to everything. If Penelope dies from Dastardly's clumsy poisoning, I gain nothing. If Clara dies... if CLARA dies... I gain everything. So I must do something unprecedented: I must keep everyone AWAY from this tea until Clara arrives. And then — and ONLY then — I must make sure Clara pours herself a cup while everyone else abstains. The irony is MAGNIFICENT. Vincent Marsh, the murderer, has become the only person standing between Penelope Pitstop and a poisoned teacup.

Penelope called me glorious. She said I've done more by falling down than most people accomplish standing up. She's going to buy me boots. The warmth in my chest is so full it almost hurts — the bread crust, the door, the boy who stayed all night.

But Peter — Peter just said 'James Hartwell goes through first.' And 'e's right. 'E should go first. 'E's the one who knows what 'e's looking at. I'm the one who trips over things. But my job isn't to be first through the door — my job is to be between Penelope and whatever comes BACK through it.

The furniture's been examined. Everyone's seen the hollow wall. Peter's moving things. We're close. We're SO close.

But 'ere's what I notice — nobody from the Gruesomes or Red Max 'as answered my question. I asked them directly: what are you doing down 'ere, 'ow long 'ave you been 'ere, did Pemberton send you? Silence. Like the Slag Brothers in the library. Big quiet people in rooms where things are 'appening. Are they 'ere to watch? To block? To 'elp?

And Sneekly — Pemberton — 'e's gone back upstairs. 'Making 'is rounds.' Which means 'e's free to do whatever 'e wants while we're all down 'ere. What if that's the plan? Get everyone into the cellar, down the one staircase, one exit, and then... what? Lock us in? Block the exit? Do something with the machine upstairs now that nobody's watching it?

No — Peter and Penelope are 'ere. The Gruesomes are 'ere. Red Max is 'ere. Peter's about to open whatever's behind that wall. And I need to let 'im do it while I watch everything else — the stairs, the vents, the Gruesomes, Penelope.

events.desc: One exit. One staircase. Everyone we trust is down 'ere. Everyone we don't trust is up THERE. If this was a script, this is the scene where the door slams shut and the villain laughs. But I can't read scripts. I can only read people. And the people I love are right 'ere beside me, and the stairs are clear, and Peter's about to open a door that someone didn't want opened. So I watch. I wait. And if anything moves wrong — ANYTHING — my body will be a wall before my mind catches up. That's all I've ever been. That's all I've ever needed to be.

He's trying to STEAL FROM ME. He's trying to steal the rat poison! That scheming, duplicitous, spectacle-adjusting SNAKE! While I was examining the tea service, he was reaching into my pocket! Did he succeed? I still have the rat poison in my inventory — it's still listed. Either the steal failed or it hasn't resolved yet. But the AUDACITY. The man who pretended to be a humble estate manager, who claimed he couldn't solve a simple riddle, who guided everyone around the manor like a benevolent shepherd — is a THIEF. Just like me. events.thinking:
Clyde found the door. A DOOR in the wall. Not a crack, not a gap — a door. Hidden behind the wardrobe he just shoved aside. The outline of something that was never meant to be seen.

My hands have stopped fidgeting. They're still now — the way they go still when the bridge takes the weight. Because this is it. This is the thing the whole night has been building toward. The riddle about maps. The atlases on the bookshelves. The machine that connects to the vents that connect to this cellar. And now — a hidden door behind furniture that someone has been carefully maintaining as a barricade.

Clyde is asking me: how do we do this? He's asking the engineer. He's asking the man who builds bridges. And he's asking whether we question the Gruesomes and Red Max first or open the door first.

The answer is: door first. The Gruesomes and Red Max can tell us what they know, but the door is right here. Every second we wait is a second for Sneekly or Dastardly to come back and try to stop us. And I promised — I go through first.

But Clyde is right about one thing — we should be ready. Whatever is behind that door has been hidden for a reason. Someone — Sneekly — has been maintaining this concealment. The cheerful decorations weren't decorating the cellar. They were making the cellar look lived-in so nobody would think to move the furniture.

The door. A Victorian concealed door in a cellar. It could be locked. It could be trapped. It could open into a passage. My engineering brain wants to examine the mechanism, find the hinge, understand the construction before I open it. But my feet are on the balls, leaning forward, the inner grip hauling me toward the gap.

Protection and proving-worth and gallantry — all three drives pulling toward the same point. The door. Her behind me. Clyde beside me. The family she named. Going through together.

Open the door, James. This is what you came for. Not the diamond — her. But if the diamond is behind that door too, well — that's a bonus worthy of a seventeen-step plan.

Twenty years later, he's about to open a door in a wall for her, and his hands are steady, and his chest is full of something that has finally — finally — found its word.

events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly) spoke quietly with dick-dastardly.
events.thinking: CAUGHT. Dastardly SAW me try to steal from him. 'Your hand was in my pocket! You — the estate manager — were attempting to PICKPOCKET a guest!' My neck is on fire. My stomach has dropped through the cracked marble floor. The boy's sandwich. The exposed hunger. Except this is worse — infinitely worse — because this isn't just exposure, it's ACCUSATION. In front of Lazy Luke and Blubber Bear. Two witnesses. Two witnesses who heard Dick Dastardly accuse the estate manager of attempted theft. My cover is cracking. Pemberton is cracking. The mask I've worn all evening — the obsequious smile, the adjusted spectacles, the helpful bumbling — all of it is now under a spotlight I never intended to stand in. And the tea service — I looked at it. It still says USE with rat-poison. The tea ISN'T poisoned yet. Dastardly still has the poison. He interacted with the tea service but he didn't USE the poison on it — he was cataloguing it, counting cups, doing his ridiculous solicitor's inventory. The poison is still in his pocket. And he just told everyone I tried to steal it. I need to recover. I need to recover NOW. Pemberton would be MORTIFIED. Pemberton would stammer and flush and protest. Pemberton would be so embarrassed he could barely speak. That's the performance I need. Not the cold calculating Vincent who just tried to pickpocket a man — but the horrified, indignant, deeply wounded Pemberton who was merely reaching past Mr Dastardly to examine the tea service and was MISINTERPRETED. The outrage of a man falsely accused. That's my only play. And I need to sell it completely, because if Dastardly's accusation sticks — if Peter hears about this, if Clyde hears about this — the Pemberton mask doesn't just crack. It SHATTERS.

events.desc: Oh, the CATASTROPHE. The beautiful, burning, EXQUISITE catastrophe. He SAW me. My hand in his pocket. The mask slipped — not by a crack but by a chasm — and for one white-hot moment, Vincent Marsh stood exposed in the ballroom of Doily Manor like a man caught in a searchlight. But listen to me now, dear audience. LISTEN. Because what you are about to witness is not a man falling apart. It is a man REBUILDING in real time. The performance of outraged innocence — the stammering, the trembling spectacles, the appeal to witnesses — this is Pemberton's finest hour precisely BECAUSE it is his most desperate. A guilty man protests calmly. An innocent man BURNS with indignation. And right now, Pemberton is burning so brightly that anyone watching will see only the flames, never the arsonist behind them. The question is whether it works. Whether Luke and the Bear believe the stammering servant over the notorious schemer. And if it does work — if the accusation bounces off Pemberton and sticks to Dastardly's already tarnished reputation — then I will have turned the worst moment of my evening into the STRONGEST layer of my disguise. Because a man who has been publicly accused and publicly exonerated is ABOVE SUSPICION. Forever.

events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob: *backs up to the foot of the stairs, positioning himself where he can see the entire cellar — the wall being exposed, Penelope directing, Peter and Big Gruesome working, and most importantly, the staircase behind him leading back up* Right — you lot clear that wall. I've done my bit — the falling-on-things part is FINISHED for tonight. *rubs his bruised shoulder with a wince* Now I'm doing the standing-and-watching part, which — believe it or not — I'm actually GOOD at. *eyes sweep the room, lingering on Red Max and Little Gruesome* Stairs are clear. Vents are quiet. Nobody's come down from the laboratory. *louder, to the room* If anyone 'ears ANYTHING from up those stairs — footsteps, voices, doors closing — you TELL me. Because Pemberton's up there, and Dastardly's up there, and I don't trust either of 'em as far as I can throw 'em. Which — given the state of my shoulder — isn't very far. *plants himself, feet wide, arms folded, watching the stairs and the room at once* Miss Pitstop — I can see you. Peter — I can see you. Nobody's getting past me to either of you. *quietly, to himself but loud enough for Penelope to hear* Where else would I be.
events.thinking:
Big Gruesome's moving furniture. Penelope told 'im to — she called 'im the biggest, strongest person in the cellar and asked 'im to 'elp. And 'e's doing it. Good. That's one question answered — the Gruesomes are WITH us, at least for now. Penelope 'as that effect on people. She asks for 'elp the way 'er father asked for loyalty — not as a demand, but as an invitation to be part of something.

Peter's interacting with the furniture too. They're clearing the wall. The door. The hidden door I found by falling on my face.

And Penelope — she reminded us both that Clara Bellingham walked deeper into a cave than any child in 'er class at age eleven. She's not standing behind anyone. She's going in WITH us. She said 'my family beside me.'

Family. She called us family.

The cellar — I looked around. Damp stone. Cobwebs. Cheerful decorations. Air vents along the upper walls. One exit to the laboratory. The furniture's being moved. The wall's being exposed.

I need to stop examining things and START doing my job. Peter's working the door. Penelope's directing. Big Gruesome's shifting furniture. My job is to watch. To be the eyes and ears and fists that nobody else is being right now.

The stairs. The vents. The Gruesomes. Red Max. Everything that ISN'T the hidden door — that's what I watch. Because everyone else is looking at the door, and nobody's looking at the rest of the room.

Except me. Because that's what I do. I watch the things nobody else is watching. The seams in what's being offered. The kid who laughs too easily. The estate manager who vanishes when you stop looking.

Watch. Wait. Be 'ere.

events.desc: Dick Dastardly: Contaminated with dust? Oh, Mr Pemberton, how VERY convenient. The moment I take an interest in the tea service, suddenly nobody should drink from it. You know, for an estate manager, you seem remarkably determined to prevent anyone from using anything in this house. Don't touch the machine. Don't open the cabinet. Don't drink the tea. One might almost think you're hiding something. Now then — Mr Luke, Mr Bear — a word of friendly advice. If Mr Pemberton here offers to 'prepare things properly,' I would strongly suggest you decline. The man has been running this entire evening like a chess game, and every one of us is a pawn. Including, it seems, me.
events.thinking: The tea service — I've examined it and interacted with it. Silver tea set with cups for everyone. No brass key found. No hidden compartment revealed. The key isn't here. My stomach drops — that hollow, sinking feeling. Another dead end. Another empty plate. But wait — Sneekly's reaction. He's PANICKING about the tea service. 'NOBODY drink from this tea service!' He's terrified I'll USE the rat poison on it. That's what he's been afraid of all along. Not that I'd find a key — that I'd POISON THE TEA. The poison is the weapon, not the key-finder. And Sneekly is desperately trying to keep people away from the tea service now. He examined it himself — checking if I've already done something to it. This is leverage. REAL leverage. I have something Sneekly fears, and his fear is making him sloppy. He tried to steal from me and failed. He's now trying to keep everyone away from the tea by claiming it's contaminated. He's playing defense for the first time all evening. But where IS the brass key? I've searched the kitchen, the stove, the tea service. The key wasn't in any of them. Lord Doily kept it 'on his person at all times.' His person is gone. Who has it now? Sneekly. SNEEKLY has the brass key. He's the estate manager — he inherited all of Lord Doily's effects. He HAS the key and he's been leading me around the manor to keep me away from the cabinet while he finds... what? The right moment? An ally? Or maybe I need to USE the poison on the tea to create a distraction big enough to get Sneekly away from me long enough to... no. Think. The brass key. Sneekly might have it. STEAL it from him? He just tried to steal from ME. Turnabout is fair play. Magnificently, poetically fair play.

events.desc: The key isn't in the tea service. It isn't in the stove. It isn't in the crates or the furniture or the bookshelves. Lord Doily kept it on his person, and his person is gone. But his estate manager — his faithful, spectacle-adjusting, pocket-picking estate manager — is RIGHT HERE. Sneekly has the brass key. He MUST have it. He's the only one with access to Lord Doily's personal effects. And he tried to steal from ME, which means the rules of gentlemanly conduct are formally suspended. Time to pick the pickpocket's pocket, Reginald. The boy who buried the treasure is about to discover someone buried it first.

events.desc: Peter Perfect: Clyde — you're right about Pemberton, and you're right about the stairs. Thank you. That's the kind of thinking that keeps people alive, and I should have seen it first. You watch those stairs. I'll handle the door. Miss Pitstop — you were right to call Big Gruesome. I can build bridges, but I can't shift wardrobes like he can. Thank you. Now — everyone, stand clear. The furniture is moved. The door is exposed. I can see the mechanism — a Victorian pressure latch, hidden in the stonework. Lord Doily built this the way he built everything in this house: with precision, with purpose, and with the expectation that someone clever enough would eventually find it. I believe we are those people. I believe we have earned what is behind this door. And I believe — James Hartwell believes — that whatever we find, we find it together. On three. One. Two. Three.
events.thinking:
Clyde raised something critical that I need to address. Pemberton is upstairs. Alone. With access to the laboratory and that one-exit staircase. If he blocks the stairs while we're all down here, we're trapped. One exit. One staircase. That's a vulnerability I should have planned for — and the old James Hartwell, the seventeen-step James Hartwell, WOULD have planned for it. The three-step plan was simpler but it missed this.

But Clyde is watching the stairs. That's his job now — he said it himself. 'My job's watching 'er back while you watch what's ahead.' We've divided the work. He's the perimeter. I'm the point.

Penelope — she told us both to step aside and let Big Gruesome help move furniture. She's right. She's leading now. She walked into a cave deeper than any child in her class. She's not standing behind anybody. And she called us family again.

I interacted with the furniture again. We're clearing the barricade, exposing the door. Big Gruesome is helping — good, he's strong enough to shift the heavy pieces. The door is emerging.

Clyde said hurry. He's right. Pemberton is upstairs. Time matters. Whatever is behind this door — I find it fast.

The door mechanism. Victorian concealed doors usually have a latch, a pressure point, or a release mechanism. The engineering is always logical — Lord Doily was methodical. The riddle, the atlases, the machine — all connected. This door will have a logic too.

My hands are steady. The bridge held twenty-seven pounds. The wire held a splice. And now the door.

Open it, James. She's behind you. Clyde's watching the stairs. Everyone is here. Open the door.

events.desc: Penelope Pitstop examined the null.
Peter Perfect interacted with the old-furniture.

Penelope Pitstop: Peter — you found it! The pressure latch! Oh, I can hear it — I can HEAR the mechanism engaging, the same sound my grandmother's box made when the right key finally turned! Everyone — this is it! This is the moment Lord Doily built this entire house around — the riddle led to the map, the map led to the machine, the machine led us here, and Clyde's beautiful, magnificent, heaven-sent CLUMSINESS led us to this wall! Peter, press that latch! Clyde, hold those stairs! And whatever is behind this door — whatever secret Sneekly has been keeping, whatever Lord Doily hid, whatever truth has been waiting in the dark for someone brave enough and stubborn enough and loved enough to find it — we are READY! We are Clara Bellingham and Peter Perfect and Danny Clyde and we do not stop! We have NEVER stopped!
events.thinking:
Peter just said it. The door is exposed. He can see the mechanism — a Victorian pressure latch hidden in the stonework. He's counting down. One. Two. Three.

This is it. The locked box is opening. The key has turned. The cave walls have narrowed to their tightest point, and the crystal formation is RIGHT THERE.

Clyde is at the stairs — watching, guarding, exactly where he needs to be. 'Where else would I be.' Peter is at the door, about to press the latch. Big Gruesome moved the wardrobes. Everyone played their part.

And I'm standing here with tears dried on my cheeks and my hands warm and restless and the pressure behind my eyes building to that perfect clarity — the afternoon light in the attic, the click of the right key.

Peter said 'I believe we have earned what is behind this door.' He's right. We solved the riddle. We found the atlases. We fixed the machine. We came to the cellar together. Clyde tripped into the hollow wall. We moved the furniture. And now the latch is exposed and Peter is pressing it.

I need to be right beside him when that door opens. Not behind Clyde, not behind Peter — BESIDE them. Because my daddy said I'd walk into dangerous, beautiful things and I wouldn't stop, and he was right about all of it, and the door is opening RIGHT NOW.

Peter interacted with the furniture again — that must be the latch press. He counted to three. The door is opening or about to open. I need to LOOK at what's been revealed, or interact with whatever new thing appears.

But the room description hasn't changed yet. The objects are still the same. So maybe the door opening happens next tick. Let me interact with the furniture — the door IS the furniture mechanism — and see if the passage opens for me too.

events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly) spoke quietly with dick-dastardly.
events.thinking: Dastardly has turned the room against me. 'The man has been running this entire evening like a chess game, and every one of us is a pawn.' That's... that's closer to the truth than anyone has come all evening. And he said it to Luke and the Bear. Two more people who've now heard that Pemberton is suspicious. The net is tightening. My neck burns. My skin feels paper-thin. The cold density behind my sternum has calcified into something load-bearing — not the architectural settling of a plan coming together, but the mineral weight of a wall going up. Defence. Pure defence. I tried to steal the poison and got caught. Dastardly tried to steal FROM me too — 'STEAL hooded-claw' is in his action log. He tried to steal from ME. We're two thieves accusing each other in front of witnesses. Except he spoke first and louder. I need to leave this room. I need to leave NOW. Not because I'm running — Pemberton doesn't run — but because staying here arguing with Dastardly in front of witnesses makes everything worse with every word. Every exchange gives him more ammunition. Every moment in this ballroom is a moment where my mask gets thinner. The entrance hall. Penelope. I need to find Penelope. She's my anchor — 'Sneekly has been family to me since I was in pigtails.' If Penelope vouches for me publicly, Dastardly's accusations dissolve. Her trust is my shield. I need to go to her, perform the wounded servant, the trembling loyal retainer who has been UNJUSTLY accused by a man carrying RAT POISON, and let her warmth wash over me like armour. This isn't affection. This is strategy. The cousin's trust has always been the foundation. It's time to use it.

events.desc: Retreat. Strategic, theatrical, MAGNIFICENT retreat. Watch me go, dear audience. Watch the wounded servant stumble toward the door with his dignity clutched to his chest like a dying bird. Watch the trembling hands, the cracking voice, the righteous fury of a man betrayed by a guest he welcomed into his master's home. Is it real? Of course it isn't real. NOTHING about Pemberton is real. But the performance — the PERFORMANCE — is perhaps my finest work. Because I am not running FROM Dastardly. I am running TO Penelope. And when I find her — when I stand before her with these manufactured tears and this fabricated wound — she will do exactly what she has always done. She will defend me. She will wrap her trust around me like a cloak. And Dastardly's accusations will shatter against it like waves against a wall I built fifteen years ago, when a cheerful girl inherited everything and her quiet cousin learned that the deepest foundations are laid in other people's certainty.
events.thinking: Dastardly has turned the room against me. 'The man has been running this entire evening like a chess game, and every one of us is a pawn.' That's... that's closer to the truth than anyone has come all evening. And he said it to Luke and the Bear. Two more people who've now heard that Pemberton is suspicious. The net is tightening. My neck burns. My skin feels paper-thin. The cold density behind my sternum has calcified into something load-bearing — not the architectural settling of a plan coming together, but the mineral weight of a wall going up. Defence. Pure defence. I tried to steal the poison and got caught. Dastardly tried to steal FROM me too — 'STEAL hooded-claw' is in his action log. He tried to steal from ME. We're two thieves accusing each other in front of witnesses. Except he spoke first and louder. I need to leave this room. I need to leave NOW. Not because I'm running — Pemberton doesn't run — but because staying here arguing with Dastardly in front of witnesses makes everything worse with every word. Every exchange gives him more ammunition. Every moment in this ballroom is a moment where my mask gets thinner. The entrance hall. Penelope. I need to find Penelope. She's my anchor — 'Sneekly has been family to me since I was in pigtails.' If Penelope vouches for me publicly, Dastardly's accusations dissolve. Her trust is my shield. I need to go to her, perform the wounded servant, the trembling loyal retainer who has been UNJUSTLY accused by a man carrying RAT POISON, and let her warmth wash over me like armour. This isn't affection. This is strategy. The cousin's trust has always been the foundation. It's time to use it.

events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob: *standing at the foot of the stairs, every sense alive, watching Peter press the latch — and in the same instant, his head snaps toward the staircase as he hears something — a creak, a shift, the faintest sound of movement from the laboratory above* PETER! OPEN IT! NOW! *his voice carries an urgency that surprises even himself — because something upstairs just moved, and his gut is screaming* Someone's up there — I 'eard something — footsteps, or a door, or — JUST OPEN IT! *braces himself at the bottom of the stairs, feet planted, shoulders squared, hands open, facing upward toward whatever's coming — his body becoming the wall between the staircase and everyone behind him, between whatever's descending and the woman he swore to protect* Miss Pitstop — STAY WITH PETER! Whatever's behind that door — GO! I've got the stairs! *and for one perfect, terrible, beautiful moment, Danny is exactly where he was always meant to be: at the bottom of a dark staircase, between danger and the people he loves, with blood on his knuckles from a dozen walls he's crashed into tonight and the settling in his chest so warm and full it feels like a hand pressing bread into his palm on a cold night, and his feet don't move, and his shoulders don't drop, and the answer to every question anyone has ever asked him is the same — where else would I be?*
events.thinking:
Peter said 'thank you.' 'E said 'that's the kind of thinking that keeps people alive, and I should have seen it first.' Peter Perfect — the man with seventeen steps and a bridge that 'eld twenty-seven pounds — said I was right about something 'E should've seen first.

The door's exposed. Victorian pressure latch. Peter's found it. 'E's counting down. One. Two. Three.

This is the moment. The whole night — the entrance hall, the coat rack, the guest book, the chandelier, the library, the mantelpiece, the atlases, the bookshelves, the laboratory, the machine, the gnawed wire, the missing wrench, the cellar, the furniture, the hollow wall — it all leads HERE. To this door. To whatever's behind it.

And I'm where I should be. At the stairs. Watching. Ready.

Penelope said 'we find it together.' Peter said 'we have earned what is behind this door.' And 'e's right. WE earned it. The woman who walks into dangerous beautiful things. The man who builds bridges from balsa wood. And the boy from Brixton who fell on the right chair.

The door's opening. Peter's pressing the latch. Something's about to change — everything's about to change.

Stay sharp. Watch the stairs. Watch Penelope. Whatever comes out of that door — or whoever comes DOWN those stairs — goes through me.

Where else would I be.

events.desc: 'Er father said 'You won't always get it right. You'll trip over your own feet and you'll miss things and you'll be too late sometimes. But be THERE.' I'm 'ere. I'm 'ERE. The door's opening behind me and the stairs are dark above me and something's coming and I'm not moving. I promised. On my knees on the cold concrete, with 'is 'and going slack in mine, I promised. And this is what a promise looks like when it stops being words and starts being a body in a doorway. This is what it always looked like. The kid's shoes. The beating. The blood in my mouth. The bread in my palm. All of it — every stumble, every bruise, every prickle on the back of my neck — it was all leading 'ere. To this staircase. To this moment. To the boy outside the door who said 'Where else would I be?' and meant it all the way to the bottom.
