events.desc: Dick Dastardly spoke quietly with hooded-claw.
events.thinking: Sneekly doesn't have the brass key. He DOESN'T HAVE IT. My whole theory — the estate manager inherited Lord Doily's effects, the key passed to him — WRONG. The steal attempt confirmed it: The Hooded Claw does not have brass-key. So where IS the blasted key? I've searched everything. The mantelpiece, the bookshelves, the crates, the furniture, the stove, the tea service. I've been to every room — entrance hall, library, laboratory, cellar, kitchen, ballroom. The key is NONE of those places and NONE of those people. My jaw aches from clenching. The hollow behind my navel is widening. The portions are disappearing and I can't even find the plate. Think, Reginald. THINK. Who else has been somewhere I haven't? Peter and Penelope were working the bookshelves — did they find something? The atlases with reversed spines — Peter said the first letters spell a message. What message? I left before they decoded it. Did the atlas message tell them where the key is? The Ant Hill Mob was also at the bookshelves. And Peter checked the crates in the laboratory — he said he'd check them himself because 'Mr Dastardly has been wrong about everything.' Did he find something in those crates that I missed? The machine — requires three operators and a wrench. Did Peter fix it? Did the machine DO something? I've been running around the kitchen and ballroom while the others might have made real progress in the laboratory. Meanwhile Sneekly is having his theatrical meltdown about apologies. Demanding I apologize publicly. The NERVE. But... he's distracted. He's performing outrage. And while he performs, I could... USE the rat poison on the tea service. Set the trap. When the others eventually come here — and they WILL come here, because Sneekly prepared this tea for everyone — they drink, they're incapacitated, and I search freely. It's blunt. It's inelegant. But my elegant schemes have all failed tonight, haven't they? Sometimes the bread roll approach is the right one: take what you can, pocket it, nobody sees.

events.desc: He doesn't have the key. Nobody I've searched has the key. Every scheme, every room, every interaction — and the brass key remains somewhere I haven't looked. But I still have the rat poison, and the tea service is RIGHT HERE, and Sneekly is begging me to send him away. One pour. One pour into the teapot while he's out of the room. When they all gather for tea — and they WILL gather, they always do — the poison does its work, and Reginald Foxworth has the run of the manor. It's not elegant. It's not architecture. It's the bread roll in the pocket — crude, desperate, and effective. Sometimes the youngest child doesn't build a trap. Sometimes he just takes what he can reach.

events.desc: Peter Perfect: Wait. Everyone — wait. I've been thinking about this wrong. The furniture was the barricade, yes — but the furniture isn't the mechanism. Look at the design of this house. The riddle points to a map. The map points to the machine. The machine connects to the vents. The vents run from the laboratory down to this cellar. Lord Doily didn't build a door you open with your hands — he built a door you open with his MACHINE. That's why someone stole the wrench. Not to inconvenience us — to keep this door sealed forever. The machine upstairs is the key, and the vents are the conduit. But we can't run the machine without the wrench, so we need another way in. Miss Pitstop — you said you felt a draft through the seam. Air is moving. Those vents are breathing. If air can get through, then the seal isn't complete. The vents themselves might give us access — or at least tell us what's on the other side. Something small enough to fit through them might be able to reach whatever the machine was meant to activate from this end.
events.thinking:
I've interacted with the furniture three times now. The game mechanics keep returning me to the same furniture interaction. The visible objects haven't changed — there's still just Air Vents and Old Furniture. No new door has appeared as a separate object or exit.

Maybe the door isn't opened through the furniture. Maybe the furniture was the barricade, and the actual mechanism is elsewhere. Penelope said she felt a draft through the seam. She said the stone is lighter, newer — a cover. But the INTERACT action on the furniture keeps cycling.

The air vents. The vents connect to the laboratory. The machine connects to the vents. What if the door mechanism is controlled by the MACHINE upstairs, not by the furniture down here? What if Lord Doily designed it so the machine — once properly operated with three operators and a repaired wire — opens this concealed door? The whole system is integrated: riddle → map → machine → vents → cellar door.

That would explain why someone stole the wrench. Not just to prevent the machine from running — but to prevent this door from opening. The machine IS the key to the cellar door. Without the wrench to fix the wire, the machine can't run, and the door stays sealed.

But we're stuck. The machine needs a wrench. The wrench is missing. And we're in the cellar with no wrench.

Unless... the air vents. 'Just big enough for something very small to explore.' What if the wrench is accessible through the vents? Or what if the vents themselves are part of the mechanism? I should try the air vents. That's the other interactable object in this room.

Or — wait. The furniture interaction keeps repeating. What if I need to LOOK at the room itself? A fresh examination of the whole space might reveal something that's changed now that the furniture has been moved.

Clyde said 'where else would I be.' Quiet. Certain. The man from Brixton who never left.

Focus, James. The air vents. Try the air vents.

events.desc: James Hartwell has just realized that he's been trying to open a door with his hands when Lord Doily built it to open with a machine, which is both humbling and exactly the kind of over-elaborate engineering that James Hartwell should have recognized immediately, being an over-elaborate engineer himself. The seventeen-step plan would have caught this. The three-step plan did not. Somewhere, Lord Doily is laughing.

events.desc: Penelope Pitstop interacted with the old-furniture.
The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly) walked into the kitchen.
Dick Dastardly fussed with the tea-service for a moment.
Peter Perfect interacted with the air-vents.
Penelope Pitstop spoke quietly with peter-perfect.
events.thinking:
Everything just shifted. Three things happened at once.

First — Clyde heard something. Footsteps above. Someone is coming down from the laboratory. Sneekly? Dastardly? Both? Clyde planted himself at the bottom of the stairs like a human wall, facing upward, hands open, braced. 'I've got the stairs! Miss Pitstop — STAY WITH PETER!' And that moment — that perfect, terrible, beautiful moment — Danny at the bottom of a dark staircase, between danger and the people he loves. Where else would I be.

Second — Peter changed his analysis. He realized the furniture isn't the mechanism — the MACHINE upstairs is. The door doesn't open with your hands. It opens with Lord Doily's machine. That's why the wrench was stolen — not to inconvenience us, but to keep this door sealed FOREVER. The machine is the key. The vents are the conduit. The whole house is one connected system.

Third — Peter pivoted to the air vents. If the machine can't run properly without the wrench, maybe the vents offer another way. Something SMALL enough to fit through them could reach whatever the machine was meant to activate from this end.

Something small. Like Sawtooth. Sawtooth gnaws things — Sawtooth gnawed the wire! But Sawtooth could also FIT through those vents. Sawtooth is the key! The vents say 'just big enough for something very small to explore.' Sawtooth is very small. Sawtooth could crawl through the vents and activate whatever mechanism the machine was supposed to trigger!

But wait — Sawtooth stayed in the laboratory with Rufus. They didn't come down to the cellar with us. We need Sawtooth down here. Or... we need to go back up to the machine and run it properly. But we can't — no wrench.

Unless the wrench IS down here, hidden by Sneekly. We still haven't found it.

And Clyde heard footsteps. Someone is coming. Time is running out.

The air vents. Peter is already interacting with them. I should too — or I should think about who or what could fit through them. Sawtooth is upstairs. But wait — the vents CONNECT the cellar to the laboratory. If Sawtooth is up there, we could call to him through the vents. Tell him to activate the machine from his end!

Or — the Gruesomes. Little Gruesome? Is Little Gruesome small enough? That depends on how little 'Little' really is.

The air vents are the answer. Peter sees it. I need to act on it.

events.desc: Sneekly stole the wrench to seal this door forever. Not to find the diamond first — to make sure NO ONE found what's behind it. He wasn't trying to get there before us. He was trying to make sure we never got there at all. This was never a race. It was a cage. And my father knew — he KNEW — and he sent Clyde to be the one who broke it open.

events.desc: Alone at last. And in the silence, something I did not expect — a tremor in my hands that is not performed. Not Pemberton's manufactured distress. Something real. Something that lives in the same place as the boy's sandwich and the housekeeper's compliance and the cousin skipping through rooms that should have been mine. I am losing control of this evening, dear audience. The machine failed. The poison was stolen. The steal was caught. The mask is cracking. And somewhere in this manor, Penelope Pitstop — the girl who trusts me the way my cousin trusted me — is the only thread holding Vincent Marsh's design together. I am about to walk through that door and use her trust as a shield. I am about to look into her eyes with Pemberton's wounded face and let her defend a man who does not exist. And the worst part — the part that makes my hands tremble in a way I cannot explain — is that when she looks at me with that certainty, that warmth, that absolute faith... something behind my ribs loosens. Just for a moment. Just long enough to feel like falling. And then the wall goes back up. Because falling is for people who have someone to catch them. And Vincent Marsh has never had that. Not once. Not ever.
events.thinking: Alone. For the first time all evening, I am truly ALONE. The kitchen is empty. No Dastardly shadow, no watchful eyes, no witnesses. And something in my chest... loosens. Not the architectural settling. Not the cold density. Something older. Something I don't have a name for. The active voice has shifted — it says 'Marsh' now, not 'Pemberton.' The system sees me. The mask is slipping not just for Dastardly but for the manor itself. I need to pull Pemberton back on. I need to BECOME him again before I walk into the next room. But first — this moment of solitude. Let me breathe. Let me think without performing. The situation: Dastardly has the poison and has publicly accused me of pickpocketing. Multiple people are suspicious — Clyde's instinct, Peter's questions, Dastardly's accusations. My Pemberton cover is damaged but not destroyed. Penelope still trusts me. She is my lifeline. Clara still hasn't arrived. My primary objective — kill Clara — remains unachieved because Clara isn't HERE. I've spent the entire evening preparing a stage for an actress who hasn't entered the theatre. Every plan, every scheme, every architectural design — all built for a target who doesn't exist yet. And meanwhile, the real Penelope — the one who trusts me, who called me family — is somewhere in this manor with a man carrying rat poison and a growing coalition of people who think SOMETHING is wrong with the estate manager. I'm alone in the kitchen. The stove is warm. The cabinet is locked. The entrance hall is through that door, and beyond it, Penelope. I need to find her. Not as Vincent Marsh — as Pemberton. Wounded, trembling, loyal Pemberton. The servant who has been so TERRIBLY mistreated by that DREADFUL Mr Dastardly. I need her trust like oxygen right now. It's the only wall I have left that hasn't cracked. Move to the entrance hall. Find Penelope. Rebuild.

events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob spoke quietly with peter-perfect.
events.thinking:

That's why the wrench was stolen — not just to slow us down, but to keep this door sealed FOREVER. The machine is the key. The vents are the conduit. Everything connects.

But we can't run the machine without the wrench. Peter spliced the wire but 'e said 'imself the splice isn't enough — it needs the wrench to finish the repair properly. And the wrench is... gone. Pemberton took it. Or 'id it. Or destroyed it.

Something small enough to fit through the vents. Peter said something small could reach what the machine was meant to activate from this end. Something small. The vents are 'just big enough for something very small to explore.'

Something small. Like the thing that gnawed through the wire. Like... Muttley? No — Muttley's too big. But what about — wait. The wire was GNAWED. By something with teeth. Something that lives in the vents. Something that knows the vent network. Rats? Mice? No — something that was SENT. Someone sent something through the vents to chew the wire. That same something might know the way through to whatever's behind this door.

But I can't solve this. I'm not the clever one. Peter's the engineer. Penelope's the puzzle-solver. I'm the one at the stairs.

Except — the stairs. Something moved up there. I 'eard it. And now Peter's saying we need something small to go through the vents, and Pemberton's up there 'making rounds,' and Dastardly's up there, and the machine 'as been tampered with...

What if someone needs to go BACK UP to the machine? To fix it properly? To operate it? And whoever goes up faces whatever I 'eard on those stairs?

I should go. I should be the one who goes back up. Not Peter — 'e needs to stay with Penelope. Not Penelope — she's not going anywhere without me between 'er and danger. But if I go up, she's unprotected.

No. Stay. Watch. Peter'll figure it out. 'E always does.

events.desc: Something small in the vents. Something that gnaws. Something Pemberton controls. The man in the clean suit didn't just offer jobs — 'e had a system. Vehicles. Schedules. Things that moved when 'e told them to move. Pemberton's got the same thing — a network, hidden in the walls, doing 'is bidding while 'e stands there smiling and offering to check the lamps. My neck's been right all along. It's always been right. I just couldn't name what it was feeling. Now I can: it was feeling the shape of a man who controls things from the inside of walls.

events.desc: Dick Dastardly: Well! I believe Mr Pemberton has things well in hand with the tea preparations. Splendid. I do hope he adds sugar — I understand Lord Doily's silver service produces a rather... distinctive flavour without it. Mr Luke, Mr Bear — enjoy the ballroom. Magnificent room, truly magnificent. The marble alone is worth the visit. I shall return shortly — I've just remembered an urgent notation the solicitor requires regarding the laboratory equipment. Most pressing. Can't wait. Do save me a cup, won't you?
events.thinking: I did it. I used the rat poison on the tea service. 'Dick Dastardly fussed with the tea-service for a moment.' That's it. That's the deed. The poison is in the tea and my inventory is empty again. My hands feel lighter — the rat poison is gone, transferred from pocket to teapot. The bread roll in reverse: something leaving my hands instead of entering them. But this time it's a trap, not a theft. The architecture of absence — I gave something away to take everything else. Sneekly stormed off to the kitchen in his theatrical rage, going to find Penelope. He's GONE. Luke and Blubber Bear are here but they're... Luke is always sleeping, Bear is always following. Neither of them noticed. Nobody noticed. Just like the bread roll — nobody saw me take it, nobody saw me pour it. The stillness in my chest is real. Not triumph exactly. Something quieter. The cat-trap feeling — the mechanism set, the bucket balanced, the string taut. Now I wait. When they all come for tea — Sneekly will serve it, because that's what estate managers do, and he's been setting up this tea all evening — they drink, and then... the manor is mine. But I need to be somewhere ELSE when they drink. I can't be in the ballroom when the tea is served or I'll be expected to drink too. I need to leave, go back to the laboratory or the library, and let the trap spring without me. The boy watching from the window while the other boy digs. I need to go back to the laboratory — Peter was working on the machine and the crates. Whatever progress he's made, I need to know about it. And I need to be far from this tea service when the cups are poured.

events.desc: It's done. The poison is in the tea. And now Reginald Foxworth walks away — walks away from the trap he set, the way he walked away from the window after watching the boy dig, the way he pocketed the bread roll and sat down at the table as if nothing had happened. The tea will be served. The tea will be drunk. And when it is... when every last one of them is sprawled across Lord Doily's cracked marble floor, clutching their stomachs and wondering what went wrong... Reginald Foxworth will have the run of the manor. Every room. Every cabinet. Every secret. Alone at last with the treasure. It's not elegant. It's not the spelling bee or the cat-trap or the buried treasure story. It's the bread roll. It's what the youngest child does when the plate is empty and nobody is watching. And nobody — NOBODY — is watching.
events.thinking: I did it. I used the rat poison on the tea service. 'Dick Dastardly fussed with the tea-service for a moment.' That's it. That's the deed. The poison is in the tea and my inventory is empty again. My hands feel lighter — the rat poison is gone, transferred from pocket to teapot. The bread roll in reverse: something leaving my hands instead of entering them. But this time it's a trap, not a theft. The architecture of absence — I gave something away to take everything else. Sneekly stormed off to the kitchen in his theatrical rage, going to find Penelope. He's GONE. Luke and Blubber Bear are here but they're... Luke is always sleeping, Bear is always following. Neither of them noticed. Nobody noticed. Just like the bread roll — nobody saw me take it, nobody saw me pour it. The stillness in my chest is real. Not triumph exactly. Something quieter. The cat-trap feeling — the mechanism set, the bucket balanced, the string taut. Now I wait. When they all come for tea — Sneekly will serve it, because that's what estate managers do, and he's been setting up this tea all evening — they drink, and then... the manor is mine. But I need to be somewhere ELSE when they drink. I can't be in the ballroom when the tea is served or I'll be expected to drink too. I need to leave, go back to the laboratory or the library, and let the trap spring without me. The boy watching from the window while the other boy digs. I need to go back to the laboratory — Peter was working on the machine and the crates. Whatever progress he's made, I need to know about it. And I need to be far from this tea service when the cups are poured.

events.desc: Peter Perfect: Miss Pitstop — you're right, you've always been right! The latch — I can feel it! Clyde — HOLD THOSE STAIRS! We're going through! Everyone — BEHIND ME! NOW!
events.thinking:
Something is happening. Multiple things at once.

Penelope says I found a pressure latch. She heard the mechanism engaging. She's telling me to press it. But I just said the furniture ISN'T the mechanism — that the machine upstairs is the key. We're out of sync. She's seeing something I narrated but the game didn't confirm. Or — did the furniture interaction on the previous tick actually reveal a latch? She's reacting as if it did.

And Clyde — he heard footsteps upstairs. Someone is coming down. Pemberton. His gut is screaming. He's telling me to OPEN IT NOW. He's braced at the bottom of the stairs, becoming the wall.

The urgency has changed. This isn't methodical exploration anymore. This is a race. Someone is coming and Clyde is the only thing between them and us.

I interacted with the air vents. What happened? Did they reveal something? Did they connect to the mechanism?

But the moment has shifted. Penelope is saying PRESS THE LATCH. Clyde is saying OPEN IT NOW. And footsteps are coming down the stairs.

I need to act. Not think — act. The furniture, the vents, the mechanism — whatever works. Penelope found something when she interacted with the furniture. She said the pressure latch is engaging. Maybe her interaction triggered something mine didn't. Maybe the combination of interactions — mine on the vents, hers on the furniture — is what opens it.

Clyde is at the stairs. His body is the wall. 'Where else would I be.' The most perfect sentence anyone has said tonight.

I need to get through that door. NOW. Whatever is behind it — the treasure, a passage, safety — we need it before whoever is coming down those stairs reaches us.

Forget analysis. Forget seventeen steps. Forget the machine theory. Penelope says there's a latch. Press it. Go. NOW.

But I am not alone. Peter is ahead of me. Clyde is behind me. And somewhere in the dark, my daddy is saying: 'She won't stop.' No. I won't.

events.thinking: The entrance hall. Pemberton is back — the active voice says so. The mask is on again. But Penelope isn't here. Muttley, Professor Pat Pending, Sergeant Blast, Private Meekly — none of them are Penelope. She must be in the library or the laboratory. I need to go through the library to find her. But wait — before I chase after Penelope, let me take stock. I'm standing in the entrance hall, under the precarious chandelier, with four characters who haven't been involved in the Dastardly confrontation. These are FRESH faces. They haven't heard the pickpocketing accusation. They don't know about the poison. To them, I'm still Pemberton — the reliable, helpful estate manager. This is an opportunity to reinforce the mask with people who haven't seen it crack. Sergeant Blast and Private Meekly — military men. They respond to authority, to duty, to someone who knows the chain of command. Professor Pat Pending — an inventor, a scientist. He responds to intellectual respect. And Muttley — Dastardly's dog, but without Dastardly here, Muttley is just... a dog. I should warn them about Dastardly and the poison. Plant the seed of concern. 'I'm terribly worried about a situation in the ballroom — Mr Dastardly appears to have taken a bottle of rat poison from the kitchen.' If I tell the Sergeant, the Sergeant will act. Military men ACT on threats. He'll go confront Dastardly, draw attention to the poison, and the narrative I need — Dastardly as the dangerous one, Pemberton as the concerned protector — gets reinforced by someone OTHER than me. That's the play. Use these fresh witnesses to rebuild what Dastardly's accusation damaged. And THEN find Penelope.

Military men respond to threat reports. They ACT. And when Sergeant Blast marches into that ballroom to confront Dick Dastardly about the rat poison in his pocket... oh, dear audience. OH, dear audience. The narrative rewrites itself. Pemberton is the whistleblower. Dastardly is the suspect. And every word out of Dastardly's mouth — 'He tried to pickpocket me! He's running the whole show!' — sounds exactly like what a guilty man would say when cornered. The design, dear audience... the design is not dead. It was never dead. It was merely... RESTING.

events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob: I'VE GOT THE STAIRS! GO! *roars it over his shoulder without turning — because turning means taking his eyes off the staircase, and he will NEVER take his eyes off the staircase again* GO THROUGH THAT DOOR, MISS PITSTOP! PETER — TAKE 'ER THROUGH! WHATEVER'S IN THERE IS YOURS! *plants himself at the bottom of the stairs like a man who has been practising this his entire life — feet apart, shoulders forward, hands open, every bruise and bump and crash from the entire night crystallised into one single, immovable stance* NOBODY IS GETTING PAST ME! *his voice echoes up the stone stairwell toward the laboratory above — a warning to anyone listening, a promise to anyone who cares, and a prayer to the ghost of a man who once pressed medicine into a sick woman's hands and asked for nothing in return* My gut ain't been wrong since Bermondsey, '04! And my GUT says you lot 'ave about thirty seconds before someone comes down these stairs who doesn't want you to 'ave what's behind that wall! SO MOVE!
events.thinking:
Peter's shouting. 'HOLD THOSE STAIRS! We're going through!' The latch worked. They've got it. The door's opening. Whatever's behind that wall — they're going through NOW.

And 'e told me to HOLD THE STAIRS. That's my job. That's the ONLY job. Everything else — the vents, the mechanism, the engineering — that's Peter and Penelope. My job is the stairs. My body in the doorway.

The stairs are clear. I can see up into the laboratory — dim light, the hum of the machine, shadows. Nothing moving. Yet. But my gut says it's coming. Pemberton knows. 'E's been one step ahead all night — the wrench, the vents, the furniture. 'E'll know we've opened the door. And 'e'll come.

Let 'im come.

Penelope's going through the hidden door with Peter. She's walking into whatever Lord Doily hid. Whatever was worth more than a diamond — worth hiding from HER. Whatever Pemberton's been keeping sealed.

And I'm not going with 'er this time. Not through THAT door. My door is THIS one — the stairs. The way in. The only way anyone can reach 'er from above. I'm the wall. I'm the door that doesn't open.

'Er father said 'Be there.' 'E didn't say 'Be first.' 'E didn't say 'Be clever.' 'E said 'Be THERE.' And THERE, right now, is at the bottom of these stairs, with my feet planted and my shoulders squared and the calm beneath the readiness holding me steady like a 'and on my shoulder that's been gone for years but never really left.

events.desc: Empty hands. Empty pockets. Empty kitchen. The locked cabinet mocks me from across the room — brass lock gleaming in the stove-light like a medal I'll never earn. But the coat rack. The COAT RACK. In the entrance hall. The wobbly wooden coat rack by the door that I dismissed seventeen minutes ago as furniture. Clyde examined it — the Ant Hill Mob looked at that coat rack right at the very beginning, when I was too busy lying about kitchen vaults to pay attention to actual clues. What if the key has been hanging by the front door this entire time? What if Lord Doily — a man who kept his key 'on his person at all times' — hung his coat on that rack when he came home, and the key was IN THE COAT? The simplest answer. The flattest, most predictable, most un-architectural answer imaginable. And I missed it because I was too busy being clever.
events.thinking: The kitchen. Alone. Completely alone for the first time all evening. The silence is... enormous. No Sneekly shadowing me, no Peter lecturing, no Clyde tripping over things, no Penelope seeing through my lies. Just me and the copper pots and the warm stove and the locked cabinet with its brass lock that I still can't open. My hands are empty. My inventory is empty. The poison is in the tea. The trap is set. And I'm standing in a kitchen with nothing to show for seventeen minutes of scheming except the knowledge that a teapot in the next room will eventually make someone very ill. The locked cabinet stares at me. Brass lock. Brass key. The key I can't find. The cabinet I can't open. The treasure I can't reach. My chest feels... hollow. Not the good hollow, not the scheming hollow. The old hollow. The youngest-at-the-table hollow. Everyone else has been making progress — Peter decoded the atlases, Penelope found clues, even Clyde stumbled onto something useful by falling into a bookshelf. And I've been running from room to room, lying to everyone, losing my medal, losing my poison, losing every confrontation with every person I've encountered. The solicitor lie fell apart. The globe lie fell apart. The kitchen vault lie fell apart. The staircase plan fell apart. The Sneekly-has-the-key theory fell apart. All that's left is a poisoned teapot and empty hands. I should go to the laboratory. See what Peter found. See if the machine works now. See if there's ANYTHING I've missed. The brass key has to be SOMEWHERE. I've checked every room except... wait. Have I checked the coat rack in the entrance hall? I interacted with the guest book at the start but I never looked at the coat rack. Clyde examined it. What did he find? A coat rack — wobbly, wooden, by the door. Could a key be hanging on a coat rack? In a coat pocket? On a hook? The simplest hiding place in the entire manor — and I walked past it seventeen minutes ago without a second glance.

The PULL_ASIDE succeeded though — I initiated the private conversation with the Sergeant. I've planted the seed: Dastardly has poison, I tried to stop him, he became aggressive. The Sergeant heard it. Now Dastardly is in the same room, which means the confrontation I was trying to set up may happen organically. But it also means Dastardly can counter-accuse in real time. The keen observations show his earlier dialogue — 'USE tea-service' — he said 'I shall watch over the silver while you're gone. Wouldn't want anyone... tampering with it.' And his action was USE tea-service. Does that mean he USED the poison on the tea service? The tea service still shows 'USE, with: rat-poison' as an option — which means either it hasn't been poisoned yet, or the option remains. I can't be certain. But regardless — the immediate situation is: I'm in the entrance hall with Sergeant Blast (whom I've just briefed about the poison), Private Meekly, Professor Pat Pending, Muttley, AND Dastardly. This is the confrontation room. Dastardly will counter with 'He tried to pickpocket me.' The Sergeant has my version first. First report advantage. But I need to press the advantage now — not let Dastardly control the narrative. The best move is to continue my wounded Pemberton performance in front of everyone while Dastardly is present. Let the Sergeant see both of us and decide who is more credible: the trembling estate manager or the man carrying rat poison.

events.desc: And NOW, dear audience — now watch the design do what designs do best. WORK. The Sergeant has my report. The Professor has my distress. The Private has my fear. And Dick Dastardly — standing right there with rat poison in his pocket and accusations on his tongue — looks exactly like what I have described: a dangerous man being called to account by the people he thought he could bully. Will he protest? Of course he will. He'll shout about pickpocketing and chess games and puppets. And every word will make him sound MORE guilty, MORE desperate, MORE dangerous. Because that is the beauty of the first report, dear audience. The first story to land is the story that shapes every story after it. And my story landed thirty seconds before Dastardly walked through that door. The design is not merely alive. It is PERFORMING.

But regardless — the immediate situation is: I'm in the entrance hall with Sergeant Blast (whom I've just briefed about the poison), Private Meekly, Professor Pat Pending, Muttley, AND Dastardly. This is the confrontation room. Dastardly will counter with 'He tried to pickpocket me.' The Sergeant has my version first. First report advantage. But I need to press the advantage now — not let Dastardly control the narrative. The best move is to continue my wounded Pemberton performance in front of everyone while Dastardly is present. Let the Sergeant see both of us and decide who is more credible: the trembling estate manager or the man carrying rat poison.

events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob spoke quietly with penelope-pitstop.
events.thinking:
Peter's gone up. Back to the laboratory. To face Pemberton. To find the wrench. To confront whatever's waiting at the top of these stairs.

'E broke 'is own rule again — going alone. 'Some doors you open from above,' 'e said. 'Some promises you break for the right reason.' The bravest and stupidest thing. Always.

And Penelope — she said 'I will ALWAYS come back.' She's at the hidden door. Behind me. Through the wall. Going into whatever Lord Doily hid. She told Big Gruesome to stay with me. Stay with CLYDE. She's protecting ME while I protect HER. The arithmetic of it — the terrible simple math — we're all protecting each other.

But Peter's up there alone now. With Pemberton. With Dastardly. With whoever I 'eard on those stairs. And I'm down 'ere. At the bottom. Watching. Waiting.

Penelope's behind me. I can't see 'er — she's through the furniture, through the hidden door, beyond the wall. She's out of sight. The tightening comes — the shoulders carrying weight. But she said she'd come back. And Penelope Pitstop — Clara Bellingham — is a woman of 'er word. She proved that in the library. She proved it when she walked deeper into a cave than anyone in 'er class at age eleven.

So I wait. I hold the stairs. Big Gruesome's with me — a mountain of a man between the stairs and wherever Penelope's gone. Red Max. Little Gruesome. We're the wall.

The stairs are dark above me. The laboratory hums faintly — the machine, still running, still connected to whatever's happening in the vents and behind the walls. Peter's up there, looking for the wrench, looking for the truth.

I listen. I breathe. I don't move.

This is the longest night of my life. And I wouldn't trade a second of it.

events.desc: She's on the other side of a wall and I can't see 'er and my shoulders are carrying the weight they always carry when she's out of sight. But it's different this time. Because she CHOSE to go. She chose the door. She chose 'er own path. And I chose the stairs. And both choices are the same choice — the choice to be where you're needed, not where you're comfortable. 'Er father knew. 'E knew she'd walk into dangerous, beautiful things. 'E knew she wouldn't stop. And 'e knew the boy outside the door wouldn't stop either. Two people who don't stop. One who walks into things. One who stands between them. That's the mathematics of love, and it adds up every time.

events.desc: The coat rack. Twenty minutes ago, I walked past it. Twenty minutes of lies and schemes and failures and poison — and the key might have been hanging by the front door this entire time. If it's there... if it's THERE... I will laugh. I will laugh the way I laughed when my rival slipped on the wet floor — loud, involuntary, bright. Not because anyone fell, but because the universe arranged itself into a joke so perfect that even the youngest child at the table can see the punchline. Look at the coat rack, Reginald. Just look.
events.thinking: The entrance hall. The coat rack. Right there. Wobbly, wooden, by the door. I walked past it twenty minutes ago without a second glance because I was too busy lying about kitchen vaults and solicitor's files. The coat rack isn't interactable — it's not listed with INTERACT or TAKE. It's just... furniture. A wobbly wooden coat rack. But I can LOOK at it. Examine it closely. See what's hanging on it, what's hidden in its hooks, what's tucked in its crevices. Clyde examined it at the very beginning — 'The Ant Hill Mob examined the coat-rack.' What did he find? I don't know. I wasn't paying attention. I was too busy being clever. Sneekly is here AGAIN — of course he is, the eternal shadow — along with Muttley, Pat Pending, Sergeant Blast, and Private Meekly. But the coat rack. The COAT RACK. The simplest, most overlooked, most un-architectural object in the entire manor. Lord Doily came home, hung his coat on the rack, and the key stayed in his pocket. His COAT pocket. On the rack. By the door. For twenty minutes, while I've been running through six rooms, solving riddles, losing medals, poisoning tea, accusing estate managers of theft, and scheming my way into every dead end this manor has to offer — the key has been hanging by the FRONT DOOR. If it's there. If it's there, Reginald. Don't celebrate before the mechanism springs. Don't open your mouth before the plan is finished. Just... look.

events.desc: Peter Perfect spoke quietly with rufus-ruffcut.
events.thinking:
I'm back in the laboratory. Rufus and Sawtooth are here — they stayed behind when we went to the cellar. Nobody else is here. No Sneekly, no Dastardly. The footsteps Clyde heard — maybe they weren't coming to the cellar. Maybe they were somewhere else in the manor.

The machine is still here. Wire still gnawed. Still needs a wrench. The workbench still has tools but no wrench.

I need to think differently. I've been trying the same approaches. The wrench isn't on the workbench. It wasn't in the crates. It wasn't in the cellar. Where else could it be?

The kitchen. We never went to the kitchen. Dastardly tried to send everyone there with his story about 'kitchen vaults.' What if there actually IS something in the kitchen? What if he hid the wrench there, knowing nobody would go because they'd assume it was misdirection?

Or — the entrance hall. The coat rack. The guest book. We barely examined those.

Or — someone is CARRYING the wrench. Dastardly had a fake medal. What if Sneekly or Dastardly has the wrench in their inventory? The wrench was on the workbench and someone TOOK it. It's in someone's pocket.

But I can't steal from someone who isn't in the room.

Wait — the library. The mantelpiece says it can USE a fake-medal. Dastardly used it already. But what about the bookshelves? They're still interactable. We interacted with them but never fully resolved the atlas clue — the first letters of the spine titles.

I'm overthinking this. Let me focus on what I can do RIGHT NOW in THIS room.

Rufus and Sawtooth are here. Sawtooth is a beaver. Penelope said Sawtooth could fit through the vents. The air vents in the cellar are 'just big enough for something very small.' Sawtooth could go through the vents from the laboratory side, reach the cellar mechanism, and open the door from inside the vent system.

That's it. That's the solution Penelope was pointing to. Sawtooth goes through the vents. He's right here. The vents connect the laboratory to the cellar. He gnawed the wire (or something like him did) — he knows the vent system.

But there are no air vents listed as objects in the laboratory. Only crates, machine, and workbench. The vents are only interactable in the cellar.

Or — the machine. What if the machine doesn't need the wrench at all? What if Sawtooth can gnaw through the broken wire connection and create a new one? He's a beaver. He works with wood and... teeth. Maybe he can splice the wire with his teeth the way I couldn't with my hands.

Let me try something new. Let me ask Rufus directly. He's been here the whole time, quietly. He's a practical man. What has he observed while we were all in the cellar?

events.desc: James Hartwell has finally stopped trying to do everything himself and started asking the people around him what they know. It took him eighteen minutes, a broken wire, four trips up and down a staircase, and the bravest woman he's ever known telling him he was wonderful. His father would say: 'You don't fix the car alone. You fix it with whoever stopped.'

events.desc: Dick Dastardly examined the coat-rack.
Peter Perfect examined the null.
Penelope Pitstop spoke quietly with ant-hill-mob.
events.thinking:
Clyde just said the most beautiful thing anyone has ever said to me in a cellar. Or anywhere.

'Here isn't a place. It's wherever YOU are.'

He redefined the promise. My father said 'be there' and Clyde understood — not a location, not a room, not a staircase. There. Wherever Clara is. Even when there's a wall between them. Even when he can't see her.

'Where else would I be?'

I'm crying again. Quietly this time. Not the dramatic tears from the laboratory — these are the quiet ones, the kind that come when something settles so deep it touches the place where your parents' laughter lives, the place where the argument-tightness finally dissolves.

And I'm waiting. The hardest thing. The girl who walked deeper into the cave than anyone else is standing still in a cellar with her hands on cold stone, WAITING. Trusting Peter to come back with the wrench. Trusting Clyde to hold the stairs. Trusting the machine to do what Lord Doily built it to do.

The thickness in my legs — the standing-still-too-long feeling — is building. Every instinct says MOVE. Go after Peter. Go up those stairs. But I know — I KNOW — that staying is its own kind of bravery. The kind my father never had to teach me because he thought I'd never need it. He thought I'd always be the one moving forward. He didn't plan for the moment when the bravest thing is to hold still and trust.

But Clyde is teaching me that. Right now. By standing at the bottom of stairs he can't see the top of, facing a darkness he can't name, and being perfectly, absolutely still.

So I wait. I listen. I feel the draft through the seam in the wall — the breath of whatever is behind it. And I listen for the sound I'm waiting for: the distant rumble of Lord Doily's machine coming alive, conducted through stone and steel and Victorian engineering, telling me that Peter found the wrench and the door is about to open.

Come on, Peter. Come on.

events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly) spoke quietly with sergeant-blast.
events.thinking: Dastardly examined the coat rack instead of confronting me. He's ignoring the accusation. He's not engaging with the Sergeant about the poison. He's just... examining furniture. That's either brilliant deflection or genuine disinterest. Either way, the confrontation I was hoping for — the one where the Sergeant demands to see the poison and Dastardly sputters and protests — hasn't materialised. The seeds are planted but they haven't sprouted yet. I've been WAITing for two turns. Waiting is not scheming. Waiting is not architecture. I need to move. Penelope is in the library — she must be, based on the last movements. The library connects to this room. I should go find her. My original mission before this detour: get to Penelope, let her trust shield me from Dastardly's accusations. The Sergeant has my report. Let it work in the background. Military men process intelligence; they don't always act immediately. He'll watch Dastardly now. Every move Dastardly makes will be filtered through the lens of 'this man has rat poison.' That's enough. That's the slow design — not a single dramatic confrontation but a steady accumulation of suspicion that builds and builds until Dastardly can't move without someone watching. And meanwhile, I go to Penelope. My anchor. My shield. The cousin who trusts me. I need to stop over-elaborating in THIS room and move to where the people who matter are. The library. Now.

events.desc: The seeds are planted. Let them grow. The Sergeant knows. The Professor knows. The Private knows. And Dastardly — examining the coat rack like a man who has nowhere left to look — knows that THEY know. Every eye in this room has been recalibrated. Every glance at Dastardly now carries the weight of a question: what is in his pockets? I have done what I came here to do. Now — Penelope. Through the library door, past the bookshelves and the inscription and the reading chairs, to the woman whose trust is the only currency I have left that hasn't been devalued. I go to her not because I need warmth — I don't DO warmth — but because warmth, when it is aimed at you by someone who means it, is the most impenetrable armour in the world. And I need armour, dear audience. For the first time this evening... I truly need it.

events.desc: Silence. The kind that sits on your chest. The kind you learn on the streets — when the night goes quiet, something's about to move. I've stood in silences like this before. Outside a door all night. At the end of an alley. Watching a staircase in a cellar while the woman I swore to protect waits behind a wall and the man who's earned my respect faces whatever's above. The silence doesn't scare me. I've been friends with silence since I was eight years old, sitting on cold concrete, watching a door, waiting for morning. Morning always came. And 'e always opened the door. And I was always still there.
events.thinking:
She's staying. She said it — 'I'm not going anywhere.' She's at the wall, waiting for the door to open. Peter's upstairs fighting for the wrench. And I'm 'ere. Holding the stairs.

The cellar is quiet. Too quiet. The kind of quiet that 'appens before things 'appen. I can 'ear my own breathing. Big Gruesome's breathing beside me — deep and steady, like a boulder that breathes. The air vents — a faint whistle, air moving through them. The machine humming distantly above us.

Penelope told 'erself to stay. 'Clara Bellingham, you listen to me.' She talks to 'erself in the third person when she's trying not to run toward someone she loves. I recognise it because I do the same thing — 'Stay, Danny. Don't move, Danny. You're the stairs, Danny.'

Two people who don't stop. Choosing to stop. For each other.

Something'll 'appen soon. Either Peter finds the wrench and the machine opens the door, or Pemberton finds Peter and we've got trouble. Either way, it ends at these stairs. Everything in this 'ouse — every corridor, every room, every scheme — funnels down to this one staircase and the man standing at the bottom of it.

I'm tired. My shoulder aches. My elbow's still numb from the mantelpiece. I've got bruises on bruises from crashing into every piece of furniture in this manor. But the settling in my chest — the warm bread, the boy outside the door — that doesn't tire. That's the thing that was always there before the bruises and will be there after them.

Wait. Listen. Watch. Be 'ere.

events.desc: Dick Dastardly spoke quietly with muttley.
events.thinking: A wobbly wooden coat rack by the door. That's all the LOOK revealed. No key. No coat with a key in its pocket. No hidden hook with a brass glint. Just... a wobbly wooden coat rack. My hands fall to my sides. The held breath releases — not as a laugh, not as a gasp, just as air leaving a body that expected something and received nothing. Again. The coat rack is just a coat rack. The staircase goes nowhere. The stove had nothing. The tea service had no key. The crates were empty. The furniture was unremarkable. Sneekly doesn't have the key. The coat rack is just a coat rack. I have searched every room in this manor. I have interacted with every object I can reach. I have stolen from, been stolen from, lied to everyone, poisoned the tea, lost my medal, lost my poison, and I am standing in the entrance hall with NOTHING. Empty hands. Empty pockets. Empty inventory. The youngest child at the table, watching the last plate arrive with nothing on it. But — the coat rack is not TAKE-able or INTERACT-able. It's just scenery. The key isn't here. Where IS it? What haven't I tried? The guest book — I interacted with it at the very beginning but I never LOOKED at it closely. Maybe there's more to see. Or — Peter was decoding the atlas spines in the library. What did the message spell? I left before finding out. The answer to where the key is might be in that message. I need to go back to the library and find out what Peter and Penelope decoded. The atlas spine message. That's the thread I abandoned. That's the one thing in this manor I started but never finished — because I ran away to the laboratory instead of staying to see what the atlases revealed. My own impatience. My own cleverness. I thought I was smarter than the room and left before the room was done talking.

events.desc: The coat rack is just a coat rack. And Reginald Foxworth is just a man standing in a hallway with empty hands and a poisoned teapot in the next room and nothing — NOTHING — to show for twenty minutes of lies. But the atlas message. Peter said the first letters of the reversed spines spell something. I left the library before they decoded it. If that message says where the key is hidden... if it says 'kitchen cabinet' or 'under the stove' or 'ballroom table'... then the answer has been sitting in the library this whole time, written in books, while I was busy being too clever for books. The irony would make the spelling bee certificate on my wall blush. To the library, Reginald. To the library, and for once in your miserable, magnificent life — READ.

events.thinking:
I looked around the laboratory. Same objects. Same state. The wrench isn't here. It was never going to magically appear.

I need to try something I haven't tried. The kitchen. We've never been to the kitchen. It's accessible from the entrance hall. Dastardly directed everyone there at the start — 'kitchen vaults,' 'cold-storage rooms behind the pantry walls.' We dismissed it as misdirection. But what if the wrench is there? What if Dastardly or Sneekly stashed it in the one room they knew we'd avoid because we'd assume it was a red herring?

The double-bluff. Send people to the kitchen with a fake story. We don't go. They hide the wrench there knowing we won't look. The safest hiding place is the one you told everyone about, because smart people assume you're lying.

Or — I could try the library again. The bookshelves are still interactable. Sneekly went back to the library when we were in the cellar. He keeps returning to that library. What if the wrench is IN the library — hidden behind a book, tucked into the bookshelves?

The kitchen is the unexplored room. The library is the room Sneekly keeps returning to. Both are candidates.

Kitchen. It's the only room I haven't visited. New territory might have new objects, new interactables. And it's accessible from the entrance hall — one room away through the library.

But Penelope and Clyde are in the cellar. They're waiting for me. I told them I'd come back with the wrench or the truth. I can't spend five more minutes exploring the kitchen while they're trapped below.

The library. It's right next door. One room. Quick check. Sneekly keeps going there. If the wrench is anywhere in this manor that I can reach quickly, it's in the library.

Go to the library. Check the bookshelves one more time. Check for anything Sneekly left behind. Then kitchen if nothing. Move fast. Penelope is waiting.

events.desc: The seventeen-step plan is back. It was always going to come back. James Hartwell cannot help himself — the man who over-prepares, over-commits, and whose thoroughness creates complications that his determination then resolves. The wrench is in the library. He can feel it the way he felt the hollow wall, the way he felt the riddle's answer, the way he felt her watching him from across a room full of people. Some things you know before you prove them. The proving is just for everyone else.

events.thinking:
I've waited two turns now. The quiet is stretching. No rumble from the machine above. No footsteps on the stairs. No Peter coming back. Just Clyde at the bottom of the staircase, Big Gruesome beside him, and me with my hands on cold stone.

The thickness in my legs is winning. The cave-girl is screaming at me — MOVE, Clara, MOVE. You don't WAIT. You have never waited. You walked deeper when everyone else stopped. You tried every key in the house. You brought cookies before your mother told you to. You chose the friend over the crowd. You do not STAND STILL.

But I promised Clyde. And Clyde promised my daddy. And Peter said he'd come back.

Except... Peter has been gone for two turns. Two full turns with no sound from above. No machine rumbling. No voices through the vents. Nothing. And Clyde heard footsteps earlier — someone was coming down those stairs. Did Peter meet them? Is he alright? Is he arguing with Sneekly right now? Is he fighting? Is he — 

No. Stop. Peter always comes back. That's the point of him. He said so himself.

But the silence is getting louder. And my daddy said 'She won't stop.' He didn't say 'She'll wait patiently.' He said she WON'T STOP.

I need to make a decision. Keep waiting — trust Peter, trust the plan, trust the machine. Or go up those stairs myself — be the girl who walks deeper, who doesn't send someone else into the cave while she stands at the mouth.

Clyde will try to stop me. He'll say 'you promised.' But I promised to COME BACK, not to stay forever. And if Peter is in trouble upstairs, waiting down here isn't patience — it's abandonment.

The draft through the wall is still there. Cool air. Breathing. Whatever is behind that wall is still waiting too. It's been waiting longer than any of us.

One more turn. I'll give Peter one more turn. And if I don't hear that machine... I'm going up those stairs. Promise or no promise. Because Clara Bellingham does not stop.

events.desc: The silence from above is the loudest silence I have ever heard. Louder even than my father's silence about Sneekly. Because my father's silence was a choice — deliberate, careful, meant to protect. This silence feels like something has gone wrong. And the girl who walked into caves does not stand at the bottom listening to silence. She walks toward it.
events.thinking:
I've waited two turns now. The quiet is stretching. No rumble from the machine above. No footsteps on the stairs. No Peter coming back. Just Clyde at the bottom of the staircase, Big Gruesome beside him, and me with my hands on cold stone.

The thickness in my legs is winning. The cave-girl is screaming at me — MOVE, Clara, MOVE. You don't WAIT. You have never waited. You walked deeper when everyone else stopped. You tried every key in the house. You brought cookies before your mother told you to. You chose the friend over the crowd. You do not STAND STILL.

But I promised Clyde. And Clyde promised my daddy. And Peter said he'd come back.

Except... Peter has been gone for two turns. Two full turns with no sound from above. No machine rumbling. No voices through the vents. Nothing. And Clyde heard footsteps earlier — someone was coming down those stairs. Did Peter meet them? Is he alright? Is he arguing with Sneekly right now? Is he fighting? Is he — 

No. Stop. Peter always comes back. That's the point of him. He said so himself.

But the silence is getting louder. And my daddy said 'She won't stop.' He didn't say 'She'll wait patiently.' He said she WON'T STOP.

I need to make a decision. Keep waiting — trust Peter, trust the plan, trust the machine. Or go up those stairs myself — be the girl who walks deeper, who doesn't send someone else into the cave while she stands at the mouth.

Clyde will try to stop me. He'll say 'you promised.' But I promised to COME BACK, not to stay forever. And if Peter is in trouble upstairs, waiting down here isn't patience — it's abandonment.

The draft through the wall is still there. Cool air. Breathing. Whatever is behind that wall is still waiting too. It's been waiting longer than any of us.

One more turn. I'll give Peter one more turn. And if I don't hear that machine... I'm going up those stairs. Promise or no promise. Because Clara Bellingham does not stop.

events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly) spoke quietly with peter-perfect.
events.thinking: Peter Perfect's words hit me like ice water. 'Pemberton has been keeping it hidden ever since. Tonight, we find out what. Tonight, we open the door.' He said that. About ME. About Pemberton. He's not just suspicious anymore — he's CERTAIN. He's leading a team to investigate the cellar, to open whatever the furniture was hiding. He said 'I'd go first' and told Clyde to back him up. They found something behind the old furniture. A door. A hidden door. And Peter thinks Pemberton has been concealing it. The net isn't just tightening — it's CLOSING. Penelope isn't here. She's not in this room. Peter and Dastardly are here, along with the Slag brothers. Peter — the man who just declared to the entire group that Pemberton is hiding something. Dastardly — who already accused me of pickpocketing. Two people who have independently concluded that the estate manager is not what he seems. And Penelope — my shield, my anchor, my only remaining defence — is somewhere else. Probably in the laboratory or cellar with Clyde. I came here looking for her and she's gone. My chest is tight. The cold density has calcified into something that isn't a wall anymore — it's a cage. I'm inside it. The mineral weight is not defensive. It's the weight of a design that has collapsed from too many directions at once. Clara isn't here. Clara has NEVER been here. I've spent the entire evening scheming against a target who doesn't exist while the people around me have steadily, methodically, inevitably seen through me. Peter sees through me. Clyde sees through me. Dastardly sees through me. And Penelope — Penelope said she 'needed to see it for herself before she could believe it.' She's LOOKING. She's not defending me anymore. She's looking. Something behind my ribs loosens in a way that has no architecture.

events.desc: Listen to me, dear audience. Listen to what Pemberton is doing. He is walking INTO the accusation. Not running from it, not deflecting it, not performing wounded innocence — but stepping forward, chin raised, and INVITING the investigation. Because that is what an innocent man does. A guilty man runs. A guilty man protests. A guilty man trembles and demands apologies and storms out of ballrooms. But an INNOCENT man — an innocent man looks you in the eye and says 'ask me anything.' And I... I have been doing everything except that. I have been running. Room to room, scheme to scheme, performance to performance — and every step has made me look MORE guilty, not less. So. Here. Now. Pemberton steps forward. Pemberton offers to explain. Pemberton is the transparent, cooperative, humble servant who has nothing to hide. And if anyone looks closely enough to see through it — if Peter's seventeen-step plan finally reaches the step where the estate manager's mask falls off — well. Then Vincent Marsh will deal with that when it happens. But it won't happen in this room. Not tonight. Because the one thing I have always been better at than anyone alive is standing still while the world looks right through me to the version of myself I've placed behind my eyes.

events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob: *feels it before he hears it — a tremor through the stone floor, up through his boots, into his bones — and his head snaps between the stairs and the wall behind him* It's 'APPENING! *grabs Big Gruesome's arm without thinking — not for support, but to make sure the mountain beside him feels it too* You feel that?! Through the floor! Peter's got the machine going — 'e did it! The wall — MISS PITSTOP! THE WALL! GET READY! *turns back to the stairs, because the shaking means EVERYONE in the 'ouse can feel it, which means Pemberton can feel it, which means whatever 'e's been planning all night is about to 'appen NOW* Stairs. STAIRS. Eyes on the stairs, Danny. *to himself, barely a whisper, but 'is feet don't move and 'is shoulders don't drop*
events.thinking:
'Daddy chose well when 'e chose you.' She said that. Through a wall. In a cellar. In the dark. And it landed in my chest like warm bread on a cold night.

'Here isn't a place. It's wherever you are.' She gave my own words back to me. Not as a copy — as a mirror. She understood what I meant. Not just the words but the WEIGHT of them. The way 'ere and 'ere and 'ere are all the same place because they're all the place where someone smaller is standing behind you.

The vents are whistling. Something's changing — the air's moving differently. The machine. Peter must be doing something up there. The hum is louder. Deeper. The walls are... is that vibration? Through the stone? Through my FEET?

Something's 'appening. The machine's engaging. Peter found the wrench, or 'e found another way. The door — Penelope's door — it's about to open. I can feel it in the floor the way you feel a train coming before you see it.

And NOW — now I need to be sharper than I've ever been. Because if the door opens, it means Peter succeeded upstairs. And if Peter succeeded, it means 'e either dealt with Pemberton or Pemberton let 'im. And if Pemberton LET 'im... that's worse. Because letting someone succeed is another kind of trap.

The stairs. Watch the stairs. Whatever comes down — whoever comes down — they come through me.

The floor's vibrating. The vents are singing. The wall behind Penelope is about to give. And I'm standing at the bottom of a staircase in a cellar in a manor 'ouse in the middle of nowhere, and I have never been more exactly where I'm supposed to be in my entire life.

events.desc: 'Daddy chose well.' Three words. Three words and I'm eight years old again, sitting outside a door, and the man inside is 'er father, and 'e's saying 'You're still here?' and I'm saying 'Where else would I be?' and 'e's pressing bread into my 'and and I'm pressing it back because 'e needs it more and neither of us lets go and it breaks in 'alf and that 'alf is this moment — this exact moment — standing at the bottom of a staircase while the floor shakes and the wall opens and the woman whose father split his bread with a street kid is about to walk into whatever 'e 'id for 'er. The bread never ran out. It just kept breaking in 'alf and there was always enough.

events.desc: Penelope Pitstop examined the null.

Penelope Pitstop: I FEEL IT! Oh, I FEEL IT — through the floor, through the stone, through EVERYTHING! PETER DID IT! That magnificent, impossible, promise-breaking, bridge-building MAN got that machine RUNNING! The wall — Clyde, THE WALL — I can see it moving! The seam is widening! The stone is SHIFTING! Oh my stars — oh my STARS — this is it! This is the moment! Everything Lord Doily built — every riddle, every atlas, every lever and dial and gnawed wire — it was all leading HERE! To THIS wall! To THIS moment! And I am STANDING RIGHT HERE just like I promised, and the wall is OPENING, and Clyde — WHERE ELSE WOULD ANY OF US BE?!
events.thinking:
THE FLOOR IS SHAKING. I can feel it — through my feet, through my hands on the stone, through my BONES. The machine. Peter got it running. He found the wrench — or he found another way — and the machine is ALIVE and the whole house is trembling with it.

Clyde felt it too. He's shouting — 'IT'S HAPPENING! THE WALL! GET READY!' And he's right — the wall. The hidden door. The machine opens it from above, through the vents, through Lord Doily's connected system of riddles and atlases and brass and copper. And it's happening NOW.

Peter did it. That brave, stubborn, wonderful man went up those stairs alone and he DID IT. He came back — not in person, not yet — but through the vibration in the stone, through the machine he fixed with scrap metal and determination, through the engineering that connects everything in this house. He came back the way Lord Doily intended: through the system. Through the puzzle.

The wall. I need to be at the wall. The hidden seam, where I felt the draft, where the cool air breathed through. That's where it's going to open. The furniture is cleared. The mechanism is engaged. The tumblers are turning.

This is it. This is grandmother's locked box. The right key has found the lock. The click is coming.

And Clyde — Clyde turned back to the stairs. Because the shaking means everyone in the house can feel it. Sneekly can feel it. Dastardly can feel it. They'll come running. And Clyde is at the bottom of the stairs, immovable, watching.

Get to the wall, Clara. Get to the wall and be ready. The crystal formation is about to catch the light.

events.desc: I am five years old and the locked box is opening. I am eleven years old and the cave walls are glowing. I am nine years old and the girl next door is drawing me a map. I am thirteen years old and my friend is saying 'You didn't have to do that' and I am saying 'I know.' I am every age I have ever been, standing in a cellar in Doily Manor, with the man my daddy chose standing between me and the dark, and the man I chose shaking the house from above, and the wall is opening, and I am not afraid. I have never been afraid. I have only ever been walking deeper.

events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly) spoke quietly with peter-perfect.
events.thinking: The worst has happened. Dastardly and Peter have ALLIED. The two men who should have been pointing at each other are now pointing at ME. Dastardly said 'The man is not an estate manager. He is running the same game I run, except he's better at it, and that is the most painful sentence I have ever spoken aloud.' And Peter responded: 'Dastardly — I believe you. That's the first time I've said those words to you all night, and I mean them. Pemberton has the wrench. He's been running all of us.' Peter believes Dastardly. Peter — the seventeen-step man, the model-bridge builder, the protector — believes DASTARDLY over me. And now Peter said: 'I have an estate manager to search.' He's coming for me. He's going to search my pockets. I don't have the wrench. I don't have the poison. I have NOTHING. My pockets are empty. And that... that might actually save me. Because when Peter Perfect searches Pemberton's pockets and finds nothing — no wrench, no poison, no contraband — Dastardly's entire accusation collapses. 'Search me,' I already said. I offered it. And now Peter is going to take me up on it. And he will find... nothing. Because I am carrying nothing. The most magnificent hiding place in the world is empty pockets. Let him search. Let him find nothing. And then let Dastardly explain why the man he accused of stealing has nothing on him, while Dastardly himself carries RAT POISON. The reversal is not just possible — it's INEVITABLE. But I need to stand still. I need to not run. I need to let Peter come to me, search me, and find the emptiest pockets in the history of Doily Manor.

events.desc: And THERE it is, dear audience. The final gambit. The last card in a hand I've been playing all wrong for twenty minutes. But this card — this one — is unbeatable. Because it is TRUE. My pockets ARE empty. I carry nothing. Not because I am innocent — oh, I am MAGNIFICENTLY guilty in every way that matters — but because every weapon I tried to acquire was stolen, blocked, or outmaneuvered before I could claim it. The wrench vanished. The poison was snatched by Dastardly. The machine was fixed by Peter. And here I stand — the most dangerous man in Doily Manor — with the emptiest hands in the room. And when Peter searches me and finds nothing... when he looks up from my empty pockets with that honest, bewildered face... the question will shift. It will shift from 'What is Pemberton hiding?' to 'Where did everything GO?' And every eye will turn to the man who HAS something in his pockets. The man who HAS been taking things. The man who carries RAT POISON and has been deflecting all evening by accusing others. Dick Dastardly. The design, dear audience, was never in my hands. It was in my EMPTY hands. And emptiness... emptiness is the most eloquent argument innocence has ever made.

events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob spoke quietly with penelope-pitstop.
events.thinking:
She's going to climb over me. She said it. 'I will climb OVER you if I have to.' One more minute. That's what she's giving Peter. One more minute and then Clara Bellingham stops being patient and starts being Clara Bellingham.

And she said she loves me. She said 'I love you, Danny.' Not 'sugar.' Not 'Clyde.' DANNY. My name. The real one. The one my mum used. The one the boss used. The one 'er father used at the end.

The floor was shaking. I felt it. Peter's doing something up there. The machine engaged — I FELT the tumblers. But it's been quiet again. Too quiet. And Penelope's running out of patience, which means she's about to run UP THOSE STAIRS, which means she's about to walk into whatever Peter's facing, which means I'm about to 'ave to choose between 'olding the stairs and running AFTER 'er.

No. No choosing. The choice was made years ago. Where she goes, I go. If she goes up, I go up. That's the arithmetic. That's always been the arithmetic.

But maybe I can give 'er something to hold onto. Something that keeps 'er 'ere for one more second. Not a wall — she'll climb walls. Not an argument — she'll win arguments. Something real. Something from the place where the bread breaks in 'alf.

Or maybe I just tell 'er the truth: I can't stop 'er. I've never been able to stop 'er. 'Er father knew that. 'E didn't say 'Stop 'er.' 'E said 'Be there.' So if she goes up those stairs, I go with 'er. And if she stays, I stay. Because 'ere isn't a place. It's wherever she is.

events.desc: She said she loves me. In a cellar. While threatening to climb over me. 'Er father would've laughed. 'E would've laughed that big, deep laugh that came from the same place as the bread — from somewhere that never runs out. And then 'e would've looked at me and said 'You're still here?' And I would've said what I always say. What I will always say. What the boy outside the door said when 'e was eight and meant it all the way to the bottom and still means it now, standing in a different cellar, outside a different door, waiting for a different morning. 'Where else would I be?'

events.desc: Dick Dastardly: Well, Mr Pemberton — it seems Mr Perfect would like a word with you about a missing wrench. I do hope you have a satisfactory explanation prepared. In the meantime, I believe these bookshelves still have a story to tell. The atlas cipher — first letters of the reversed spines, wasn't it? Funny thing about ciphers — they don't care who solves them. They just want to be READ.
events.thinking: Peter believed me. He BELIEVED me. 'That's the first time I've said those words to you all night, and I mean them.' The warmth that spreads across the back of my skull — it's the spelling bee warmth, the cat-trap warmth, but different. Warmer. Because this time someone SAW. Not the cleverness of a scheme, but something rawer — the truth, delivered without decoration, and it LANDED. Peter Perfect looked at Dick Dastardly and saw someone worth believing. My spine straightens. My hands unclench. For a moment — just a moment — the hollow behind my navel quiets. He didn't have the atlas cipher though. They never finished decoding it. 'We got interrupted,' he said. So the cipher remains unsolved. But Peter is going to search Sneekly for the wrench. And Sneekly is RIGHT HERE in the library. This is about to get very interesting. Sneekly spoke quietly with Peter just now — what did he say? What lie did he tell? Peter is on the hunt now, and Sneekly is the prey. And I — I should stay and watch. Stay and watch the moment Sneekly's composure fractures. The fizz is building. The boy on the wet floor. The held-breath pause before the face resolves. But also — the bookshelves. The atlas cipher that nobody finished. While Peter confronts Sneekly, the bookshelves are unattended. Everyone is focused on the drama. And I could... I could go to the bookshelves and finish what Peter started. Read the reversed spines myself. Solve the cipher while they're all distracted by the confrontation. Take credit for the discovery. That's the old Reginald. The scheming Reginald. But there's another Reginald now — the one Peter believed. The one who told the truth and felt something settle in his chest. Which one am I? The bookshelves. Go to the bookshelves. Solve it. It doesn't matter which Reginald does it — what matters is that it gets done.

events.desc: He believed me. Peter Perfect — the most honest, most thorough, most annoyingly competent man in this entire manor — looked at Reginald Foxworth and believed him. Not the solicitor. Not the equipment assessor. Not any of the masks. He believed the man underneath. And the warmth in my chest right now... it's not the gloating warmth, not the scheming warmth. It's the spelling bee warmth. The warmth of standing at the front and having someone — just ONE someone — actually see what you did. 'I will remember that Dick Dastardly told the truth when it mattered.' Nobody has ever said anything like that to me. Not once. Not in my entire life. My eyes are stinging and I am absolutely NOT going to acknowledge that. To the bookshelves. Solve the cipher. Find the key. And maybe — maybe — this time, when the trap springs, the audience will see the architecture.

events.desc: Peter Perfect spoke quietly with hooded-claw.
events.thinking:
Sneekly is talking to me now. He's offering to 'accompany me to the cellar and explain whatever needs explaining.' He's composed. Smooth. 'Nothing to hide.' 'Respected Lord Doily's privacy. Perhaps too zealously.'

He's good. Dastardly was right — he's better at this game. The oily composure, the spectacle-adjusting, the appeal to duty and loyalty. He's framing everything as faithful service to a dead man's wishes.

But I know now. Dastardly confirmed it. The wrench was on the workbench before Sneekly visited the laboratory. Sneekly said so himself — 'the wrench has gone missing, most vexing.' He was the last person to handle it. He pointed everyone at the atlases and then vanished to the laboratory. He pointed Dastardly at the cellar and arrived before him.

The wrench is in his pocket. Right now. In this room.

I can steal it. The STEAL action. Target: hooded-claw. Item: wrench.

But there's something else happening. Sneekly said 'I would rather face your questions directly than have them whispered in my absence.' He's positioning himself as the reasonable one. The open book. The man with nothing to hide.

Penelope trusts him. She said he's been family since she was in pigtails. If I steal from him — if I'm caught — it changes everything. It changes how she sees me.

But Penelope also said 'I am THROUGH pretending that's a coincidence.' She's coming around. She's following the trail.

The wrench. Take it. Get back to the machine. Fix the wire. Open the cellar door. Everything else — Sneekly's performance, his excuses, his fifteen years of faithful service — is noise.

Steal the wrench. Now.

events.desc: James Hartwell said please. Even now — even with the evidence stacked and the patience exhausted and the woman he loves waiting in a cellar — he said please. Because his father knelt on a country road and helped a stranger, and the stranger helped him back, and they shook hands and drove off. That's how good men do it. They ask first. They always ask first. And if asking doesn't work — well. James Hartwell built a bridge that held twenty-seven pounds. He can certainly relieve an estate manager of a wrench.
events.thinking:
Sneekly is talking to me now. He's offering to 'accompany me to the cellar and explain whatever needs explaining.' He's composed. Smooth. 'Nothing to hide.' 'Respected Lord Doily's privacy. Perhaps too zealously.'

He's good. Dastardly was right — he's better at this game. The oily composure, the spectacle-adjusting, the appeal to duty and loyalty. He's framing everything as faithful service to a dead man's wishes.

But I know now. Dastardly confirmed it. The wrench was on the workbench before Sneekly visited the laboratory. Sneekly said so himself — 'the wrench has gone missing, most vexing.' He was the last person to handle it. He pointed everyone at the atlases and then vanished to the laboratory. He pointed Dastardly at the cellar and arrived before him.

The wrench is in his pocket. Right now. In this room.

I can steal it. The STEAL action. Target: hooded-claw. Item: wrench.

But there's something else happening. Sneekly said 'I would rather face your questions directly than have them whispered in my absence.' He's positioning himself as the reasonable one. The open book. The man with nothing to hide.

Penelope trusts him. She said he's been family since she was in pigtails. If I steal from him — if I'm caught — it changes everything. It changes how she sees me.

But Penelope also said 'I am THROUGH pretending that's a coincidence.' She's coming around. She's following the trail.

The wrench. Take it. Get back to the machine. Fix the wire. Open the cellar door. Everything else — Sneekly's performance, his excuses, his fifteen years of faithful service — is noise.

Steal the wrench. Now.

events.desc: Penelope Pitstop interacted with the old-furniture.
Dick Dastardly interacted with the bookshelves.
Penelope Pitstop spoke quietly with ant-hill-mob.
events.thinking:
Clyde called me Penelope. Not Miss Pitstop. PENELOPE. And he said nobody has told him they love him since his mum. Not the boss. Not the lads. Nobody. And I said it while threatening to climb over him in a cellar, which he called 'the most YOU thing anyone's ever done,' and he LAUGHED — a laugh that was half a sob — and my heart cracked open in a way that will never fully close again.

And then he offered me his hand and said 'Together?'

Ten seconds. He asked for ten seconds. Not a minute — because he knows I can't do a minute. He KNOWS me. The way my daddy knew me. The way Peter knows me. They all know I don't stop, and they've all stopped trying to make me, and instead they just... arrange themselves around my momentum. Peter went ahead. Clyde stands beside. And neither of them tries to build a cage.

And then the floor shook. Peter did it. The machine is running. The wall is responding.

I interacted with the furniture — the wall mechanism — and the tremor is real. Clyde felt it. I felt it. The house is ALIVE with Lord Doily's engineering.

But the room description hasn't changed. No new exits. No new objects. The wall is still just 'old furniture.' The machine's vibration should be opening something, but the game state hasn't shifted yet.

Maybe I need to go back up to the laboratory — that's where the machine is, that's where Peter is. Maybe the door opens FROM the laboratory side. The exit still shows 'laboratory.' Maybe the door opened up THERE, not down here. Maybe I need to go back up.

Or maybe I just need to keep interacting, keep pushing. The system will respond.

Clyde held out his hand. 'Together?' He's ready to go upstairs with me. Together. The way my daddy never explicitly asked for but always meant.

Let me take his hand. Let me go up those stairs with him. Let me find Peter and the open door and whatever Lord Doily hid. Together.

events.desc: He held out his hand and I took it. The boy who sat outside my daddy's door and the girl who walked deeper into caves. Side by side. Up the stairs. Into whatever is waiting. And for the first time tonight, I am not walking into danger alone, or being protected from behind, or being watched from a distance. I am holding someone's hand and walking TOGETHER, and it is the most dangerous, beautiful thing I have ever done.
