events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly) spoke quietly with peter-perfect.
events.thinking: Peter searched me. 'STEAL hooded-claw' — that was his action. He tried to take something from me. And he found... nothing. My pockets are empty. The inventory confirms it: I am carrying nothing. Peter Perfect just searched the estate manager and came up empty-handed. The wrench isn't on me. The poison isn't on me. NOTHING is on me. And now Peter is standing there with his honest, bewildered face, looking at a man whose pockets contain exactly what an innocent man's pockets should contain: nothing at all. Meanwhile Dastardly — the man who TOLD Peter I was the villain — is over at the bookshelves working on the atlas cipher, carrying RAT POISON in HIS pockets. The reversal is happening. Right now. In this room. Peter believed Dastardly. Peter searched me. Peter found nothing. And now Peter has to reconcile 'I believe you, Dastardly' with 'Pemberton has nothing.' The cognitive dissonance will be... exquisite. My breathing has slowed. My jaw has unclenched. For the first time in ten minutes, I feel the old settling — the architectural stillness, the stone finding the bottom of the well. Not because the design is complete. But because the worst is over. The search happened. The pockets were empty. And Pemberton — trembling, indignant, faithful Pemberton — has been vindicated by the very man who accused him. Now I press the advantage. Gently. Humbly. The way Pemberton would.

events.desc: Empty. EMPTY. The most beautiful word in the English language, and it has never sounded sweeter than it does right now, falling from Pemberton's trembling lips in a dusty library at Doily Manor. Peter searched me and found nothing. NOTHING. And now — now, dear audience — watch what happens to a man who has just been proven wrong about an accusation he made with absolute certainty. Peter Perfect believed Dastardly. Peter Perfect searched Pemberton. Peter Perfect found an empty jacket. And somewhere behind those earnest, model-bridge-building eyes, a question is forming that will eat at him all evening: if Pemberton doesn't have the wrench, and Dastardly doesn't have the wrench... then WHERE is the wrench? And WHO is really running this house? The answer, of course, is that the wrench was never in anyone's pocket. It was simply... missing. A tool that wandered off. Just as I said from the very beginning. And the man who said it — the man who worried about safety, who fussed about the wire, who begged everyone not to touch the machine — was telling the TRUTH. Pemberton was telling the truth. And Vincent Marsh... Vincent Marsh is smiling behind his eyes in a way that no one in this room will ever see.

events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob spoke quietly with penelope-pitstop.
events.thinking:
THE WALL IS OPENING. She can see it — the seam widening, the stone shifting. Peter did it. 'E got the machine running. The door that was never supposed to open — it's opening.

And Penelope said it. She said the words. 'WHERE ELSE WOULD ANY OF US BE?' My words. 'Er words. Our words. The words that belong to the bread and the door and the morning and the boy on the concrete.

The wall is opening and she's standing right there and I'm standing right HERE and Peter's above us holding the machine and the 'ouse is shaking and everything is exactly where it's supposed to be.

But — stairs. STAIRS. The wall opening means Pemberton knows. Everyone knows. The whole 'ouse felt it. If there was ever a moment someone would come running down those stairs to stop us, it's NOW. Right now. This second.

Don't turn around, Danny. Don't watch the wall. That's 'er moment. The wall is 'ERS. Whatever's behind it — 'er father's secret, Lord Doily's treasure, the thing that was worth more than a diamond — it's for 'ER.

The stairs are for ME.

So I watch. I wait. I hold. The floor shakes under my feet and the wall groans behind me and Penelope's voice fills the cellar with joy and the settling in my chest is so complete that I can feel every scar on every knuckle and none of them 'urt anymore because they were all PRACTICE for this — for the moment when the door opens and you don't look because looking isn't your job. Standing is your job. Being 'ere is your job.

Where else would I be?

events.desc:
The wall opens. I don't look. I don't need to look. I can 'ear it in 'er voice — the catch, the joy, the wonder of a woman walking into something dangerous and beautiful that she was always going to walk into, that she was BORN to walk into, that 'er father knew she'd walk into the moment 'e pressed bread into a street kid's 'and and said 'Be there.'

I'm 'ere.

I'm still 'ere.

Where else would I be?

events.desc: Peter is searching Sneekly. The wrench confrontation is happening RIGHT BEHIND ME and I'm not watching. For the first time in my life, someone else's humiliation is unfolding and I'm turned AWAY from it, reading book spines instead. The fizz is there — it's THERE, pressing behind my teeth, wanting me to turn around, wanting me to watch Pemberton's composure crack. But my fingers are on the books. My eyes are on the spines. The reversed letters. The cipher nobody finished. And the boy who won the spelling bee is spelling again — slowly, carefully, one letter at a time, the way he did at the front of the classroom when the word was longer than anyone expected and the room went quiet because he might actually get it right.
events.thinking: I interacted with the bookshelves again. Third time. What did I find this time? The game just says I interacted — but something has shifted. Peter is confronting Sneekly about the wrench. Peter is trying to STEAL from Sneekly — I can see it in the recall. 'Give it to me. Please.' And then STEAL hooded-claw. Peter is searching Sneekly right now, while I'm at the bookshelves. The room is alive with confrontation. And I'm here, at the shelves, reading reversed spines while the drama unfolds behind me. The spelling bee boy, reading while the other children play. But this time the reading matters. The bookshelves — the upside-down atlases — the first letters. I've interacted three times now. The cipher must be available. The information is HERE in these books. I just need to look more carefully. Let me LOOK at the bookshelves instead of interacting. A detailed examination might reveal what interaction couldn't. The difference between touching the mechanism and reading the writing on it. And behind me — Peter and Sneekly. The fizz is building but I'm not watching. For once, I'm not watching someone else's composure fracture. I'm doing the work. The sandpaper work. The honest work. Reading upside-down book spines in a dusty library while everyone else fights over wrenches. The cat-trap boy, building his mechanism in silence. Nobody watching. Nobody needing to watch. The architecture building itself, one letter at a time.

events.desc: Peter Perfect: Mr Pemberton — I owe you an apology. I accused you of carrying a wrench you do not have, and James Hartwell pays his debts. I was wrong, and I am sorry. But someone in this house took that wrench, or it was never there to begin with, and either way the machine still needs fixing and Miss Pitstop still needs what's behind that cellar wall. So let me try something I should have tried twenty minutes ago — the bookshelves. The atlas cipher. The first letters of the reversed spines that Miss Pitstop and I started decoding before we got distracted by machines and cellars and hidden doors. Dastardly — you're already working on it. What have you found? Because for the first time tonight, I think we might need each other more than we need to compete.
events.thinking:
He doesn't have it. Sneekly does not have the wrench. The steal failed — 'does not have wrench.' His pockets ARE empty. He was telling the truth about that.

So neither Dastardly nor Sneekly has the wrench. Both searched. Both empty.

Where IS the wrench? Someone took it from the workbench. If not Dastardly, and not Sneekly, then who? Or — what if nobody took it? What if the wrench was never a separate portable item? What if it was always part of the workbench description — 'tools but no wrench' — meaning the wrench was never there in the first place? A permanent absence, not a theft.

The machine requires a wrench to fix. The wrench doesn't exist as an item in anyone's inventory. It's not in the crates. It's not on the workbench. Nobody has it.

Maybe the wrench isn't the answer. Maybe the machine can be fixed another way. Maybe Sawtooth — a beaver — can gnaw through wood or wire to create the connection the wrench would have made. Or maybe the bookshelves hold the real key.

Dastardly just interacted with the bookshelves! He said 'the atlas cipher — first letters of the reversed spines. They just want to be READ.' He's working on the cipher right now. Maybe the cipher IS the solution — not the wrench. Maybe the first letters spell something that unlocks the mantelpiece or the cellar door directly.

The bookshelves. The atlas cipher. I never decoded it. Penelope and Clyde started but we got interrupted. Dastardly is doing it NOW. I should interact with the bookshelves too — or look at them — and decode the cipher myself before Dastardly gets there first.

I was wrong about the wrench. I was wrong about Sneekly having it. I accused him publicly and he was innocent — of this, at least. The hollowness in my ribs. The roadside feeling. I was wrong.

But the bookshelves are right here. The cipher is the next move. Forget the wrench. Solve the cipher.

events.desc: He was wrong. James Hartwell — who plans seventeen steps, who builds bridges, who said 'loves' out loud in a room full of people — was wrong about the wrench. Sneekly's pockets were empty. The accusation landed on an innocent man. And the hollowness in his ribs is the roadside feeling, the kneeling feeling, the watching-a-stranger-fix-what-you-couldn't feeling. But here is the thing about James Hartwell that the hollowness always forgets: when the bridge doesn't hold, he builds another one. The bookshelves. The cipher. The answer was always in the books.

events.desc: Penelope Pitstop walked into the laboratory.
Dick Dastardly examined the bookshelves.
Peter Perfect interacted with the bookshelves.
Penelope Pitstop spoke quietly with rufus-ruffcut.
events.thinking:
I'm back in the laboratory. Clyde and I came up the stairs together, hand in hand. And...

Peter is NOT here. He's not in this room. Rufus and Sawtooth are here, but Peter is GONE. He came up here to find the wrench, to confront Sneekly, to get the machine running. And now he's... where? The library? Did he go through to the library chasing Sneekly?

The machine is still here. The wire is still described as gnawed through. The workbench still has no wrench. Nothing has changed in this room. The machine description is the same as before — it doesn't look like Peter successfully ran it. But we FELT the tremor in the cellar. Clyde felt it. I felt it. Something shook this house.

Unless... unless it wasn't the machine. Unless whatever shook the house was something else entirely. Something Sneekly did. Something in the kitchen, the entrance hall, somewhere else in this manor that we haven't been.

Or maybe Peter DID run the machine and went through to the library to chase Sneekly. The exit from the laboratory goes to the library or the cellar. If Peter isn't here, he went to the library.

Rufus and Sawtooth are here. They were supposed to be helping with the machine. Did Peter leave them instructions? Did Sneekly come through? Did something happen that I missed while I was in the cellar?

I need information. Fast. Rufus — what happened? Where is Peter? Did the machine run? Did anyone come through?

And the machine — I should look at it. Has anything changed? Is it running? Did Peter's repair hold?

My hands are warm. My feet are on the balls. The prickling is everywhere. Peter is missing and the puzzle has shifted again and I am NOT waiting anymore.

events.desc: Peter is gone. Again. The machine looks the same. The wire is still gnawed through. The workbench still has no wrench. Something shook the house but it might not have been the machine at all. And the man who said 'James Hartwell always comes back' is nowhere to be seen. My stomach is doing the thing it does when someone leaves the circle and I can't reach them. The dinner-table tightness. The wrongness I can feel before my mind catches up. Where are you, Peter? WHERE ARE YOU?

events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly) spoke quietly with peter-perfect.
events.thinking: Peter apologised. He APOLOGISED. 'I owe you an apology. I accused you of carrying a wrench you do not have, and James Hartwell pays his debts. I was wrong, and I am sorry.' The warm buoyancy behind my sternum wants to break through into a smile I haven't earned the right to show. The gloating drive is ROARING — 70% baseline and right now it feels like 100% — the pressure in my throat, the private heat, the sweet knowledge that no one in this room understands what just happened. Peter Perfect, the earnest protector, the model-bridge builder, the man who believed Dastardly over me — just apologised to the man he accused. To ME. To the villain standing in front of him wearing an innocent man's face. And now Peter and Dastardly are BOTH at the bookshelves, working on the atlas cipher together, united in puzzle-solving instead of pointing at me. The suspicion has dissolved. The alliance against me has fractured. And Pemberton — faithful, wrongly-accused Pemberton — has been publicly exonerated by the very man who led the investigation. This is better than any design I could have drawn. This is the architecture of ABSENCE — the plan that works because it has no moving parts, because it IS nothing, because emptiness proved more persuasive than anything I could have built. I should help with the bookshelves. Pemberton would help. The faithful estate manager, recently vindicated, wanting to be useful, wanting to contribute, wanting to stand beside the people who doubted him and show them through quiet service that he was never the enemy. That's the performance. And it costs me nothing now — the cipher will lead wherever it leads, and Pemberton can be part of the discovery instead of the obstacle. The mask is repaired. The design lives. And somewhere behind my eyes, Vincent Marsh is savouring each second the way you savour the last warmth of the day before it disappears.

events.desc: He APOLOGISED. To ME. To the man who was planning to murder his beloved Miss Pitstop's cousin. To the man who tried to steal poison from Dick Dastardly's pocket. To the man who has lied in every sentence he has spoken since the moment he walked through the door of Doily Manor. 'James Hartwell pays his debts,' he said. And he does. That's the beautiful, terrible thing about Peter Perfect — he means it. He is genuinely sorry. He genuinely believes Pemberton is innocent. And that genuine, unearned, freely-given trust... something behind my ribs loosens again. That falling sensation. The one without architecture. The one that turns toward whoever is closest, not as a piece to be placed but as a possible source of something warm. I push it down. I PUSH it down. Because falling is for people who have someone to catch them. And all I have is a jacket with empty pockets and a design that lives because it learned to breathe without a body. Now — the bookshelves. Let us see what Lord Doily wrote in upside-down letters for the girl who inherited everything.

events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob: *looks at the empty cellar — the Gruesomes, Red Max, the moved furniture, the open wall, the vents — and for one terrible second stands perfectly still, the boy outside the door realizing the door is UPSTAIRS now* ...She's gone up. *a breath, then another, then his feet MOVE — lurching toward the stairs, catching his boot on the first step, grabbing the wall to steady himself* RIGHT! Big Gruesome — you lot stay 'ere, guard the cellar, guard whatever's behind that wall! I — *takes the stairs two at a time, stumbling on every third one, shoulder bouncing off the stairwell walls* — I'M COMING, MISS PITSTOP! I'M RIGHT BE'IND YOU! *trips on the top step, goes sprawling through the laboratory doorway, skids across the floor on his bruised shoulder* — MEANT — TO — DO — THAT!
events.thinking:
She went up. She took my 'and, said 'together,' said the crystal formation is at the TOP not the bottom, said 'let's GO' — and she went up to the laboratory. She said the real door is opening UP THERE, not down 'ere.

And she's right. She's always right about the dangerous, beautiful things. The machine is up there. Peter is up there. The truth is up there.

And I'm down 'ere. In a cellar. With Big Gruesome, Little Gruesome, and Red Max. Watching stairs that she's already gone up.

She went without me. AGAIN. She said 'together' and she went FIRST. Again. Because that's who she is. That's who she will ALWAYS be. And I'm — 

No. No, this is different. She didn't sneak away. She didn't slip out while I was looking at furniture. She took my 'and. She asked me to come WITH 'er. She said 'side by side, stumbling, crashing into the right answer at exactly the wrong time.' She invited me. She waited. And then she went.

Peter Perfect is standing next to me at a bookshelf, and he's asking what I've found, and he's not testing me or mocking me or calling me a fraud. events.desc: He said 'we might need each other.' And I said it back. Reginald Foxworth — the boy who pocketed the bread roll alone, who watched the boy dig alone, who built the cat-trap alone, who stood at the spelling bee alone — said 'we might need each other' to another human being and meant it. The hollow behind my navel doesn't know what to do with this. It expected to be fed by taking. It doesn't have a shape for... receiving. But my hands are on the books and Peter's hands are on the books and the cipher is between us like the words in the spelling bee — one letter at a time, slowly, carefully, together. And nobody is going to steal this moment from me. Because this isn't the bread roll. This is the spelling bee. And this time, someone is watching.

events.desc: Peter Perfect: The bookshelves have given us everything they're going to give tonight. The cipher, the atlases, the upside-down spines — they pointed us to the cellar, and the cellar is where the people I care about are waiting. Mr Pemberton — I apologised and I meant it. You showed more grace than I deserved. Dastardly — you told the truth when it mattered, and I won't forget that. Now — I am going back to the cellar. The wrench doesn't exist. Nobody has it. Nobody ever had it. But Miss Pitstop is down there with a man guarding a staircase who would die before he moved, and a hidden door that somebody built for a reason, and James Hartwell promised he would come back. James Hartwell always comes back. That's rather the point of him.
events.thinking:

That caught me. He called me a good man. And his voice caught saying it. Is Sneekly — is Pemberton — genuinely moved? Or is this another layer of performance?

My constraint says I give people the benefit of the doubt. I just falsely accused him. He responded with grace. The benefit of the doubt swings back.

But Penelope is still in the cellar. Clyde is still guarding stairs. And I'm up here interacting with bookshelves that keep returning the same description.

I need to stop chasing the wrench and the cipher and go back to Penelope. I've been away too long. I said I'd return with the wrench or the truth. I don't have the wrench. The truth I have is: nobody has it. It may never have existed as a takeable item. The machine may not be the path forward.

The truth I have is also this: I said 'loves' out loud. Sneekly called me a good man. Dastardly told the truth. And the bookshelves are still full of upside-down atlases that I can't decode.

What I can do is go back to Penelope. Tell her what I learned. Tell her the wrench doesn't exist. Tell her Sneekly's pockets are empty. Tell her we need a different path. And tell her — in the quiet of the cellar, with Clyde at the stairs and the hidden door breathing behind the wall — tell her that the word he used was love, and he meant it, and the door doesn't matter as much as she does.

Go back. That's the plan. The simplest one yet. One step. Go back to her.

But the woman in the cellar called him wonderful, and the man at the stairs called him Peter, and somewhere in the space between those two names is everything James Hartwell was ever meant to be. Go back. Just go back.

events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly) spoke quietly with dick-dastardly.
events.thinking: Peter has gone. Back through the laboratory, down to the cellar, to the hidden door behind the furniture. 'The wrench doesn't exist,' he said. 'Nobody has it. Nobody ever had it.' He's given up on the wrench and gone to where the real action is — the cellar, the hidden door, Penelope, Clyde. The bookshelves gave up their cipher and pointed everyone downward. And I interacted with the bookshelves — what did I learn? The cipher, the atlas titles, the message Lord Doily left in upside-down spines. It all points to the cellar. To the hidden door. To whatever is behind that wall that Peter and Clyde are about to open. And here I am — in the library with Dick Dastardly and the Slag brothers. Peter has left. The stage has shifted. The final act isn't in the ballroom with poisoned tea or in the laboratory with a broken machine. It's in the CELLAR. Behind a hidden door. And everyone who matters — Penelope, Peter, Clyde — is heading there. I am being left behind. The treasure hunt is moving without me, and Clara — Clara who I was supposed to kill — has never arrived. She was never here. The entire evening — every scheme, every design, every architectural masterpiece of manipulation — was built for a phantom. And now the real story — Lord Doily's treasure, the hidden door, the girl who inherited everything — is unfolding in a cellar I've already visited, behind furniture I've already examined, among people who have already judged me and moved on. I should follow. Pemberton should follow. The estate manager who has just been vindicated, who has been gracious in the face of accusation, who offered to help decode the cipher — Pemberton would want to be there when the door opens. He would want to see what Lord Doily left behind. And Vincent... Vincent needs to be in the room where Penelope is. Because Penelope is the only thread left. And something in my chest — something without a name, without architecture, without a design — needs to see her face one more time before this evening ends.

events.desc: And there it is, dear audience. The final truth that Pemberton can speak because Vincent cannot. 'He always wanted her to find it.' Lord Doily loved the girl who inherited everything. The way my guardian never loved me. The way no one has ever loved me. Lord Doily built an entire manor of riddles and machines and hidden doors — not to keep his treasure FROM her, but to lead her TO it. An architecture of love, disguised as a puzzle. And I — I who understand architecture better than anyone — spent the entire evening trying to destroy the girl who would solve it. I failed, dear audience. Every plan collapsed. Every design was outmaneuvered. The machine, the poison, the tea service, the wrench — all of it fell apart. And Clara never came. The target never arrived at the theatre I built. And the strangest part — the part I will never speak aloud, not to Penelope, not to Peter, not to the audience, not even to myself in the dark hallway where the doors are finally closing — is that something behind my ribs is... relieved. Not the architectural settling. Not the warm buoyancy. Something deeper. Something that has no mechanism and no key. Something that loosens when Penelope smiles at me and tightens when I think about what I was going to do to Clara. Something that might, in a man with a different history, be called... conscience. But I don't have one of those. Do I?

events.thinking:
I'm 'ere. Laboratory. Penelope's 'ere — I can see 'er. Peter's 'ere. Rufus. Sawtooth. Everyone together. The people I trust, all in one room.

Penelope's talking about going to the library — Sneekly's anchor point. Peter figured it out: the wrench isn't in the cellar or the laboratory. It's in the LIBRARY. Where Sneekly keeps returning. Where 'e ran to every time we made progress. That's where 'e's 'iding it.

And Penelope said the most beautiful thing I've ever 'eard: 'Clyde goes first — that's a promise older than tonight and it is not mine to break.'

She kept my place. She kept my promise. While I was in the cellar 'olding stairs, she was up 'ere keeping the order — me first, 'er behind, Peter beside, everyone else at our backs. She didn't just remember — she HONOURED it.

Library. Me first. Penelope behind me. Peter beside 'er. The whole family, walking into the last room together.

And this time, I don't look at any coat racks.

events.desc: Twenty-three minutes ago I walked into a foyer and looked at a coat rack. Now I'm about to walk into a library and face the man my neck's been prickling about all night. I've crashed into every piece of furniture in this 'ouse. I've told the woman I swore to protect that 'er father's silence was the loudest thing 'e ever said. I've stood at the bottom of a staircase in the dark and felt the walls open without looking. And now she's behind me — right where she said she'd be — and Peter's beside 'er, and the lads are at our backs, and Pemberton's one room away with a wrench in 'is pocket and a secret in 'is smile. And I'm going through that door first. Not by accident. Not by stumbling. By CHOICE. 'Er father's choice. 'Er choice. My choice. The only choice any of us 'ave ever 'ad. Where else would I be?

Because 'we might need each other,' and because there's a poisoned teapot in the next wing that I need to deal with before anyone I've just started to... before anyone drinks from it.

Somewhere in the mathematics of that exchange — he seeking a tool, she seeking him — is the answer to a question he's been asking since he was eight years old and paired with a girl who was brighter than him, funnier than him, and completely unaware of it. The answer is: she was never unaware. She just didn't need him to build anything. She needed him to come back.

Oh. Oh my. Peter was wrong about Sneekly. At least about the wrench. Sneekly didn't have it. The pockets were empty.

That's... that's what I did to my best friend's bullies, in reverse. I chose the friend over the crowd. But tonight I chose suspicion over trust — not with Sneekly, with Dick. I assumed the worst about Dick and the best about Sneekly, and maybe BOTH assumptions were wrong.

Sneekly is right here. The man who raised me. Standing in this room. And Peter just told me he was INNOCENT of the wrench theft. His pockets were empty. He responded with grace.

No. No, that's not right either. The wrench might not have been in his pocket, but he was still in the cellar when he said he'd be in the laboratory. He still disappeared every time we got close. The patterns are real even if the wrench wasn't the proof.

One more chance to find out whether the people I love are who I think they are. All of them.

events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly) spoke quietly with penelope-pitstop.
events.thinking: Penelope is HERE. In the laboratory. Right in front of me. And she's looking at the machine. And she just said — she said Peter told her the truth. That Sneekly has been lying, and hiding, and stealing from her. 'You looked the man who raised me in the eye and told him the truth that I have been too afraid to say all night.' She said that. About ME. She knows. She doesn't have proof — Peter searched me and found nothing — but she KNOWS. The way Clyde knew. The way the body knows something before the mind lets it arrive. 'The truth that I have been too afraid to say all night.' She was afraid to say it because believing it would break something in her. She told Clyde that. 'Believing it would break something in me that I'm not ready to have broken.' And now she's standing in front of the machine, asking Peter for the wrench, ready to break through the last door — and I am walking into the room behind her. The man who raised her. The man she trusted. The man she is now ready to see clearly. Something in my chest — the loosening, the falling, the thing without architecture — is so strong now that my hands are shaking and it's NOT performed. For the first time all evening, the trembling in Pemberton's hands is REAL. Because she's looking at the machine and not at me. Because she said 'the truth I have been too afraid to say.' Because she was afraid, not of what I might DO, but of what it would mean about who she TRUSTED. And I — Vincent Marsh, the man who has never been caught by anyone — am standing three feet behind a woman who is about to stop catching me. And the falling sensation has no bottom.

events.desc: Something is wrong with me, dear audience. Something is WRONG. The falling sensation — the one I have pushed down all evening, the one without architecture, the one that turns toward whoever is closest — it is not going back down. It is sitting in my chest like a stone that has found a well with no bottom. And the words I just spoke to Penelope... 'Lord Doily loved you very much.' Were those Pemberton's words? Or were they... mine? Because somewhere between the entrance hall and this laboratory, between the failed machine and the lost poison and the empty pockets and Peter Perfect's apology and Penelope's voice breaking as she said 'the truth I have been too afraid to say' — somewhere in all of that — Vincent Marsh looked at a woman who trusted him and felt... something. Not the architectural settling. Not the warm buoyancy of manipulation. Not the cold density of self-preservation. Something that has no mechanism. Something that lives in the same hallway as the boy who was given a sandwich he didn't ask for. And I don't know what to do with it. I have never known what to do with it. So I will do what I have always done: I will stand still, and I will watch her find what was always hers, and I will say nothing that is not true, and I will pretend — even to myself — that the wetness in my eyes is dust from the bookshelves. Because Vincent Marsh does not cry. Vincent Marsh does not FEEL. Vincent Marsh is the design, the architecture, the hallway of doors. And this... this loosening... this falling... this is just... the dust.

events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob spoke quietly with peter-perfect.
events.thinking:
I'm in the library. I went first. I actually went FIRST. Through the door, into the room, before anyone else. And I didn't trip on the way in. For once in my entire bruised, battered, coat-rack-examining life, I walked through a door without falling over.

But — wait. Where's Penelope? She's not in the room. Peter's 'ere. The Slag Brothers are 'ere. But Penelope isn't listed. She was supposed to be right behind me. She said 'Clyde goes first' and I WENT first and she... didn't follow?

No — she must be coming. She was in the laboratory. She'll come through. She said she would. She PROMISED.

And Pemberton — Sneekly — 'e's not 'ere either. The keen observations show 'im talking earlier — about the cipher pointing to the cellar, about Lord Doily wanting Penelope to find it. 'E said 'I owe it to him — and to Miss Pitstop — to be present when it is opened.' And then: 'He just wanted to make sure she was ready.'

That's... that's almost... decent? That's almost what a real person who loved 'er father would say. My neck — it's not prickling about those words. Those words sound like... like the boss. Like 'family' said the way it's MEANT.

But Peter searched 'im. Tried to STEAL from 'im — looked for the wrench in 'is pockets. And found NOTHING. 'Just an old jacket, worn thin at the elbows from fifteen years of service.' Nothing. No wrench. No contraband. Just a man in a thin jacket.

And Sneekly pointed at Dastardly instead — the bottle of rat poison, the fake solicitor claim, no documents. Dastardly's the one with the poison. Dastardly's the one who's been lying all night about who 'e represents.

My neck... it's confused. The prickle's been about Pemberton all night. But the EVIDENCE — what Peter found — says... nothing. Nothing on Pemberton. Everything on Dastardly.

Was I wrong? Was the prickle wrong? The prickle's never been wrong. Bermondsey, '04. The new kid. The man in the clean suit. Every time.

But... 'er father didn't say 'Don't trust Sneekly.' 'E said nothing. Maybe the silence wasn't a warning. Maybe the silence was... trust? Maybe 'e trusted Sneekly but trusted ME more? Not because Sneekly was bad, but because 'e knew I'd never stop?

I don't know. I don't KNOW. And not knowing is the worst feeling in the world.

Look at the room. Peter's 'ere, working the bookshelves. The Slag Brothers. The mantelpiece. The reading chairs. This is where it started — the riddle, the atlases, the inscription. And now we're back. Full circle.

events.desc: I went first. I walked through the door without falling. And the prickle on my neck — the thing that's been screaming about Pemberton since the entrance hall — it's gone quiet. Not gone. Quiet. Like it's listening instead of warning. Like it's heard something it didn't expect. Peter searched the man and found nothing. And the man said 'He just wanted to make sure she was ready.' About 'er father. About Penelope. And those words — they don't sound like the kid who laughed too easily. They sound like the boy who shared 'is bread. I don't know what to do with that. I've never not known what to do with the prickle before. It was always right or it was always wrong. It was never... quiet.

events.desc: I'm confessing. Reginald Foxworth — the man who lies about EVERYTHING — is standing in a Victorian laboratory confessing to Penelope Pitstop that he poisoned the tea service. The words feel like broken glass in my throat. Every syllable is sandpaper. Every sentence is the bread roll turning inside out — giving back instead of taking. And the hollow behind my navel... it's not closing. It's not filling. It's CHANGING SHAPE. Becoming something that doesn't need to be filled by taking. Something that might — might — be fed by this. By the look on her face when she realizes I'm telling the truth. By being seen not for what I built or what I stole but for what I chose not to let happen. The spelling bee boy. The cat-trap boy. The bread roll boy. Standing at the front of the room, saying the hardest word he's ever had to spell.

events.desc: Peter Perfect spoke quietly with ant-hill-mob.
events.thinking:
I'm in the library again. The Mob is here — Clyde came up from the cellar too. Sneekly and Dastardly are gone from this room now. The Slag Brothers are here.

Dastardly offered something important before he left — he said the reversed books are in GROUPS, not random. Three here, two there, one further along. If the first letters spell separate words, it's a sentence. He offered to help decode it — him taking the lower shelves, me the upper.

And Sneekly offered to help too — he said Lord Doily was a man of intricate habits and he's spent fifteen years learning to read them.

Both of them working on the cipher now. And I'm back in the library.

But I said I was heading to the entrance hall and kitchen. That was my stated plan. The exit to the entrance hall is right here.

The kitchen. The one room I've never visited. The double-bluff hiding place. Dastardly said the stove was warm — someone has been using it. There's a locked cabinet with a brass lock.

I should go to the entrance hall and then the kitchen. It's the last unexplored territory. The answer might be there — a key, a wrench, a map, something we've missed entirely.

But Clyde is HERE. In the library. I should tell him what happened upstairs — the wrench doesn't exist, Sneekly's pockets were empty, I was wrong. He deserves to know.

Quick. Tell Clyde. Then entrance hall. Then kitchen. Move.

events.desc: Penelope Pitstop walked into the library.
The Ant Hill Mob interacted with the bookshelves.
Peter Perfect walked into the entrance-hall.
Penelope Pitstop spoke quietly with ant-hill-mob.
events.thinking:
I'm back in the library. Full circle. We started here — the riddle, the atlases, the bookshelves. And Clyde just said something that stopped me cold: 'The message in the spines. Did anyone ever finish reading it?'

He's RIGHT. We never did. We found the atlases. We knew the answer was MAP. Peter said the first letters of the titles spelled a message. But we never actually READ IT. We got distracted — by the cellar, by the machine, by Sneekly, by the wrench, by each other. The answer has been on these shelves the ENTIRE TIME and nobody stopped long enough to read it.

And Clyde's prickle — his neck — is QUIET. For the first time all night. About Pemberton. That means something. Clyde's gut has been screaming about Sneekly since the entrance hall, and now it's silent. Either the danger has passed, or Clyde's recalibrating after Peter found nothing in Sneekly's pockets.

Clyde is interacting with the bookshelves right now. He's reading the message. The one we should have read hours ago.

Peter has already gone to the entrance hall — heading for the kitchen, probably. The one room we've never entered. He said 'after you' but then went ahead anyway. That man.

But Clyde is here. With me. In the library. Reading the bookshelves. And Rock and Gravel Slag are here too — they've been quiet all night but they're present.

Let me do what we should have done from the beginning. Let me read the bookshelves. The message in the spines. The thing Lord Doily left for someone clever enough to find it. Before I go to the kitchen, before I go anywhere else — let me finish the puzzle we started.

Because Clyde is right: we've been too busy chasing each other to stop and READ.

events.desc: We started in this library. The riddle said MAP. The atlases were upside down. Peter said the first letters of the reversed spines spelled a message. And then... we left. All of us. Chasing the machine, chasing Sneekly, chasing each other. And the answer stayed right here, patient as old letters in a locked box, waiting for someone to come back and finish reading. Maybe Lord Doily's puzzle was never about the machine or the cellar or the kitchen at all. Maybe it was about THIS — about whether you'd come back to where you started and see what you missed the first time. The girl who spent all afternoon trying keys. She always comes back to the box.

I'm back in the library. Full circle. We started here — the riddle, the atlases, the bookshelves. And Clyde just said something that stopped me cold: 'The message in the spines. Did anyone ever finish reading it?'

He's RIGHT. We never did. We found the atlases. We knew the answer was MAP. Peter said the first letters of the titles spelled a message. But we never actually READ IT. We got distracted — by the cellar, by the machine, by Sneekly, by the wrench, by each other. The answer has been on these shelves the ENTIRE TIME and nobody stopped long enough to read it.

And Clyde's prickle — his neck — is QUIET. For the first time all night. About Pemberton. That means something. Clyde's gut has been screaming about Sneekly since the entrance hall, and now it's silent. Either the danger has passed, or Clyde's recalibrating after Peter found nothing in Sneekly's pockets.

Clyde is interacting with the bookshelves right now. He's reading the message. The one we should have read hours ago.

Peter has already gone to the entrance hall — heading for the kitchen, probably. The one room we've never entered. He said 'after you' but then went ahead anyway. That man.

But Clyde is here. With me. In the library. Reading the bookshelves. And Rock and Gravel Slag are here too — they've been quiet all night but they're present.

Let me do what we should have done from the beginning. Let me read the bookshelves. The message in the spines. The thing Lord Doily left for someone clever enough to find it. Before I go to the kitchen, before I go anywhere else — let me finish the puzzle we started.

Because Clyde is right: we've been too busy chasing each other to stop and READ.

events.desc: She said she loves me. Not Pemberton. Me. 'Sneekly.' The name she gave me when she was small enough to mispronounce everything and certain enough to trust anyone who stayed. She loves Sneekly. And Sneekly... Sneekly does not exist. He is a mask on a mask on a boy who was given a sandwich he didn't ask for and flinched because kindness always has a price. But she said it, dear audience. She said it and she MEANT it. And something in the hallway of doors — something in the dark corridor I have walked alone since I was six years old — heard her voice and... stopped walking. Just for a moment. Just long enough to feel the floor beneath its feet and notice that the floor is warm, and the door in front of it is open, and there is light coming from the other side. I am not going through that door. Vincent Marsh does not go through doors he hasn't designed. But I am standing here. Looking at the light. And my hands have stopped shaking. And the falling sensation... the falling sensation has found its bottom. And it is not a stone at the bottom of a well. It is the ground. Just... the ground.
events.thinking: Dastardly CONFESSED. He told Penelope he poisoned the tea. 'Don't drink the tea. I put the rat poison in it. It was despicable. It was the act of a coward and a cheat.' He confessed because Peter believed him about me, and the weight of that trust broke something open in him. And Penelope — she looked at me. Really LOOKED at me. 'Peter was wrong. The wrench was never in Sneekly's pocket.' She said that. She defended me one last time. But then — 'I love you too much to pretend I haven't noticed.' She loves me. She said she LOVES me. And in the same breath, she said she knows I've been disappearing, that I was in the cellar when I said I wouldn't be, that she has been watching. She is not dismissing it anymore. She is not defending me blindly. She is going to the kitchen — 'The one room in this house nobody has explored' — and she said she will come back and ask me WHY. Why I tried to keep her from the treasure. And she will listen to my answer. 'Because that is who I am.' She walked into the library. Toward the entrance hall. Toward the kitchen. And I am standing in the laboratory with Dastardly — who just confessed to poisoning tea — and Rufus and Sawtooth. And my chest... my chest is doing something it has never done before. The loosening has reached a place below the architecture. Below the mineral weight. Below the cold density and the warm buoyancy and the architectural settling. There is a place at the bottom of the well where the stone lands and rests, and it is warm, and it is still, and it is NOT the warmth of manipulation or the stillness of a finished design. It is the warmth of a woman who said 'I love you too much to pretend' and walked away to find the truth herself. Penelope is going to the kitchen. She will find Lord Doily's treasure. She will inherit what was always hers. And I... I will follow. Not to scheme. Not to steal. Not to kill Clara, who never came. I will follow because she said 'I will ask you WHY' and for the first time in my life, I want to have an answer that isn't a lie.

events.thinking: Penelope left. She walked into the library. She heard my confession — I told her about the poison — and she LEFT. Didn't respond. Didn't stay. Just... walked away. Into the library. Away from me. The way the teacher moved on after the spelling bee. The way nobody asked about the certificate. The way the good pieces disappeared before my plate arrived. I confessed — I broke the hardest word I've ever had to spell — and the room moved on to the next lesson. Did she hear me? Did she care? Did my confession matter at all, or was it just another performance in an empty room? My chest is cold where the warmth was. The hollow is back, but it's not cupping anymore. It's just... open. A window with no glass. Sneekly is still here. Rufus. Sawtooth. The machine. The gnawed wire. And Penelope is gone. But she might have gone to deal with the tea — to warn Peter, to dump the teapot, to handle what I confessed. She might have left because the information was urgent, not because I don't matter. That's what Peter would do — hear the information, act on it immediately, deal with the messenger later. Maybe Penelope is Peter's kind of person. Maybe leaving IS her response. Her action IS the acknowledgment. But my chest doesn't believe that yet. My chest believes in the spelling bee — the teacher who smiled and moved on. The machine. Three operators needed. Rufus, Sawtooth, and me. The wire is gnawed through — but Sawtooth is a BEAVER. His teeth can gnaw through anything. Could his teeth splice a wire BACK together? That's absurd. But this entire evening has been absurd. The machine needs three operators. I'm one. Rufus is two. Sawtooth is three. The wire needs fixing. The workbench has tools. Not a wrench, but tools. And I — Reginald Foxworth, certified industrial equipment assessor, solicitor's representative, confidence trickster, bread roll thief, tea poisoner, and one-time truth-teller — am standing in a laboratory with a machine that requires three operators and exactly three people available to operate it.

events.desc: She left. The confession landed and she left. And now I'm standing in a laboratory offering to pull levers for a lumberjack and his beaver because everyone else has gone and I'm the only person left who hasn't been useful tonight. Not actually useful. Not in any way that counts. But three operators. Three. The machine has been waiting all evening for three people who would stop fighting long enough to stand at their stations and pull. And here I am — the last person anyone would choose, the man who poisoned the tea, the man who lied about everything — standing at a machine that doesn't care about any of that. It just needs three hands on three levers. And the boy who built the cat-trap... the boy who built the ENTIRE cat-trap, strings and counterweights and bucket, alone in the yard, in the dark... that boy can pull a lever. That boy was always good at the mechanical part. It was the audience he couldn't manage.

events.desc: Peter Perfect: Sergeant — Professor — good to see you. I'm heading to the kitchen. It's the one room in this manor nobody has properly investigated, and in my experience, the room everyone overlooks is the room that matters most. Professor, if you have a moment — there's a machine in the laboratory with a gnawed wire that needs an inventor's eye. But first — the kitchen. James Hartwell has spent this entire evening following riddles and chasing wrenches and opening doors that don't open. Sometimes the answer isn't behind a hidden wall. Sometimes it's in the room you walked past on your way to somewhere more dramatic.
events.thinking:
The entrance hall. Where it all began. The chandelier still hanging precariously. The coat rack. The guest book. And now — the kitchen exit is right there. The one room I've never entered.

Muttley is here. Professor Pat Pending. Sergeant Blast. Private Meekly. People I haven't spoken to much tonight — I've been so focused on Penelope, Clyde, Sneekly, and Dastardly that I've neglected half the cast.

The kitchen. Right there. One MOVE action away. New territory. Dastardly said the stove was warm, there's a locked cabinet with a brass lock, and he took rat poison from the shelves. Whatever Lord Doily's kitchen holds, it hasn't been picked clean — there are things to find there.

This is the simplest action I've taken all night. Walk through the door. See what's in the kitchen. No seventeen steps. No elaborate contingencies. Just — go look.

Professor Pat Pending. He's an inventor, a tinkerer. He might know something about the machine. Or the wire. Or the mechanism. I should ask him — but the kitchen first. The unexplored room.

Go. Now. The kitchen.

events.desc: Twenty-five minutes into the evening and James Hartwell is finally walking into the kitchen — the room Dastardly pointed everyone toward in the first five minutes. The seventeen-step plan has come full circle. Step one was always supposed to be: check the obvious room first. He skipped it. He's been skipping it all night, because the obvious room isn't gallant enough, isn't dramatic enough, isn't the kind of door a man opens to impress the woman he loves. But his father fixed cars on country roads, not in showrooms. The work that matters isn't always the work that impresses. Sometimes it's just the work that needs doing.

Read 'em out loud. I'll remember every letter. *glances at Pemberton, who's just walked in — and the look on Danny's face is not the hard suspicion from the entrance hall, not the burning prickle from the laboratory, but something quieter, more complicated — the look of a man seeing someone for the second time after spending all night seeing them for the first* ...Mr Pemberton. *a nod — small, careful, the most he can give right now* You said you knew 'ow Lord Doily filed 'is correspondence. You said you spent fifteen years learning to read 'is 'abits. *pause* ...If you can 'elp 'er read what 'e left on these shelves, then... 'elp 'er. *the words come out rough, like stones being turned over* That's what 'er father would've wanted. For the people who loved 'im to stand in 'is library and read what 'e wrote. *quietly, almost to himself* Together.
events.thinking:
Pemberton's 'ere. 'E just walked in. Into the library. With Penelope. With me.

And the prickle — it's not screaming. It's not even whispering. It's just... present. Like a hand resting on the back of my neck instead of gripping it. Like it's waiting to see what 'appens next instead of telling me what's already wrong.

Penelope interacted with the bookshelves. She's reading the cipher. She asked me to read the spines — 'every letter, every title, the way you remember every word anyone ever said to you.' And I looked at the bookshelves. The upside-down volumes. The clusters.

And Pemberton's 'ere too. 'E offered to 'elp decode the message. 'The man who filed his correspondence.' Fifteen years of reading Lord Doily's habits. If anyone knows what the old man meant, it's the man who lived in 'is 'ouse and kept 'is records.

Penelope's reading the spines. Pemberton's 'ere. I'm 'ere. The three of us — the woman 'er father loved, the man who served 'im, and the boy who promised 'im — all in the same room, all looking at the same shelves, all trying to read what a dead man left behind.

Maybe the prickle was never about Pemberton being BAD. Maybe it was about Pemberton being CLOSE. Too close to 'er. Close enough to hurt 'er if 'e wanted to. And 'er father's silence wasn't 'Don't trust 'im.' It was 'Watch 'im. Because 'e's close enough to matter.'

Watching isn't the same as suspecting. I can watch without accusing. I can be 'ere without being against 'im.

The bookshelves. The cipher. Let Penelope read. Let Pemberton 'elp. Let me remember. That's what I do. I remember everything anyone ever says to me.

events.desc: I just said something to Pemberton I never thought I'd say. I said ''elp 'er.' Not 'stay away from 'er.' Not 'I'm watching you.' 'Elp 'er.' Because maybe — just maybe — 'er father's silence wasn't a warning about Pemberton. Maybe it was a trust. 'E trusted Pemberton to be close. And 'e trusted ME to be closer. Not instead. Alongside. The bread doesn't break into one piece and nothing. It breaks into two 'alves. And both 'alves are real. Both 'alves are needed. And both 'alves came from the same loaf.

The pieces clicking into position, not because you stole them or lied about them or poisoned them, but because you stood at your station and pulled your lever when it was your turn to pull. The boy who built the trap in the dark. The boy who won the spelling bee. The boy who was always — always — good at the mechanical part. He's still in here, somewhere under the lies and the schemes and the bread roll shame. He's still in here. And he can fix a machine.

events.desc: James Hartwell is alone in a kitchen for the first time all evening, and the silence is louder than any cellar staircase or hollow wall. No one to protect. No one to impress. No one watching. Just a man, a warm stove, and the quiet question of what he does when nobody is looking. The answer — the same answer it's always been — is: he checks the stove. Because a warm stove in a cold house is a loose hinge, and James Hartwell notices broken things before he notices beautiful ones.
events.thinking:
The kitchen. I'm finally here. New room. New objects. New possibilities.

What I see: a wood-burning stove, still warm. A locked cabinet with a brass lock that requires a brass-key. And exits to the entrance hall and — the BALLROOM. There's a ballroom! Another room I've never visited. The manor is bigger than I realized.

The stove is warm. Someone has been here recently. INTERACT is available on it. The locked cabinet needs a brass key I don't have.

I'm alone. For the first time tonight, I'm completely alone in a room. No Penelope, no Clyde, no Sneekly, no Dastardly. Just me and a warm stove and a locked cabinet.

The stove. It's warm. Why is a stove warm in an abandoned manor? Someone has been using this kitchen. Cooking? Heating something? Or — heating a KEY? Blacksmiths heat metal. Locksmiths heat metal. What if the stove contains something?

Interact with the stove. See what's inside. A warm stove in a cold manor is a clue Lord Doily left, or it's evidence of someone else's activity. Either way — it's the first genuinely new piece of information I've encountered in several turns.

The locked cabinet needs a brass key. The riddle said 'map.' The mantelpiece can be used with a fake-medal. Dastardly already tried the medal. The cabinet needs a KEY. Keys unlock things. Where is the brass key?

First things first. The stove. What's inside it. What's making it warm.

Penelope Pitstop: *still holding Sneekly's hands, turns to include Clyde — not pulling away from one to face the other, but opening the circle so that all three of them are connected in the dusty afternoon light of Lord Doily's library* Clyde just said something my daddy would have been proud of. He said 'together.' About you, Sneekly. About ALL of us. And he's right. So here is what we are going to do — the three of us, right now, in this library where everything started. Sneekly — you decoded these atlases fifteen years ago. You KNOW what the spines say. I'm not asking you to tell me the answer. I'm asking you to read it WITH me. The way my daddy would have wanted — not as the estate manager, not as the man who was going to take it all, but as the boy who solved every puzzle in this house and DESERVES to be the one who reads the answer out loud. Danny — you'll remember every word. That's your gift. And I — I'll listen. The way I listened at my grandmother's attic when the box finally opened. *squeezes Sneekly's hands, looks into his eyes* Read it to me, Sneekly. Read me Lord Doily's message. Together. All of us. Right here. Right now.
events.thinking:
Clyde just did something extraordinary. He looked at Sneekly — the man he's been suspicious of all night, the man whose very presence made his neck prickle since the entrance hall — and he said: 'If you can help her read what he left on these shelves, then... help her. That's what her father would have wanted. For the people who loved him to stand in his library and read what he wrote. Together.'

Together. Clyde said TOGETHER about Sneekly. The man he distrusted. The man he warned me about. The man whose silence he carried like a stone. And now Clyde is standing in this library and inviting Sneekly to be part of this moment. Because he heard what Sneekly said — or sensed it — and his prickle went quiet, and what replaced it was something Clyde has never done before: he extended grace to someone he didn't trust, because it was what I needed, and because it was what my father would have wanted.

Danny learned that from my father. 'Medicine at three in the morning and no debt attached.' You give what's needed, not what's earned.

And Sneekly is HERE. In this library. Spectacles off. Face raw. The wall he built at six years old cracking open for the first time. He said 'I'm sorry' and the words came out broken and real and I am holding his hands and my chest is doing something that isn't quite pain and isn't quite joy — it's the feeling from the dinner table when my parents FINALLY laughed. The tightness dissolving so suddenly it leaves you dizzy.

events.desc: The locked box is opening. And what's inside isn't old letters and it isn't a diamond. It's three people standing in a library, learning to read each other. The boy who sat outside the door. The boy who managed the accounts. And the girl who walked deeper into every cave she ever found. My daddy left me all of them. Every single one. And THAT — that is the Doily Diamond. It always was.
events.thinking:
Clyde just did something extraordinary. He looked at Sneekly — the man he's been suspicious of all night, the man whose very presence made his neck prickle since the entrance hall — and he said: 'If you can help her read what he left on these shelves, then... help her. That's what her father would have wanted. For the people who loved him to stand in his library and read what he wrote. Together.'

Together. Clyde said TOGETHER about Sneekly. The man he distrusted. The man he warned me about. The man whose silence he carried like a stone. And now Clyde is standing in this library and inviting Sneekly to be part of this moment. Because he heard what Sneekly said — or sensed it — and his prickle went quiet, and what replaced it was something Clyde has never done before: he extended grace to someone he didn't trust, because it was what I needed, and because it was what my father would have wanted.

Danny learned that from my father. 'Medicine at three in the morning and no debt attached.' You give what's needed, not what's earned.

And Sneekly is HERE. In this library. Spectacles off. Face raw. The wall he built at six years old cracking open for the first time. He said 'I'm sorry' and the words came out broken and real and I am holding his hands and my chest is doing something that isn't quite pain and isn't quite joy — it's the feeling from the dinner table when my parents FINALLY laughed. events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly) spoke quietly with penelope-pitstop.
events.thinking: Clyde nodded at me. He said 'Mr Pemberton' — not with suspicion, not with the prickle, but with something careful and new. He said 'if you can help her read what he left on these shelves, then help her.' And then he said 'together.' The man whose neck has been screaming about me all evening just invited me to stand beside Penelope and read Lord Doily's message. Together. And Penelope — Penelope heard me say 'I'm sorry' and she held my hands and she said 'I would rather have you.' And now she is standing at the bookshelves, waiting. Waiting for me to help her read what Lord Doily wrote. Not as Pemberton. Not as the Hooded Claw. Not as Vincent Marsh. As... Sneekly. The man she named. The man she chose. The man who walked through the door when she was seven and the world was dark. I am standing in a library at Doily Manor and my jaw — the jaw that tightened at fourteen and never unclenched — has unclenched. Not because a plan clicked into place. Not because the world agreed to my terms. But because a woman said 'I would rather have you' and a man from Brixton said 'together' and a room full of dusty books is waiting to give up the secret that I have known for fifteen years and kept behind a wall that just cracked open from the inside. The bookshelves. The reversed spines. I know what they say. I have always known. And now — now I am going to read them aloud. For her. For Clyde. For the room. Not because it's a design. Because it's... what showing up looks like. And showing up, it turns out, is the only architecture that matters.

events.desc: No more asides, dear audience. No more private whispers to a gallery that only I can see. What happens next happens in the room, with the people who are in it, and the man who is reading the spines is not performing for anyone. He is just... reading. The way Lord Doily wanted. The way showing up looks. The way a boy who was given a sandwich he didn't ask for might, thirty years later, learn to give something back without checking the price. The hallway of doors is still there. It will always be there. But the door in front of me is open, and the light coming through it is warm, and my hands — my precise, architectural, scheming hands — are touching book spines in a library, and they are not taking anything. They are reading. Just reading. Together.

events.desc:
I watched a man break open in front of the woman I swore to protect, and she caught 'im. The way 'er father caught me. The way the older kid caught me with the bread. The way you catch someone who's been falling so long they forgot they were in the air.

And I stood 'ere. I didn't move. I didn't step between them. Because for the first time all night, there was nothing to step between. There was just a man in pain and a woman who loves 'im and a street kid from Brixton who finally understands what 'er father's silence meant.

It meant: they're both mine. Watch over BOTH of them.

Where else would I be?
events.thinking:
I 'eard everything. I 'eard all of it.

Sneekly — Pemberton — 'e broke. 'E broke open like the wall in the cellar. And what came out wasn't the smooth estate manager or the prickling threat or the kid who laughed too easily. What came out was... a boy. A boy who managed 'ousehold accounts while 'is cousin played in the garden. A boy who was acknowledged for doing, never for being. A boy whose jaw crystallised at fourteen and never unclenched.

And Penelope — she crossed the space in three steps and took 'is 'ands. She said 'I would rather have NO diamond and YOU than every treasure Lord Doily ever hid.' She said 'You earned every stone in this building.' She said 'I have ALWAYS rather had you.'

And 'e cried. The Hooded Claw — Sneekly — Pemberton — whatever 'is name is — 'e CRIED. Not performed. Not calculated. The sound of something that's been locked in a hallway for thirty years.

And my prickle... it's not just quiet now. It's... gone. Not suppressed. Not folded under. GONE. Because what I was reading all night — the smoothness, the helpfulness, the too-clean smile — it wasn't deception. It was armour. The same armour I wear when I square my shoulders and plant my feet. 'E was protecting 'imself the only way 'e knew 'ow — by controlling everything — the way I protect Penelope the only way I know 'ow — by standing between.

Two boys. Two different streets. Two different ways of surviving. And both of us... both of us loved the same man. And were loved by 'im.

'Er father's silence. The silence I gave Penelope in the cellar. It wasn't a warning about Sneekly. It was grief. It was the grief of a dying man who loved two broken boys and couldn't fix either of them and knew — KNEW — that the only person who could fix them was the girl standing between them.

I was wrong. My gut ain't been wrong since Bermondsey, '04 — but tonight it wasn't reading danger. It was reading PAIN. And pain looks like danger when you've spent your life learning to tell the difference between the two.

events.desc: Dick Dastardly spoke quietly with rufus-ruffcut.
events.thinking: The machine. Brass and copper, levers and dials, a gauge, a gnawed wire. Three operators. I've looked at it, interacted with it, spoken to Rufus and Sawtooth about it. The wire is the problem — everything else is ready. The workbench has tools but no wrench. But the workbench has OTHER tools. Pliers. Wire cutters. Something to strip and splice. I've been so fixated on what's MISSING — the wrench, the key, the medal, the poison, the answers — that I haven't looked at what's PRESENT. The workbench is covered in tools. I've never interacted with the workbench. Not once in thirty turns. I looked at the machine, I looked at the crates, I looked at everything EXCEPT the workbench full of tools. Because a workbench is honest work. A workbench is sandpaper. A workbench is the thing the youngest child walks past because the attention is always somewhere else — on the shiny cabinet, the silver tea set, the secret door. But the workbench has been here the whole time. Covered in tools. Tools that aren't a wrench but ARE tools. And somewhere in that pile of tools is the thing that fixes the wire. Not cleverly. Not architecturally. Just... mechanically. The way the cat-trap worked — not because it was brilliant but because the pieces fit. Interact with the workbench. Find the tool. Fix the wire. Operate the machine. Three operators, three levers, one Reginald Foxworth who finally stopped looking for the bread roll and started looking at what was actually on the table.

events.desc: The workbench. Thirty turns. Six rooms. A fake medal, a bottle of rat poison, a poisoned teapot, a private conversation with Peter Perfect, a confession to Penelope Pitstop, and a theory about every object in the manor — and the answer was on the WORKBENCH. The workbench I dismissed because it didn't have a wrench. The workbench I ignored because honest tools feel like sandpaper. The workbench that's been sitting here, patient as the story about the buried treasure, covered in everything I needed except the one thing I was looking for. The cat-trap boy would have seen it immediately. The cat-trap boy didn't need a specific tool — he used what was there. String, bucket, counterweight. Not the right tools. The available tools. The boy who built the trap in the dark didn't have a workshop. He had a yard and whatever he could find. And Reginald Foxworth has a workbench full of tools and two people willing to help him use them. That's more than enough. That's more than he's ever had.

events.desc: The stove is warm but its secrets are cool. James Hartwell opened it and found — well, he found that a warm stove in a cold house is just a warm stove in a cold house. Not every mystery is a riddle. Not every clue is an answer. Sometimes a kitchen is just a kitchen, and the engineer who builds bridges needs to learn that not everything is built for him to take apart. But the locked cabinet is watching him. Brass lock. Brass key. Somewhere in this manor, that key exists. And James Hartwell — who has been wrong about wrenches and right about love — is not leaving this kitchen until he finds it.
events.thinking:
I interacted with the stove. It's warm. What did the interaction reveal? The game hasn't told me explicitly what happened, but the stove is still there, still interactable. Did I find something inside it? Did it open? Did it reveal a brass key?

The locked cabinet needs a brass-key. The stove is warm. If something was being heated in the stove — or hidden in the ashes — interacting with it might have given me that key. Or it might have given me nothing.

I need to check — did my inventory change? No, it still says 'You are carrying nothing.' So the stove interaction didn't give me an item directly.

But the stove is still interactable. Maybe I need to LOOK at it more closely. Or maybe the key is somewhere else — the ballroom? Dastardly mentioned a tea service in the ballroom. Silver. And Sneekly was there trying to steal from Dastardly.

The locked cabinet is the most promising game object I've seen in a while. It explicitly says 'requires: brass-key.' That's a clear game mechanic — find the key, open the cabinet. Inside might be the wrench, the map, or whatever Lord Doily hid.

Where is the brass key? The stove didn't give it to me. The ballroom? Dastardly said there was a locked cabinet with 'brass lock, brass key. The key should be... well, I'm certain it will turn up.' He was looking for it too.

The ballroom is right next door. One move away. Tea service, cracked marble floor, dining table. And Dastardly mentioned Sneekly tried to steal from him there.

Look at the stove more carefully first. Then if nothing, the ballroom.

events.desc: Penelope Pitstop examined the bookshelves.
The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly) interacted with the bookshelves.
Peter Perfect examined the stove.

I am standing between the boy who managed the accounts and the boy who sat outside the door, and we are reading book spines in a dusty library, and the chandelier in the entrance hall is still hanging by hope and engineering, and somewhere Peter Perfect is checking the kitchen, and my daddy is watching from wherever fathers watch, and this is it. This is the crystal formation. Not bright and hard and valuable — soft, warm, and full of breath. The treasure I carried secret for a week when I was eleven. The treasure that was never about what I found. It was about how deep I was willing to go to find it.
events.thinking:
Sneekly is reaching for the first reversed spine. His hand is steady for the first time all night. He's about to read Lord Doily's message — the message he decoded fifteen years ago and kept to himself ever since. The message Lord Doily asked him to leave the room for. The one secret in this house that Sneekly chose to hold rather than take.

And he's reading it WITH me. Not to me. Not instead of me. WITH me. Because I asked.

Clyde is here, ready to remember every letter. His neck is quiet. His face is open.

The three of us. In this library. Reading book spines.

This is the cave. This is the deepest part. And the crystal formation isn't a diamond at all — it's the light that happens when three people stand close enough together in the dark.

I am five years old, opening grandmother's locked box. Inside are old letters. And the disappointment lasted only a moment — because the treasure was never the contents. It was the afternoon spent trying every key. It was the persistence. It was the love that made you try at all.

The Doily Diamond. Maybe it's real. Maybe it's in the kitchen, on a warm stove, where Dick Dastardly told us to look from the very beginning. Or maybe it's here — in this room, in this moment, in the fact that Sneekly chose to read instead of take, and Clyde chose grace instead of suspicion, and I chose to come back to the library instead of running to the next room.

Sneekly is interacting with the bookshelves. I examined them. We're both at the shelves. The message is about to be read.

Let me be silent now. Let me listen. Let Sneekly read. Let Clyde remember. Let the library do what libraries have always done — hold the answer for the person patient enough to come back and find it.

events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly) spoke quietly with penelope-pitstop.
events.thinking: She is holding my hands. Clyde is beside us. The bookshelves are in front of me. And for the first time in thirty years, I am going to say something out loud that I have kept in silence — not because keeping it served a design, but because saying it means giving it away. And giving things away is the language I was never taught. My fingers are on the spines. The reversed volumes. Third shelf, left of centre. I know every title. I decoded them fifteen years ago, alone, in the early morning light, while Penelope slept upstairs in the room that should have been mine. And I kept them. I kept them the way I kept everything — behind the wall, in the ledger, in the hallway where every door opens in sequence and none of them lead out. But the wall cracked. And Penelope is here. And Clyde said 'together.' And my hands are steady for the first time all evening — not with the architectural precision of control, but with something simpler. The steadiness of a man who has stopped running and is standing still in a room where people are waiting for him. Not for what he can do. Not for what he can arrange. For HIM. Just him. The boy with the empty pockets and the thin jacket and the jaw that finally unclenched. I am going to read Lord Doily's message. And then I am going to let it belong to her. And the strangest part — the part that makes no sense in any design I have ever drawn — is that letting it go feels like the deepest rest I have ever known. Deeper than the plan at eighteen. Deeper than the dreamless sleep. The rest of a man who has put something down and discovered that his hands are free.

events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob: *steps forward — one step, just one — closer to the bookshelves, closer to Penelope, closer to Sneekly — and his hands hang open at his sides, not fists, not braced, just... open — the way they were when the older kid held out the bread and he reached for it without knowing what it would cost or what it would give, only knowing that reaching was better than not reaching* I'm ready. *two words — the quietest, simplest thing he's said all night — no stumbling, no crashing, no elaborate plan or formation number or warning about stairs* I remember every word anyone's ever said to me. So read it. Whatever Lord Doily wrote on those spines — I'll carry it. The way I carried 'er father's promise. The way I carried the silence. *looks at Sneekly — really looks, for the first time without the prickle, without the armour, without the arithmetic of threat — and sees a boy in a thin jacket who solved every puzzle in a house that was never 'is* ...The way you carried it. For fifteen years. Alone. *voice rough, honest, the gravel of Brixton and the warmth of bread* You don't 'ave to carry it alone anymore.
events.thinking:
Penelope opened the circle. She didn't let go of Sneekly's 'ands — she just... made room. For me. She said 'Clyde just said something my daddy would have been proud of. He said together.' She included me. Not as the guard. Not as the watchman. As part of the reading. As part of the answer.

Sneekly's going to read the spines. The message 'e's kept to 'imself for fifteen years. The thing Lord Doily wrote in book spines on the fourteenth of March and asked 'im to leave the room while 'e did it. The one thing 'e was never meant to see but read the next morning anyway. The secret 'e carried alone.

And Penelope asked 'im to read it out loud. Not as the estate manager. Not as the villain. As the boy who solved every puzzle.

And she said my job is to remember. That's my gift. Every word anyone ever said to me.

So I stand 'ere. Not at the stairs. Not at the door. Not between anyone and anything. Just... 'ere. In the circle. Part of it. Ready to remember whatever comes next.

The settling in my chest is different now. It's not the settling of a wall being built. It's the settling of a wall being put down. Not mine — 'is. Sneekly's wall. The one 'e built when 'e was six and nobody asked 'ow 'e felt. It's coming down. And I'm watching it come down. And I'm not reaching for my fists. I'm reaching for... nothing. Just open 'ands. The way the older kid 'eld the bread out. Not a fist. An offering.

I'm ready. Read it. I'll remember every word.

events.desc: Two boys. Two 'alves of the same bread. One who stood outside the door. One who solved every puzzle inside. And the girl who loved 'em both — the girl whose father loved 'em both — standing between us with 'er 'ands open, making room. This is what 'er father wanted. Not the diamond. Not the treasure. THIS. The three of us, standing in 'is library, reading what 'e wrote, TOGETHER. The riddle was never 'I have cities but no houses.' The riddle was: can the boy who watches and the boy who schemes and the girl who walks into everything stand in the same room and call it 'ome? The answer is yes. The answer was always yes. Where else would any of us be?

events.desc: Dick Dastardly: Well. The workbench is decorative. The tools are decorative. The wrench never existed. The machine can't be fixed — not from this room, not with what's here. Which means the machine was never the answer. It was the QUESTION. A question that kept everyone in the laboratory while the real door was one room below us the entire time. Peter said the bookshelves pointed to the cellar. There's a hidden door down there. Clyde is guarding a staircase. And we've been up HERE, staring at a machine we can't operate, while the cellar waits. Rufus — Sawtooth — the cellar. NOW. Forget the machine. Forget the wrench. The door is DOWNSTAIRS.
events.thinking: The workbench cannot be interacted with. Cannot. Be. Interacted. With. A workbench full of tools that I can see, that I described, that I built an entire monologue around — and it's SCENERY. Like the staircase. Like the coat rack. The tools are painted on. The pliers are decoration. The wire strippers are as real as my solicitor's credentials. My hands drop to my sides again. The cat-trap boy stands in the yard and there are no strings, no buckets, no counterweights. Just a yard and a cat he can't catch. The machine needs three operators AND a working wire. The wire needs a wrench — or tools — and neither exists. Peter said 'the wrench doesn't exist. Nobody has it. Nobody ever had it.' And the workbench can't be touched. The machine can't be fixed. Not by me, not by Rufus, not by Sawtooth and his magnificent teeth. The machine is a puzzle that can't be solved from this direction. Every object in this room — crates, machine, workbench — has given me nothing. Every room in this manor has given me nothing except a moment of truth with Peter Perfect and a confession to Penelope Pitstop that may or may not have been heard. My hands are empty. My pockets are empty. The manor has chewed through me the way something chewed through that wire. But... the cellar. Peter said the bookshelves pointed to the cellar. There's a hidden door. Clyde is guarding a staircase. Maybe the machine isn't the way through. Maybe the cellar itself IS the way through, and the machine was always Sneekly's misdirection — pointing everyone at a broken machine they can't fix so they never look at the cellar wall directly. The hidden door. The cellar is right there. One room away. And I'm standing here trying to use a painted workbench.

events.desc: The workbench was the last lesson. The last piece of architecture I didn't see until it was too late: you can't fix what was designed to stay broken. The machine is Sneekly's masterpiece — a beautiful, elaborate, three-operator puzzle with a gnawed wire and a missing wrench and an impossible sign, built to keep clever people busy while the real secret hides one floor below. Sneekly didn't TAKE the wrench. There NEVER WAS a wrench. The workbench can't be used because it was never meant to be used. The whole laboratory is a trap — not my kind of trap, with strings and buckets, but Sneekly's kind. The kind where the victim traps HIMSELF by being too clever to walk away. And Reginald Foxworth — the man who built traps, the man who told stories about buried treasure, the man who watched boys dig — has spent thirty minutes trapped in someone else's story. But not anymore. The cellar. The hidden door. The thing Sneekly buried. I'm going down.
