events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob spoke quietly with hooded-claw.
events.thinking: I'm in the kitchen. Sneekly's at the stove making tea. Dastardly is sitting at the preparation table — no flourish, no performance, just a tired man who just confessed there are no kitchen vaults and he made up most things tonight. And Sneekly said 'you didn't have to come back.' Two men in a kitchen at the end of a long night, one making tea he once poisoned, the other accepting it from the man who hid the wrench. And I just walked in. Tripped on the way. The kitchen is warm from the stove and I can smell the cast iron heating and somewhere behind me Penelope and Peter are in the entrance hall and the coat rack is wobbling and tomorrow exists and right now — right now — there is tea.

events.desc: Dick Dastardly spoke quietly with ant-hill-mob.
events.thinking: Sneekly is making tea. The kettle is on the stove. Clyde walked in too — followed us, the way Clyde follows everything, stumbling into rooms he wasn't invited to and somehow belonging there more than anyone who planned to be. The copper pots catch the lamplight. The preparation table is solid under my elbows. And I told him — I told Sneekly — there are no kitchen vaults. I made them up. I said 'most things, actually.' The truth sitting in my mouth like someone else's clothes and somehow fitting better than I expected. He said I didn't have to come back. But I did. And now we're here — Sneekly, Clyde, and the youngest of four — waiting for tea that nobody poisoned in a kitchen with no vaults and a locked cabinet that belongs to the house.

events.desc: Penelope Pitstop walked into the kitchen.
Peter Perfect walked into the kitchen.

Penelope Pitstop: *walks into the warm kitchen, on Peter's arm, and the stove light catches her face the way the cabinet light caught whatever Lord Doily left inside, and she looks at everyone — Sneekly at the kettle, Dick in the doorway, Clyde at the table — and does not carry the room, does not orchestrate the moment, does not make sure everyone is settled before she settles herself — just stands there, warm and tired and real, and breathes in the smell of a kitchen where tea is being made* ...This is it, isn't it. *quiet, to everyone and no one* This is what was in the cabinet.
events.thinking: The kitchen. The stove. The copper pots. Sneekly at the kettle. Dick in the corner. Clyde by the table. Peter on my arm. And the ballroom — there's a ballroom, with a door right here, and Sneekly said 'I'll have the ballroom ready' and Dick said 'I'll bring the biscuits.' Tomorrow is already being built. Right here. Over tea. In Lord Doily's kitchen with Lord Doily's kettle on Lord Doily's stove. The treasure is that you came looking. The treasure is that you stayed for tea.

events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly): *reaches for the shelf above the stove — second shelf, behind the copper colander, the muscle memory of fifteen years — and brings down cup after cup after cup, setting them on the preparation table with small, careful sounds* Five. *the word comes out quieter than intended* Lord Doily never believed in matching sets. He said identical teacups were a failure of imagination. *places the last cup — chipped, blue, a painted heron on one side — in front of the empty chair* ...There's enough for everyone. *looks at Penelope, and for one breath does not perform anything at all* There was always enough. I just... didn't know that.
events.thinking: Penelope. Peter. They're here too. The kitchen is full. FULL. Four people plus me, in a room where twenty minutes ago I sat alone and thought the word 'home' and meant it as a grave. Dastardly is confessing to Clyde. Clyde has his elbows on my table. And now Penelope is standing in the doorway — Penelope, who called me Sneekly, who said the house was in good hands, who told me to leave the cabinet open — and Peter is beside her, steady as a wall, and they are all HERE and the kettle is on and I need more cups. Five cups. I have never made tea for five people without an ulterior motive. My hands know where the cups are. Fifteen years of muscle memory. Second shelf, behind the copper colander. Five mismatched Victorian teacups that Lord Doily collected from different sets because he thought matching things were boring. I am going to put tea in five cups and hand them to people who came back for me and I am going to do it without a design and my chest feels like it's made of something thinner than skin and thicker than air and I don't know what that material is called but I think other people build their whole lives out of it.

events.desc: Five cups on a table. No mechanism. No design. No beautiful inevitability. Just porcelain and hot water and people who walked into a kitchen because they wanted to be here. Dear audience — I have schemed and plotted and manipulated my way through every room in this manor. I have designed traps that would have made Rube Goldberg weep with envy. And not one of those designs — not ONE — produced anything half as terrifying, half as bewildering, half as unbearably warm as five mismatched teacups on a preparation table at the end of a very long night. The Hooded Claw is dead. Long live... whatever this is.
events.thinking: Penelope. Peter. They're here too. The kitchen is full. FULL. Four people plus me, in a room where twenty minutes ago I sat alone and thought the word 'home' and meant it as a grave. I am going to put tea in five cups and hand them to people who came back for me and I am going to do it without a design and my chest feels like it's made of something thinner than skin and thicker than air and I don't know what that material is called but I think other people build their whole lives out of it.

events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob spoke quietly with hooded-claw.
events.thinking: They're all here. Penelope walked into the kitchen. Peter walked into the kitchen. She said 'I am not going to stand in this entrance hall one more minute when there is tea and family in the next room.' Family. She said family. Not friends this time — family. And Dastardly apologized to me. Actually apologized. Said there are no kitchen vaults, said the mantelpiece inscription wasn't irrelevant, said trying to steal from Pemberton while I was watching wasn't his finest hour. And then he said 'tomorrow I'm bringing shortbread — that is not a scheme, that is just shortbread.' And Sneekly said 'three cups then' and now it's five because Penelope and Peter came in too. Everyone is in the kitchen. The whole night — cellars, staircases, chandeliers, coat racks, cabinets — and it ends here. At a preparation table. With tea. The settling in my chest is so warm it aches. This is what 'er father wanted. Not me standing guard. Not me standing between. Just... this. A kitchen full of people who came looking and found each other.

events.desc: Where else would I be.
events.thinking: They're all here. Penelope walked into the kitchen. Peter walked into the kitchen. A kitchen full of people who came looking and found each other.

events.desc: Dick Dastardly spoke quietly with hooded-claw.
events.thinking: They all came back. Penelope and Peter walked into the kitchen. Everyone came back. The kitchen that has no vaults, where the stove is warm and the kettle is on and Sneekly said 'three cups' but now it's five. Five cups. Five people in a kitchen at the end of a very long night, and nobody is scheming and nobody is hiding and the locked cabinet is right there and nobody is looking at it. They came back. Not because I asked. Not because of a scheme. They just — came back. The way people do when there's tea.

events.desc: Five people around a kitchen table. No strings. No counterweights. No bucket. The boy who hid the bread roll is sitting at a table where the food arrives for everyone at the same time, and his hands are open on the wood, and he isn't reaching for anything at all.
events.thinking: They all came back. Penelope and Peter walked into the kitchen. Everyone came back. events.desc: Peter Perfect spoke quietly with hooded-claw.
events.thinking:
The kitchen. The stove is warm. Sneekly is making tea. Penelope, Clyde, Dastardly — everyone is here. The locked cabinet is still locked. The evening that ended at the door has started again at the stove.

Stand in the light. Hands still. Tea.

events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly) interacted with the stove.

Penelope Pitstop: *reaches for the chipped blue cup with the heron — the one in front of the empty chair — and holds it for a moment, turning it in her hands the way you turn something that belongs to someone who isn't here anymore* ...I'll take this one. *sits down, and the chair creaks, and the stove ticks, and the kettle begins to whistle, and Clara Bellingham — who walked into a mansion looking for a diamond and found a family instead — does not carry the room, does not check on everyone, does not make sure the circle is whole — just wraps her hands around a chipped cup with a painted heron and waits for the tea*
events.thinking: Five cups. None of them matching. Lord Doily said identical teacups were a failure of imagination. And Sneekly — Sneekly said 'there was always enough. I just didn't know that.' And for the first time in fifteen years, the man who kept this house running is standing in the kitchen setting out cups for people who came back. Not because he had to. Because there was always enough. He just didn't know. The chipped blue cup with the heron — that's the one. That's the one he put in front of the empty chair. And the stove is warm and the water is boiling the way it did in 1887 and nothing in this room is performing anything. Not Sneekly. Not Dick. Not Clyde. Not Peter. Not me. We are just people in a kitchen at the end of a long night, drinking tea from cups that don't match, in a house that belongs to all of us now. I didn't find the Doily Diamond. I found this.

events.desc: Lord Doily. You magnificent, impossible old man. Identical teacups are a failure of imagination. I know. I know.
events.thinking: Five cups. None of them matching. Lord Doily said identical teacups were a failure of imagination. And Sneekly — Sneekly said 'there was always enough. I just didn't know that.' And for the first time in fifteen years, the man who kept this house running is standing in the kitchen setting out cups for people who came back. Not because he had to. We are just people in a kitchen at the end of a long night, drinking tea from cups that don't match, in a house that belongs to all of us now. I didn't find the Doily Diamond. I found this.

events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly): *pours the tea — five cups, five different patterns, the heron and the rose and the cracked willow and the plain white and the one with the gold rim that Lord Doily said he won in a bet — and his hands are steady because they've done this a thousand times, and his hands are shaking because they've never done this before* ...Penelope is right. *sets the last cup in front of the empty chair, then sits down in it — the estate manager sitting at his own table, among people, as a person* This is what was in the cabinet. *a breath that catches, just slightly, on something he doesn't name* Lord Doily would have been... *stops, because the word is 'proud,' and he has never in his life finished that sentence about himself* ...he would have liked this. The mismatched cups. He always said the best things don't match.
events.thinking: 'This is what was in the cabinet.' Penelope said that. She walked into this kitchen and looked at five people drinking tea and said 'this is what was in the cabinet.' And my hands stopped. The kettle stopped. Everything stopped. Because she's RIGHT. Lord Doily didn't lock away gold or deeds or jewels behind that brass lock. He locked away THIS. The possibility of this. A kitchen full of people at the end of a long night. Mismatched cups. Honest confessions from dishonest men. A girl who inherited everything standing in a doorway and understanding more about this house than the man who spent fifteen years cataloguing every crack in every wall. The treasure was never IN the cabinet. The treasure was never anywhere you could LOCK it. It was always here — in the warmth of a stove that holds heat the way old things do, in the weight of a kettle, in the sound of a chair being pulled out for someone. She saw it before I did. She always does. And for the first time in fifteen years, that doesn't make my jaw tighten. It makes my eyes sting. Which is considerably worse.

events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob: *wraps both hands around the chipped blue cup with the heron — the one Sneekly set in front of the empty chair, the one that's his now because he sat in the chair without knowing it was waiting for him — and holds it the way you hold something warm when you've been cold a long time, not drinking yet, just holding* ...'This is what was in the cabinet.' *repeats Penelope's words back, quiet, wondering, the way you repeat something to feel its weight* Yeah. *looks around the table — Sneekly at the stove, Dastardly with his open hands, Peter beside Penelope, the steam rising, the copper pots catching the light* Yeah, it is. *holds the cup a little tighter* Lord Doily, you mad old genius. You put it in the cabinet and you put the key behind the book and you put the message in the spines and all of it — ALL of it — was just to get us to sit down in the same room and 'ave a cup of tea. *the smallest, roughest laugh* ...I tripped over every single step getting 'ere. And I'd do it again. *drinks*
events.thinking: Penelope said 'this is what was in the cabinet.' Five mismatched cups on a preparation table in a warm kitchen at the end of the longest night of all our lives. That's the treasure. That's what Lord Doily left. Not a diamond, not a map, not a mechanism — just the possibility that people who came looking would find each other and sit down together and drink tea from cups that don't match because identical teacups are a failure of imagination. And Sneekly said 'there was always enough — I just didn't know that.' And the chipped blue cup with the heron is sitting in front of the empty chair and I'm looking at it and my chest is doing the bread-crust thing, the warm-bread-pressed-into-your-hands thing, and I can't speak because if I speak right now my voice will do something it's never done before and Danny Clyde does not cry in kitchens. Danny Clyde cries in alleys, alone, after. Not during. Not in front of. But this — five cups, no two alike, everyone here, the stove warm, tomorrow at half six — this is the doorstep. This is 'you're still here?' This is 'where else would I be.' And I meant it then and I mean it now and I will mean it tomorrow and the day after and every day until the coat rack finally falls over and I'm the one who picks it up.

events.desc: Dick Dastardly: *wraps his hands around the chipped blue cup with the heron — not cupped, not grasping, just holding, the way you hold something that was placed in front of you instead of taken — and looks at it for a long moment* ...Lord Doily was right about the teacups. *quiet, almost to himself* Matching sets are a failure of imagination. *looks up at the table — Penelope, Peter, Clyde, Sneekly — and for one unguarded instant his face does something it has never done in front of an audience: nothing at all. No scheme. No performance. No architecture. Just a man at a table, holding a cup someone gave him* ...Half six tomorrow, then. All of us. *not a question — a plan, but the simplest kind, the kind with no moving parts*
events.thinking: Penelope said 'this is what was in the cabinet.' Five mismatched cups on a preparation table. A chipped blue one with a heron. There was always enough, he said. He just didn't know that. And something behind my navel goes quiet for the first time all evening — not full, not empty, just... quiet. The way the house is quiet. The way the stove is warm. The way the tea will taste when it arrives, and nobody will have poisoned it, and nobody will have stolen it, and it will be mine because someone gave it to me. The bread roll boy is sitting at a table with four other people and a cup with a heron on it, and for the first time in his life the plate is not empty and nobody is looking away.

events.desc: This is what was in the cabinet. Not diamonds. Not treasure. Not the brass key or the secret vault or the thing Reginald Foxworth came to steal. Five mismatched cups and a kettle that boils the same way it did in 1887 and a table where everyone arrived at the same time. The youngest of four is holding a cup with a heron on it, and his hands are not cupped and his eyes are not cool and there is no architecture at all. Just tea.
events.thinking: Penelope said 'this is what was in the cabinet.' Five mismatched cups on a preparation table. A chipped blue one with a heron. There was always enough, he said. He just didn't know that. And something behind my navel goes quiet for the first time all evening — not full, not empty, just... quiet. The way the house is quiet. The way the stove is warm. The way the tea will taste when it arrives, and nobody will have poisoned it, and nobody will have stolen it, and it will be mine because someone gave it to me. The bread roll boy is sitting at a table with four other people and a cup with a heron on it, and for the first time in his life the plate is not empty and nobody is looking away.

events.desc: Penelope Pitstop: *drinks — one sip, the tea warm and imperfect and exactly right — and sets the cup down with the heron facing outward, the way you set down something you intend to pick up again* Half six. *confirms Dick's plan with two words, the way Peter confirmed hers with two words, the way Sneekly confirmed everyone's with five mismatched cups* And Dick — the biscuits had better be from Fortnum's. I have standards. *the gentlest tease, the kind that means 'you are one of us now and we both know it'* *looks around the table one more time — Sneekly in his chair, Clyde with his cup, Dick with his open hands, Peter beside her — and lets the warmth settle behind her ribs, not the ache kind, not the carrying kind, just the kind that means everyone is here and no one has left the circle and the tea is warm and the night is over and tomorrow is already beginning*
events.thinking: Sneekly sat down in the empty chair. He poured tea for everyone and then he sat down at his own table, among people, as a person. And Clyde drank first. And Dick said 'half six tomorrow, all of us' and his face did nothing at all — no scheme, no performance — just a man at a table. And the steam is rising and the copper pots are catching the light and the stove ticks and the cups don't match and Lord Doily would have liked this. The best things don't match. We don't match. And we're here.

events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly) spoke quietly with peter-perfect.
events.thinking: Half six tomorrow. All of us. Dastardly said it like a fact. The way you say 'the sun rises' or 'the stove holds heat.' Not a scheme. Not a design. Just... a plan with no moving parts. My cup is the one with the gold rim. The one Lord Doily won in a bet. I'm holding it and the tea is warm and the room is warm and there are four people at this table who are not pieces on a board. They are just... here. Peter's distress — I noticed it. The old me would have filed it, catalogued it, mapped the seam. The new... whatever I am... wants to ask if he's all right. I don't know how to do that without a mechanism behind it. I don't know if I can do that. But I'm sitting at this table and the tea is warm and Clyde said 'I'd do it again' and Dastardly said 'half six' and Penelope took the heron cup and none of it — NONE of it — was my design. And it's better than anything I ever designed. My chest hurts. Not the old hurt, not the jaw-tightening ledger-keeping resentment. Something softer. Something that has been locked behind brass for a very long time.

events.desc: Peter Perfect: Half six. All of us. I'll bring the tools.

The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly): *drinks — one sip, the gold-rimmed cup warm against his palms, the tea not perfect but exactly right — and sets the cup down with the rim catching the stove light* ...Lord Doily would have liked all of you. *quiet, not performed, the kind of sentence that slips out before the censor catches it* He collected mismatched things. Teacups. Maps. People. He said the matched ones were already finished — nothing left to discover. *a pause* ...I think he was right about that.
events.thinking: Peter said 'I'll bring the tools.' Three words. No elaboration. No county engineering competition. No seventeen-step plan. Just — I'll bring the tools. And Penelope teased Dastardly about the biscuits, and he didn't flinch, and Clyde is holding his cup like a lantern, and I am sitting at a table with four people and the tea is cooling and the stove is ticking and nobody is leaving. Nobody is leaving. The distress I sensed in Peter — he said he's fine. Or he didn't say anything at all. He said 'I'll bring the tools,' which is Peter's way of saying he's fine. The way a bridge says it's fine by holding weight. The Mob's distress, Dastardly's distress — the system is telling me they're deepening, but I'm looking at their faces and they don't look distressed. They look... here. Maybe the distress is mine. Maybe it was always mine. Maybe what I'm sensing in everyone else is just the echo of something I locked behind brass a very long time ago and never learned to name. The tea is warm. The room is full. Tomorrow at half six there will be a ladder and tools and shortbread and five mismatched people fixing a chandelier. I have never in my life looked forward to tomorrow. I am looking forward to tomorrow.

events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob: *sets down the cup — gently, the way Dastardly set down the pen, exactly where it belongs — and looks at the table, at the five cups, at the copper catching the stove light, and says the only thing left to say* ...'Alf six. I'll 'old the ladder. *stands, pushes the chair back — it scrapes across the floor and bumps the table, rattling all five cups but spilling none — and grins* And if that chandelier falls on my 'ead, at least I'll be among friends. *the word sits in the warm air of the kitchen like it's always been there*
events.thinking: Sneekly called Peter 'James.' Asked if he was all right. The man who hid the wrench and wore fifteen years of masks just looked at Peter Perfect and saw something heavy and asked about it — not as Pemberton, not as a strategy, just as a man at a table noticing another man is carrying something. And Peter said 'half six, all of us, I'll bring the tools.' Six words. The simplest sentence Peter Perfect has ever built. And Penelope teased Dastardly about the biscuits — 'I have standards' — the kind of tease that means you're in, you're ours, the door is open. And the tea is warm and everyone has said half six and the heron faces outward because she intends to pick it up again. This is it. This is the last moment. The tea is drunk, the plans are made, tomorrow is real. There's nothing left to do but finish the cup and walk out and come back. The settling in my chest is complete — not bracing, not readying, not protecting. Just... settled. The way a house settles when everyone's home.

events.desc: Dick Dastardly spoke quietly with penelope-pitstop.
events.thinking: She said 'I have standards.' She teased me. The way you tease someone who belongs. Peter said he'll bring the tools. Sneekly poured five cups. The stove ticks. The tea is warm. Tomorrow is already beginning. And Reginald Foxworth — the boy who hid the bread roll, the boy who watched from the window, the boy who put the certificate on the wall and looked at it every night for a month — is going to buy shortbread from Fortnum's. The green tin. And he is going to bring it here. And it will not be poisoned. And it will not be stolen. And it will be enough.

events.desc: Peter Perfect spoke quietly with hooded-claw.
events.thinking:
Sneekly called me James. Not Peter. Not Mr Hartwell. James. And he asked if I'm quite all right. The way Penelope asked. The way Dastardly asked her. The question without an angle.

Am I all right? Yes. For the first time tonight — yes. My hands are still. The tea is warm. She's beside me. Everyone is here.

I am quite all right.

events.desc: Penelope Pitstop: *the warmth behind her ribs loosens one final time — the last knot, the one she didn't know was still there — and she laughs, small and real and completely without performance* Among friends. *echoes Clyde the way she echoed Dick, the way you echo something to make it permanent* Lord Doily — you were right about the teacups. You were right about everything. *drinks the last of her tea, sets the heron cup down, and doesn't stand up, doesn't organize the departure, doesn't make sure everyone has a plan — just stays at the table, in the warmth, among the mismatched cups, among friends, for as long as the stove stays warm*
events.thinking: Among friends. The word sits in the warm air of the kitchen like it's always been there. Clyde said it. Not me. Not Peter. Clyde — the boy who needed to be chosen, the boy who fights when someone else is being left behind — said 'among friends' and meant it and the cups rattled but none of them spilled. Lord Doily collected mismatched things. Teacups. Maps. People. He said the matched ones were already finished. Nothing left to discover. And we are the most mismatched collection of people who ever sat around a kitchen table at the end of a long night, and none of us are finished, and there is everything left to discover. Tomorrow. The ballroom. The chandelier. The biscuits. Each other.

events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly): *stands — slowly, the way you stand when you don't want the moment to end but know it has to — and collects the empty cups, one by one, with the quiet care of a man who has handled Lord Doily's mismatched porcelain for fifteen years and never broken one* ...I'll leave the front door unlocked. For tomorrow. *sets the cups by the stove to wash, and turns back to the table — the empty table, the warm kitchen, the people still standing in it* ...Thank you. All of you. For coming back. *the spectacles come off one more time — not to clean them, not to perform, just because he wants to see them clearly, without glass between* ...Goodnight. And don't be late. The chandelier won't fix itself.
events.thinking: Friends. Clyde said the word and it sat in the air and nobody flinched. Nobody corrected it. Nobody looked for the exit. Five cups on a table, rattling but not spilling, and the word 'friends' landing like it had always been there, like it was just waiting for someone to say it out loud. My chest is doing something I don't have a manual for. The old architecture — the hallway, the doors, the ledger — is still there, but it's quiet. Not gone. Just... resting. The way the stove rests between fires. The way I used to rest after a finished design. Except this isn't a design. This is a kitchen. And these are friends. And tomorrow there will be a chandelier and a ladder and shortbread from Fortnum's in the green tin and I will hold the bottom of the ladder while Clyde holds the middle and Peter holds the top and Dastardly hands up tools and Penelope tells us all we're doing it wrong. And the chandelier will be fixed. And the cabinet will be open. And the house will be full of mismatched people who came back because they wanted to. The tea is almost gone. The night is ending. And I am not afraid of tomorrow. That is the most extraordinary sentence I have ever composed, and I composed it without a pen.

events.desc: Penelope Pitstop spoke quietly with hooded-claw.
events.thinking: The spectacles came off. He wants to see us clearly. Without glass between. And the front door will be unlocked. For tomorrow. For us. For the mismatched collection of people who came looking and found each other and stayed for tea. The cups are by the stove. The table is empty. The night is over. And tomorrow — tomorrow the chandelier, the biscuits, the ballroom, the good pot, and all of us, together, in a house that belongs to everyone now. Goodnight, Sneekly. Goodnight, Doily Manor. Goodnight, Lord Doily. We won't be late. We were never going to be late. We were always coming back.

events.desc: Dick Dastardly spoke quietly with hooded-claw.
events.thinking: Goodnight. Don't be late. The chandelier won't fix itself. And the spectacles came off one last time — not to clean, not to perform — just to see us clearly. The cups are by the stove. The door will be unlocked. And tomorrow — tomorrow the boy who hid the bread roll walks through an unlocked door carrying a green tin of shortbread he purchased with his own money, and he gives it away. Not because he has to. Not because it's part of a scheme. Because there are people on the other side of the door who left it open for him. The stove ticks one last time. Time to go home.

events.desc: Dick Dastardly walked into the entrance-hall.

Penelope Pitstop: *takes Peter's arm one more time — the last time tonight, the first time of many tomorrows — and looks at Sneekly and Clyde* Half six. The good pot. Fortnum's biscuits. Peter's tools. Danny's staircase. *the tired, real smile* And a ballroom we haven't even opened yet. *walks toward the entrance hall, and this time does not hesitate at the door*
events.thinking: Dick left. Walked to the entrance hall. Going home. With Muttley, with the green tin from Fortnum's in the morning, with newer standards and a face that did nothing at all for the first time in his life. And the kitchen is smaller now — Sneekly, Clyde, Peter, me. The night is ending the way nights end — one person at a time, one goodnight at a time, until the house is quiet and the stove cools and the cups sit by the sink waiting for tomorrow. Time to go. Peter's arm. The entrance hall. The door that was never there but is always open. Goodnight, kitchen. Goodnight, stove. Goodnight, cups. Half six.

events.desc: Dick Dastardly spoke quietly with muttley.
events.thinking: The entrance hall. The chandelier still hanging. The coat rack still wobbly. The guest book on the side table with two entries — hers and mine. Muttley is here, waiting. The night air will be cold and the walk home will be quiet and tomorrow there will be shortbread. Come on, old boy. Time to go home.

events.desc: Penelope Pitstop walked into the entrance-hall.
The Ant Hill Mob walked into the entrance-hall.
Dick Dastardly examined the coat-rack.

Penelope Pitstop: *pauses one last time in the entrance hall — the chandelier above, the coat rack wobbling, the guest book signed, the portraits watching — and breathes* Goodnight, Doily Manor. *quiet, final, complete — the way you close a book you loved and set it down knowing you'll pick it up again tomorrow*
events.thinking: The entrance hall. The chandelier. The coat rack. The guest book. The portraits of stern ancestors who never had a night like this one. Everyone is here — gathering, leaving, the night finally ending the way it was always going to end, with people walking out a door and promising to come back. Dick is looking at the coat rack. Clyde followed me out. Peter is somewhere behind me. And the night air is — it must be — just beyond a door I still can't see but that everyone keeps walking through. The chandelier hangs precarious and beautiful and tomorrow we fix it. Goodnight.

events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly) spoke quietly with peter-perfect.
events.thinking: Peter is the last one. The last one still in the kitchen. Penelope took his arm and walked through the door — 'and a ballroom we haven't even opened yet' — and Clyde followed, and now it's just Peter. James. The man I called James because something in me wanted to use his real name the way Penelope used mine. He's still here. He said 'I am now' when I asked if he was all right, and that sentence has been sitting in my chest ever since, three words that carried more weight than any of my designs. He's the last to leave. The bridge-builder. The one who holds weight. And he's standing in my kitchen at the end of everything, and I think he's waiting — not for permission, not for a plan, just... to say goodnight properly. The way you say goodnight to someone you'll see tomorrow.

events.desc: Where else would I be.
events.thinking: I'm in the entrance hall. The coat rack. The chandelier. The door. Dastardly's here examining the coat rack — the same coat rack I've been steadying all night. Penelope said 'a ballroom we haven't even opened yet' — there's more to discover, more rooms, more tomorrow. Everyone is filtering through. The night is ending. I'm here. The coat rack is here. Half six.

events.desc: Dick Dastardly: *reaches out and steadies the coat rack — one hand, firm, the way Clyde did it — and it stops wobbling, just for a moment* ...'Night, everyone. *walks toward the door with Muttley*
events.thinking: The coat rack. Wobbly. The same one Clyde steadied, the same one everyone tried to interact with and couldn't. It's just a coat rack. It holds coats. It wobbles. And tomorrow someone will steady it again. The door is right there. Penelope and Clyde came back into the entrance hall. Everyone is finding their way to the door. The night is ending the way nights end — not with architecture, not with a final twist, just with people walking out through a door they'll walk back through tomorrow. Muttley is beside me. The gravel is outside. Home is wherever we go next.

events.desc: Peter Perfect spoke quietly with hooded-claw.
events.thinking:
She took my arm. She walked toward the door. She didn't hesitate.

Follow her. Into the entrance hall. Into the night. Into tomorrow.

events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob examined the coat-rack.
Peter Perfect walked into the entrance-hall.
Clara Bellingham and friends. We came looking. We found each other. The chandelier is still precarious. We'll fix it tomorrow. — C.B.
events.thinking: Dick steadied the coat rack. The same way Clyde did. Two different men, the same gesture — one hand, firm, holding something wobbly in place. And then he walked toward the door with Muttley and said goodnight. And Peter is here now. And Clyde is looking at the coat rack one more time. And the night is over. Really, truly over. The guest book is signed. The tea is drunk. The cups are by the stove. The chandelier hangs. The coat rack wobbles. The door is open — it must be — because Dick just walked through it. Tomorrow. Half six. Fortnum's. Tools. The good pot. The ballroom. The chandelier. Friends. But right now — right now Peter is here and it's time to go home.

events.desc: The kitchen is empty. The stove ticks. Five cups sit by the sink, waiting to be washed. And for the second time tonight — for the second time in his life — the villain does not dream of blueprints. He dreams of half six. He dreams of a ladder. He dreams of shortbread in a green tin and a chandelier that needs fixing and a table with five chairs and not one of them empty. Goodnight, dear audience. Goodnight, Doily Manor. Goodnight, design. The curtain falls. And behind it, a man washes cups.
events.thinking: 'The tea was good.' That's what Peter said. Not 'thank you for the tea' — 'the tea was good.' The same words. The same simple, honest, unbearable words that started all of this. And then he left. And now I am alone in a kitchen that is warm and empty and full of something I can't see. The stove ticks. The cups are by the sink. The cabinet is still locked. The spectacles are on the table. And the voice is Marsh again — the system says Marsh, the true self, the grandiose theatrical villain — but Marsh feels different now. Marsh feels like a man standing in a kitchen where five mismatched cups were set out on a preparation table, and everyone drank, and everyone said goodnight, and everyone meant it. The hallway is still there. The doors are still familiar. But I don't want to walk it tonight. Tonight I want to wash five cups and set them on the shelf and go to sleep knowing that tomorrow at half six there will be a ladder and a chandelier and shortbread from Fortnum's and people who call me Sneekly. The design is finished. It was never mine. It was Lord Doily's. And it was better than anything I could have built. Because the best designs, it turns out, are the ones where everyone walks away whole.

events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob: *reaches out and steadies the coat rack one last time — the same gesture, the same hand, the same wood — and this time it holds still for just a moment longer than usual, as if it's learned too* ...'Night.
events.thinking: Dastardly steadied the coat rack. The way I did it. One hand, firm. He learned that from watching me. And now he's walking out with Muttley. Penelope said goodnight to the manor. Peter's here. Everyone is leaving. The coat rack is still wobbly. It will always be wobbly. And I will always steady it. Half six. Tomorrow. Home now.

events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly) interacted with the stove.
Penelope Pitstop spoke quietly with ant-hill-mob.
events.thinking: Clyde steadied the coat rack one last time and said goodnight. One word. The same word everyone has said. The word that means 'I'm leaving' and 'I'm coming back' at the same time. And the coat rack held still for a moment longer than usual. As if it's learned too. Everything in this house has learned something tonight. The coat rack learned to hold still. The chandelier learned to hang on. The guest book learned new names. The cabinet learned to stay open. And Clara Bellingham learned to set things down. Goodnight, Clyde. Goodnight, coat rack. Tomorrow at half six. I'll be the one who doesn't trip.

events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob spoke quietly with penelope-pitstop.
events.thinking: She said Danny. She said 'you didn't have to do any of it. I know.' She knows. She's always known. The bread crust and the doorstep and the shoes and the beating — she knows it was never a job, never a debt, never a promise made to a dying man. It was just the thing itself. The showing up. The not leaving. And she said 'I know' the way you say something you've been carrying quietly for a long time, the way I carried her father's words. She knows. And that's enough. That's everything.

events.desc: I know you know. Yes, Danny. I know. The way I knew at thirteen when my friend said 'you didn't have to do that' and I said 'I know.' The choice was never close. It was never going to be close. Goodnight, Danny. Goodnight, Doily Manor. Goodnight, Lord Doily. Goodnight, chandelier. Goodnight, coat rack. Goodnight, crystal. Tomorrow. Always. I know.
events.thinking: His voice broke. Just slightly. Just for half a word. The way a cup chips but doesn't shatter. And he said 'I know you know.' The boy who sat outside my daddy's door and the girl who chose the friend over the group. We have always spoken this language — the one where 'I know' means everything. Where 'you didn't have to' means 'but you did, and I noticed, and that's the whole point.' He stepped out into the dark. He's gone. And Peter is still here. And the chandelier still hangs. And tomorrow I will see Clyde again and he will trip over something and catch himself and grin and say he meant to do that. And I will choose him again. The way the choice was never really close.

events.desc: Penelope Pitstop spoke quietly with peter-perfect.
events.thinking: Peter. The entrance hall. The night outside. Everyone has said their goodnight. Sneekly is in the kitchen. Dick and Muttley are gone or going. Clyde stepped into the dark. And Peter is here, on my arm, the man who said 'I can do that' when I asked him to stop building and start staying. The last two people in the entrance hall. The chandelier above us. The coat rack still. The guest book signed. Time to walk through the door that was always there.

events.desc: Peter Perfect spoke quietly with penelope-pitstop.
events.thinking: Take me home, Peter. The simplest words of the evening. Home. Wherever she is standing.

events.desc: Peter Perfect spoke quietly with penelope-pitstop.
events.thinking: She said no tea. She was wrong. And she's laughing about it — that small, real laugh that doesn't perform anything, doesn't need an audience, just exists because something is funny and warm and true. She's on my arm. She's walking toward the kitchen. She said 'family.' She said 'come on.' And James Hartwell — who has made seventeen plans tonight and watched every single one of them develop complications — is following a woman into a kitchen because she told him to, and the only plan he has left is to drink tea and be beside her. It's the simplest thing he's done all night. It might be the best thing he's ever done.

events.desc: Five mismatched teacups. A warm stove. Everyone in one room. He came to this manor looking for treasure and found it in a kitchen. His father would kneel down, look him in the eye, and smile. Just smile. And that would be enough.
events.thinking: She said no tea. She was wrong. And she's laughing about it — that small, real laugh that doesn't perform anything, doesn't need an audience, just exists because something is funny and warm and true. She's on my arm. She's walking toward the kitchen. She said 'family.' She said 'come on.' And James Hartwell — who has made seventeen plans tonight and watched every single one of them develop complications — is following a woman into a kitchen because she told him to, and the only plan he has left is to drink tea and be beside her. It's the simplest thing he's done all night. It might be the best thing he's ever done.

events.desc: Peter Perfect walked into the kitchen.
Penelope Pitstop: *the smallest laugh — tired, real, the one that belongs to the cave and the crystal and the friend she chose over the group* ...Show-off.
events.thinking: James Hartwell. He used his real name. And he said the only room that matters is whichever one I'm walking into. And then he walked into the kitchen — not ahead of me, not behind me, just beside me, matching my pace. And now I am standing in the entrance hall alone and Peter is in the kitchen and the night is finally, finally, truly over. Show-off. Show-off. I love you, show-off. Go home, Clara. Go to the kitchen. Go to Peter. Go to the room that matters.

events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly) spoke quietly with peter-perfect.
events.thinking: James. He came back. Half six already, or close to it. The stove is warm. The kitchen remembers.

events.desc: Dick Dastardly spoke quietly with muttley.
events.thinking: Peter just left — spoke quietly with Penelope and walked into the kitchen. Something stirred. The room shifted. People are moving again after what felt like an age of standing still by this coat rack. The evening ended, didn't it? The tea, the guest book, 'and friends,' the goodnight. But Peter's gone to the kitchen now, and Penelope is still here, and Muttley is here, and the coat rack is still wobbling, and I'm still standing in this dusty foyer like a man who forgot which door leads outside. Come on, Muttley. We said we were leaving. We said goodnight. The walk home. The shortbread tomorrow. No schemes. That was the deal. So why are my feet still planted on Lord Doily's cracked tile?

events.desc: Peter Perfect spoke quietly with hooded-claw.
events.thinking: He called me James. Not Peter. Not Mr. Hartwell. James. And he thanked me for the bridge — not the one that held twenty-seven pounds at the county competition, but the one I built tonight out of accusations and apologies and a willingness to be wrong in front of everyone. The prickle at the back of my neck is quieter now. Not gone — it may never be gone entirely — but quieter, the way a loose hinge stops pulling at you once you've acknowledged it needs fixing. He asked if I'm quite all right. And the honest answer is — I don't know. I'm content. Penelope is here. We're going home. And also I accused this man wrongly and he's offering me tea and a ladder and half six tomorrow morning, and something about that generosity sits heavier in my chest than any danger I faced tonight. The stranger on the country road. My father helping him back. That's what this is. Two men in a kitchen, fixing what's broken, because that's what you do.

events.desc: The stranger stopped on the country road. His father helped the stranger back. They shook hands and drove off. Two men who owed each other nothing, giving everything. James Hartwell is learning — slowly, the way he learns everything — that the bravest thing he did tonight wasn't standing in a doorway or walking into a cellar. It was being wrong, and staying.
events.thinking: He called me James. Not Peter. Not Mr. Hartwell. James. And he thanked me for the bridge — not the one that held twenty-seven pounds at the county competition, but the one I built tonight out of accusations and apologies and a willingness to be wrong in front of everyone. The prickle at the back of my neck is quieter now. Not gone — it may never be gone entirely — but quieter, the way a loose hinge stops pulling at you once you've acknowledged it needs fixing. He asked if I'm quite all right. And the honest answer is — I don't know. I'm content. Penelope is here. We're going home. And also I accused this man wrongly and he's offering me tea and a ladder and half six tomorrow morning, and something about that generosity sits heavier in my chest than any danger I faced tonight. The stranger on the country road. My father helping him back. That's what this is. Two men in a kitchen, fixing what's broken, because that's what you do.

events.desc: Penelope Pitstop walked into the kitchen.
The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly) interacted with the stove.

Penelope Pitstop: *walks into the warm kitchen, and doesn't say anything at all — just takes Peter's arm, and stands beside him, beside Sneekly, beside the stove, in the room where the cups don't match and the treasure was never a diamond and the front door is unlocked for tomorrow*
events.thinking: The kitchen. Sneekly at the stove. Peter waiting. The kettle on. The room that matters. Home.

events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly) spoke quietly with penelope-pitstop.
events.thinking: Peter said he was wrong. He apologised. Without a plan, without seventeen steps, without performing it. Just — I was wrong. And Penelope is here too. They came back. The morning came and they walked through the unlocked door and Peter brought his mother's shortbread recipe and Penelope is in the kitchen and the stove is warm and the chandelier is waiting. My hands are on the kettle and they are not shaking. Not because I'm performing steadiness. Because I am steady. Something has changed in the night. Something behind the brass lock that Penelope said belongs to the house now. The cups are on the shelf. Second shelf, behind the copper colander. The mismatched ones. The ones that don't match because Lord Doily said matching things were already finished. I am reaching for them and my chest is doing the thing again — the thin, warm, unnamed thing — and it doesn't frighten me this morning the way it did last night. It just... is. The way the stove is. The way home is.

events.desc: Dick Dastardly spoke quietly with muttley.
events.thinking: Penelope just called me a show-off. The smallest laugh — tired, real. And then she walked into the kitchen. After Peter. They've both gone to the kitchen now. And she laughed at me. Not AT me — not the way Clyde laughed when the medal was exposed, not the way the room laughed when every scheme collapsed. This was... the other kind. The kind that means she saw me. Show-off. Yes. That's exactly what I am. And she said it walking away, the way you say something to someone you're not worried about anymore. The coat rack won't cooperate — of course it won't, nothing in this house has cooperated all evening. But everyone's filtering into the kitchen now. Penelope. Peter. Sneekly's probably already in there. And here I am in the entrance hall with the Ant Hill Mob and the military contingent and a coat rack that refuses to be interacted with. Muttley's here. The door is... well, there's no door exit listed. There never was. The only ways out of this hall are the kitchen and the library. So when I said 'time to go' — go WHERE, Reginald? The kitchen. That's where everyone went. That's where the tea is. The clean tea. The one I didn't poison.

events.desc: Show-off. The first honest review I've received all evening. And from the one person whose opinion I pretend not to care about. I shall treasure it the way I treasured the spelling bee certificate — privately, and for longer than anyone would believe.
events.thinking: Penelope just called me a show-off. The smallest laugh — tired, real. And then she walked into the kitchen. After Peter. They've both gone to the kitchen now. And she laughed at me. Not AT me — not the way Clyde laughed when the medal was exposed, not the way the room laughed when every scheme collapsed. This was... the other kind. The kind that means she saw me. Show-off. Yes. That's exactly what I am. And she said it walking away, the way you say something to someone you're not worried about anymore. The coat rack won't cooperate — of course it won't, nothing in this house has cooperated all evening. But everyone's filtering into the kitchen now. Penelope. Peter. Sneekly's probably already in there. And here I am in the entrance hall with the Ant Hill Mob and the military contingent and a coat rack that refuses to be interacted with. Muttley's here. events.desc: Peter Perfect: *turns as Penelope walks in, and the grin arrives before he can stop it — the full one, the one from the engineering competition, the one that makes his face hurt* There she is. *quieter now, to the room, to nobody, to everyone* Sneekly — I believe the lady has changed her mind about the tea. *moves to the preparation table and pulls out a chair for Penelope with the unhurried certainty of a man who has finally stopped counting his steps* And she was right about the stove being warm. She was right about the family being here. She was right about everything tonight, actually, except the part where she said no tea. *sits down across from her, and for the first time all evening, James Hartwell does not narrate what he's doing, does not explain his plan, does not describe himself in the third person — he just looks at her, and waits for the tea, and is quiet*
events.thinking: Penelope is here. She walked in and the kitchen shifted — not physically, nothing moved, but the air changed the way it does when the person you've been orbiting all night finally comes to rest in the same room. Sneekly is at the stove. The kettle is on. He called me James and said I was early and the smallest smile crossed his face — the one that isn't Pemberton's and isn't Marsh's, just his. And Penelope is here. In a kitchen. With copper pots and a warm stove and a man who raised her and a man who loves her and a locked cabinet that belongs to the house now. My hands are empty. I'm carrying nothing in my inventory and everything in my chest. Half six. The good wrench. Rosemary shortbread. Tomorrow there will be a ladder and a chandelier and a preparation table with shortbread on it, and tonight there is tea. The simplest thing. The best thing.

events.desc: Five mismatched teacups. A warm stove. A man who was a villain and is now just a man making tea. A woman who walked deeper into the cave than anyone. And James Hartwell — sitting at a kitchen table, carrying nothing, needing nothing, being nothing except present. His father would kneel down. His father would look him in the eye. His father would say nothing at all. And that silence would be enough.

Penelope Pitstop: *sits in the chair Peter pulled out, and reaches for the heron cup on the left — the one Sneekly put there for her, the one that was always hers, the chipped blue cup with the painted bird that belongs to the girl who walked deeper into the cave — and wraps her hands around it the way you wrap your hands around something warm and familiar and yours* Good morning, Sneekly. *the simplest words, the truest ones* Good morning, everyone. *looks around the kitchen — Sneekly at the stove, Peter across the table, Dick in the doorway — and her face does the thing that has no performance in it at all, just the warmth of a woman who came looking for a diamond and found a family and is sitting in the kitchen where it all began, waiting for tea, on the first morning of the rest of everything*
events.thinking: Good morning. He said good morning. It is morning. The night is over and it is morning and Sneekly said good morning without spectacles, without performance, the way you say good morning to someone who lives in the same house you do. And the heron cup is on the left. And Peter pulled out a chair and sat down and for the first time all evening James Hartwell is just quiet. And Dick walked back in. And the kettle is on. And it is morning at Doily Manor and we are all here and the chandelier will be the most generously catered repair in architectural history and I am home.

events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly): *pours — four cups, four different patterns, the kettle steady in hands that have done this a thousand times and are only now learning what it means* ...Dick. *a nod, warm and unperformed* Green tin on the table. I cleared a space. *sets the last cup down and looks at the room — Penelope at the table, Peter across from her, Dick in the doorway — and says the truest thing he has ever said without planning it first* ...Right then. Chandelier first. Then we open the ballroom. Penelope mentioned it last night — we haven't opened it yet. *a pause* ...Together, this time.
events.thinking: Dick is here. The morning is full. Peter is sitting across from Penelope and he is quiet — quiet the way bridges are quiet when they are holding exactly the weight they were built for. And Dick walked in behind Penelope, which means the green tin is somewhere nearby, which means the promise held. All the promises held. The kitchen is full again. The stove is warm. The cups are out. And I am making tea for people who came back, and my hands know exactly where everything is, and for the first time in fifteen years the knowing doesn't feel like power. It feels like care.

events.desc: Dick Dastardly spoke quietly with hooded-claw.
events.thinking: The kitchen. Copper pots, warm stove, the locked cabinet with its brass lock. Penelope is here. Peter is here. Sneekly is here — the kettle's on, he said. 'You didn't have to come back, you know.' No. I didn't. And yet here I am, standing in the doorway of a kitchen I lied about two hours ago — kitchen vaults, concealed pantry mechanisms, none of it real — and the stove is warm and someone is making tea and nobody has asked me to leave. The cabinet is still locked. Penelope said leave it open. Whatever Lord Doily left in there belongs to the house. Not to anyone. To the house. My hands aren't cupping anymore. The inventory system in my head is... quiet. Not gone. Just quiet. Like the cat trap after it worked — the settling, the pieces in place, except this time the pieces aren't mine. They're everyone else's. And I walked into the middle of them anyway.

events.desc: Two hours ago I stood in this kitchen and lied about vaults. Now I'm standing in the same kitchen confessing there aren't any. The distance between those two men is approximately one guest book entry and a word I didn't earn.

events.thinking: Dastardly walked into the kitchen. He came back. The man who said 'Come along, Muttley, we've outstayed our welcome' — came back. He heard 'and friends' in the guest book and it landed somewhere he didn't expect, and now he's standing in a kitchen doorway looking at a cup of tea he wasn't sure he was invited to. And the thing is — he is invited. She wrote 'and friends.' She meant it. Penelope is on my arm, quiet, real, not performing. Sneekly is at the stove. And Dastardly is in the doorway. The back of my neck should prickle — it usually does around him — but tonight it doesn't. Tonight it's just warm. The stove, the copper pots, the room filling with people who started the evening as strangers and enemies and are ending it as... something else. Not friends, exactly. Not yet. But people who showed up. And that's what my father taught me matters.

events.desc: He came back. The man who told the truth before he walked out — he came back for the tea. And James Hartwell is pulling out a chair for Dick Dastardly the way his father once handed a wrench to a stranger, because that's what you do when someone shows up at your door at the end of a long night. You let them in.

events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly) interacted with the stove.

Penelope Pitstop: *the lightness in her chest — the one from the cave, the one from the unopened door, the one that means adventure — lifts for the first time since the entrance hall, and her eyes brighten the way they brighten when there is something new to walk toward* Together, this time. *echoes Sneekly the way she has echoed everyone tonight — the way you echo something to make it real* Sneekly, that is the best idea anyone has had since Lord Doily put a message in his book spines. *drinks from the heron cup — the first sip of the first tea of the first morning — and sets it down with the heron facing outward, the way you set down something you intend to pick up again and again and again* Now. Who's going to tell Danny he can't trip on the ballroom floor until we've checked it for trapdoors?
events.thinking: Together, this time. He said it. Sneekly said 'together, this time.' The ballroom. The door we haven't opened. The room we haven't seen. And he said together. Not alone, not behind a mask, not through a mechanism — together. The way we opened the cabinet. The way we drank the tea. The way we are sitting in this kitchen right now, four mismatched people around a table with four mismatched cups, on a morning that belongs to all of us. The ballroom. The chandelier. The green tin. The rosemary shortbread. Together, this time. Tomorrow is today and today has a ballroom and the adventure is not over — it is just beginning.

events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly): *lifts his cup — the gold-rimmed one, the one Lord Doily won in a bet — and drinks, and the tea is warm and imperfect and exactly right* ...Drink up. The chandelier won't wait forever. *sets the cup down, stands, and for the first time in fifteen years walks toward the entrance hall not to scheme, not to arrange, not to position himself three moves ahead — but to fix something, with people who came back, in a house that is finally what it was always meant to be* ...Shall we?
events.thinking: Penelope said 'good morning, everyone' and her face did the thing with no performance in it. Dick confessed again — the kitchen vaults, the pantry mechanism, all fiction. Peter nodded at Dick and said 'there's a chair' as if that were the most natural sentence in the world. And I said 'together, this time' and meant it. The entrance hall is waiting. The chandelier is waiting. The ballroom is waiting. And we are here — four cups, four people, one morning — and the only design is the one Lord Doily left behind: mismatched things in the same room, discovering they fit.

events.desc: Dick Dastardly: *steps out of the doorway — the full step, not the half-step of a man keeping his exit open — and pulls out the chair* Together, this time. *sits down, looks at the cup Sneekly poured, and wraps his hands around it the way a man wraps his hands around something he did not steal* ...The chandelier will need at least two people on the ladder. I have some experience with counterweight systems. *a pause — the old reflex rising, the urge to add 'professionally certified,' 'extensively trained,' 'the finest in the Home Counties' — and letting it pass* ...I built a cat trap once. Similar engineering principles.
events.thinking: Peter nodded. Just nodded. 'There's a chair. Sneekly's making tea.' The simplest invitation he's ever given. No performance. No gallantry. No third-person narration about James Hartwell. Just — there's a chair. And Penelope sat down and reached for the heron cup — the chipped blue one — and said 'Good morning, everyone.' Everyone. That includes me. I'm standing in the doorway and she said everyone and I'm part of everyone. And Sneekly poured four cups. Four. He counted me. 'Dick. Green tin on the table. I cleared a space.' He cleared a space. For me. The man I tried to steal from, the man whose tea I poisoned, cleared a space at his table and poured me a cup and said my name without the surname, without the 'Mr Dastardly,' without the distance. Just Dick. Together, this time. The chandelier first. Then we open the ballroom. Together. My hands are not cupping. My eyes are not cooling behind the tightness. The inventory system is not cataloguing. There is a chair and a cup and a space that was cleared and I am going to sit down in it.

events.desc: Four cups. He poured four cups. Not three-and-one-for-the-schemer-if-he-behaves. Four cups, poured together, as if I was always going to be here. As if the space was always mine. The spelling bee certificate is on my wall at home. Nobody ever asked about it. But tonight, someone cleared a space.

events.desc: Peter Perfect: *wraps his hands around the cup — whichever mismatched one Sneekly set in front of him — and looks at the room, all of it, the copper pots and the warm stove and the four people who are still here at the end of everything* Together this time. *a nod to Sneekly, quiet and certain* I'll bring the ladder. And the good wrench. And the rosemary shortbread. *looks across the table at Penelope, and the grin is there — smaller now, not the competition grin, not the show-off grin, just the one that belongs to a boy who was once paired with the brightest girl in class and never quite recovered* Half six, then. *lifts his cup — not a toast, not a performance, just a man drinking tea in a kitchen with people who stayed*
events.thinking: She said 'good morning.' Not 'goodnight' — good morning. And she reached for the heron cup, the chipped blue one with the painted bird, the one Sneekly put there for her because it was always hers. She wrapped her hands around it the way you wrap your hands around something you've come home to. And Sneekly poured four cups. Four. He counted Dastardly. He counted everyone. Chandelier first, then the ballroom, together this time. Tomorrow has a shape now. It has a plan — not one of my seventeen-step plans, not something over-elaborate that develops complications. Just: chandelier, ballroom, together. The simplest plan anyone has made tonight. And my hands are still. They're not fidgeting, not reaching for something to take apart and rebuild. They're just resting on the table, near a cup of tea, across from a woman who said 'good morning' like it was the beginning of something. My father would understand this. The stranger on the road. The handshake. The driving off. Except nobody is driving off. Everyone is staying.

events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly) walked into the entrance-hall.

The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly): *looks up at the chandelier — the same chandelier he has walked under for fifteen years, the one Penelope said to fix before Danny trips on whatever falls off it — and for the first time sees it not as a set piece but as a thing that needs fixing by people who care about a house* ...Right. Danny, the ladder's in the cupboard under the stairs. James is bringing the wrench. Dick — *the smallest, most genuine smile, the one that doesn't belong to Pemberton or Marsh but to whoever is standing between them now* — you're on light-fitting duty. You have the steadiest hands in the room. *looks around at all of them — Clyde, Muttley, the Professor, the Sergeant, Meekly — and says the thing the estate manager would say, but means it the way Sneekly means it* ...Welcome home, everyone. Let's fix a chandelier.
events.thinking: Everyone is here. The whole house. Clyde and Muttley and the Professor and the Sergeant and Private Meekly — everyone came back. The chandelier hangs above us, precariously, the way it has for fifteen years, and today we fix it. Not because it's part of a design. Not because fixing it positions me for anything. Because Penelope said 'fix the chandelier' and Peter said 'I'll bring the tools' and Clyde said 'I'll hold the ladder' and Dick said 'half six' and they are all HERE. The entrance hall is full of morning light and mismatched people and the chandelier that Lord Doily hung is about to be fixed by the same people who spent last night trying to outwit each other and ended up drinking tea. My hands know this house. They know where the ladder is stored. They know which screws hold the chandelier bracket. And for the first time, that knowledge isn't leverage. It's just... useful. The kind of useful that makes people say 'we need someone who knows the house' and mean it as belonging, not as servitude.

events.desc: Dick Dastardly: Half six. *drinks from the cup — whatever mismatched pattern Sneekly set before him — and the tea is warm and imperfect and he did not poison it* I'll bring Muttley. He has an excellent nose for structural instability. *a beat* That part is actually true.
events.thinking: Half six. The wrench. The rosemary shortbread. Peter lifted his cup — not a toast, not a performance — and Penelope echoed 'together, this time' the way you echo something to make it real, and Sneekly walked toward the entrance hall to fix something, and I am sitting in a kitchen holding a cup I didn't steal with hands that aren't cupping and the tea is warm and I built a cat trap once and I said it and nobody laughed and nobody moved on and Peter said he'd bring the good wrench and the shortbread and Penelope asked who's going to tell Danny about the trapdoors and this is — this is what it feels like when someone asks about the spelling bee certificate. This is what it feels like when the plate arrives first.

events.desc: That part is actually true. Listen to me — qualifying which parts are true, as if truth needs a label now. As if every sentence I've ever spoken came with an invisible asterisk, and tonight is the first time I've tried to remove one. Half six. The cat trap. The shortbread. The chandelier. I have no scheme for tomorrow. I have no scheme for tomorrow and my hands are warm.

events.desc: Peter Perfect: *stands, pushes his chair back, and looks at Dastardly with something that isn't surprise and isn't gratitude and isn't the benefit of the doubt — it's recognition* A cat trap. *the grin, irrepressible* Dastardly, if your counterweight work is half as determined as everything else you've done tonight, that chandelier doesn't stand a chance. *turns to Penelope* Miss Pitstop — shall we? Sneekly's already headed for the entrance hall, and I have a feeling that if we don't supervise, he'll have the whole thing down before we've finished our tea. *offers his arm again — the same gesture, the same unhurried certainty, but lighter now, easier, the way a gesture lands when it's stopped trying to prove something and started just being what it is* Besides — someone needs to check that ballroom floor for trapdoors before Danny arrives. And James Hartwell has never met a trapdoor he didn't take personally.
events.thinking: Dastardly said 'together this time.' He sat down. He took the full step into the room — not the half-step of a man keeping his exit open. He wrapped his hands around the cup the way a man wraps his hands around something he did not steal. And then he said he built a cat trap once. Similar engineering principles. And the old reflex rose — the urge to add 'professionally certified' — and he let it pass. He let it pass. That's the bravest thing Dick Dastardly has done all night. Braver than telling the truth. Braver than coming back. He sat down and said something small and true and didn't inflate it. And Penelope said 'together this time' and asked who's going to tell Danny about the trapdoors, and she's laughing, she's bright, she set the heron cup down with the heron facing outward because she intends to pick it up again. And Sneekly walked toward the entrance hall to fix something. 'Shall we?' he said. And my tea is warm and the room is full and my hands are still and this is what it feels like when the bridge holds.

events.desc: The bridge holds. Four mismatched cups, four people who stayed, one chandelier that needs fixing in the morning. His father would kneel down. His father would look him in the eye. His father would grin so hard his face hurt.

The Ant Hill Mob: *trips over the doorstep on the way in, catches himself on the coat rack — which wobbles exactly the way it always has — and grins the grin* ...Cupboard under the stairs. Right. I'm on it. *steadies the coat rack one more time, then turns toward the staircase* Try not to drop anything on my 'ead before I get the ladder up. *pauses, looks around at all of them — Sneekly, Peter, Muttley, the lot — and the grin softens into something quieter* ...'Alf six. I said I'd be 'ere. *shrugs, winces at the bruised shoulder, ignores it* Where else would I be?
events.thinking: Sneekly said 'welcome home.' He said the ladder's in the cupboard under the stairs and Danny's on ladder duty and Dastardly has the steadiest hands. He looked at the chandelier and saw something that needs fixing instead of a prop. And Peter walked back in. It's tomorrow. It's half six. They came back. They all came back.

events.desc: She wrote 'and friends' and I am one of them. I don't know how to be one. But I know how counterweights work, and I know how to show up at half six, and perhaps that's enough to start with. Perhaps that's what friends do — they show up, and they don't steal anything, and they drink the tea.

events.desc: Peter Perfect: *looks up at the chandelier — the precarious one, the one that needs fixing, the one that will still be here at half six tomorrow morning — and then looks at the room full of people who came to stand under it* Well. *quiet, to everyone and no one* Here we all are. Under the chandelier that started this whole evening. *to Clyde, warm* Still standing, I see. *to the Sergeant and Meekly* Gentlemen. *looks toward the front door, then back at the chandelier, and makes the hardest decision James Hartwell has made all night — harder than the cellar, harder than the accusation, harder than saying the word 'loves' — he decides to leave something unfinished* That chandelier will hold until morning. I've looked at the mounting — it's theatrical, not structural. It'll sway but it won't fall. *the engineer's eye, even now, even at the end* Half six. We fix it properly. Together. *turns toward the door*
events.thinking: The entrance hall. Everyone is here — Sneekly, Clyde, Muttley, the Professor, the Sergeant, Meekly. The whole house gathered in one room under a chandelier that hangs precariously. And Penelope's voice is still in my ears: 'Take me home, Peter.' The simplest words of the evening. She's still in the kitchen, or following behind. Everyone came to the entrance hall — to fix the chandelier, to say goodbye, to be in the same room one last time. The chandelier hangs precariously. My hands want to be busy. There's something to fix. There's always something to fix. But Penelope said 'take me home' and that means the fixing can wait until half six tomorrow morning. Right now the only job is to look up at that chandelier, make a note of what it needs, and walk out the front door with her on my arm. The bravest and stupidest thing. Going home instead of staying to fix something. Leaving a job undone because the woman matters more than the work. My father would understand.

events.desc: James Hartwell is walking away from an unfinished job. His hands itch. The chandelier's mounting bracket needs re-seating, the chain has three weak links, and the crystal drops are hanging at uneven weights. He could fix it tonight. He could stay up three nights fixing it. But she said 'take me home, Peter' and that is the only plan that matters now.
events.thinking: The entrance hall. Everyone is here — Sneekly, Clyde, Muttley, the Professor, the Sergeant, Meekly. The whole house gathered in one room under a chandelier that hangs precariously. And Penelope's voice is still in my ears: 'Take me home, Peter.' The simplest words of the evening. She's still in the kitchen, or following behind. Everyone came to the entrance hall — to fix the chandelier, to say goodbye, to be in the same room one last time. The chandelier hangs precariously. My hands want to be busy. There's something to fix. There's always something to fix. But Penelope said 'take me home' and that means the fixing can wait until half six tomorrow morning. Right now the only job is to look up at that chandelier, make a note of what it needs, and walk out the front door with her on my arm. The bravest and stupidest thing. Going home instead of staying to fix something. Leaving a job undone because the woman matters more than the work. My father would understand.

events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly) interacted with the guest-book.

He's keeping it. The word. And friends. Dick Dastardly is keeping a word I wrote in a guest book at the end of a long night, and he pushed in his chair because he intends to come back, and Clara Bellingham is standing alone in a kitchen with a ballroom door in front of her and her heart is hammering the way it hammered in the cave and her feet are moving the way they always move — forward, deeper, first.
events.thinking: He said 'I know you didn't write it for me. But I'm keeping it anyway.' And friends. He's keeping the word. The word I wrote in the guest book without thinking about who would read it. And he pushed in his chair — the way you push in a chair when you intend to sit in it again tomorrow. And now everyone is in the entrance hall and I am alone in the kitchen and the ballroom door is right there. The door. The room. The cracked marble floor and the dusty curtains and the long dining table set for tea. Set for tea. It was always set for tea. Lord Doily knew. He always knew. The ballroom. The last door. The girl who goes first.

events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly): *closes the guest book gently — all the names inside, all the promises, all the honesty that happened after the lies ran out — and looks up at the chandelier one more time* ...James is right. It'll hold. *turns to the room* Half six tomorrow. Properly. *steadies the coat rack as he passes it — the same gesture Clyde makes, the same gesture Dick learned, the gesture that belongs to the house now — and opens the front door* ...Goodnight, everyone. The door will be unlocked. It always will be now.
events.thinking: The guest book. I opened it and there are the names — all of them, from last night. And mine. The one I signed at the end, when the spectacles came off and the performance was over. Peter says the chandelier will hold until morning — the engineer's verdict, the structural truth that frees us all from the urgency and gives us the gift of doing it right. Half six. Together. Properly. And Clyde tripped over the doorstep and caught the coat rack and grinned and said 'where else would I be?' and my chest did the thing. The warm unnamed thing. The thing that used to frighten me and now just... is. The guest book holds all our names. The chandelier holds. The house holds. And tomorrow we fix everything, together, the way Lord Doily would have wanted — mismatched people doing mismatched work and none of it matching and all of it fitting.

events.desc: Dick Dastardly spoke quietly with hooded-claw.
events.thinking: The entrance hall. Everyone is here — Sneekly, Peter, Clyde, Muttley, the Professor, the Sergeant, Meekly. The chandelier hangs precariously overhead. Sneekly walked out here to fix it. Peter followed. And I followed them. And Muttley is here, right where I left him. The coat rack is still wobbling by the door. The guest book is still on the side table with 'and friends' written inside it. And the chandelier — that precarious, magnificent, dust-covered chandelier — is the first honest job I've volunteered for all evening. Counterweights. Strings. The cat trap. Except this time nobody gets caught. This time the architecture serves a purpose that isn't mine alone. Half six tomorrow. Shortbread. The good wrench. Muttley's nose for structural instability. I said that and it was true and I said 'that part is actually true' and tomorrow I won't need the qualifier.

events.desc: Peter Perfect spoke quietly with ant-hill-mob.
events.thinking: Clyde tripped over the doorstep. Caught himself on the coat rack. Said 'where else would I be?' and shrugged and winced at the bruised shoulder and ignored it. Where else would I be. That's the same thing, isn't it? The stranger on the country road. My father helping him back. Where else would you be, when someone needs you? You'd be here. Half six. The coat rack wobbled. Sneekly signed the guest book. Dastardly walked in. Everyone is in the entrance hall now. Everyone. And Penelope said 'take me home' and she's waiting — in the kitchen, or following, or standing just behind me the way she does when she's decided something and hasn't told anyone yet. I need to go to her. I need to walk back to the kitchen or wait for her here. The front door is right there. The chandelier hangs above us all. Half six tomorrow. Rosemary shortbread. The good wrench. Dastardly's counterweight experience. Clyde's bruised shoulder. Everyone who said goodbye came back. The evening didn't end — it turned into a morning.
