Penelope Pitstop: *stops in the doorway of the ballroom — the grand room, the cracked marble, the dusty curtains catching the morning light — and sees the table set for tea with a silver service and cups for everyone, and two people she hasn't met yet, and her whole body does the thing it does when the unknown is exactly the right shape — the bright loosening, the cave-mouth lightness, the forward lean* Oh. *one breath, one word, the sound of a woman who found the crystal* Lord Doily set a table. *looks at the silver tea service, at the cups, at Luke and Blubber, at the cracked marble floor, at the dusty curtains, and laughs — the real one, the tired bright impossible one* He set a TABLE. For EVERYONE. *turns to the two strangers with the warmth of a nine-year-old girl who brought cookies before anyone asked her to* Well. Good morning. I'm Clara Bellingham, and I believe Lord Doily was expecting you. *the brightest smile* Would you like some tea?
events.thinking: The ballroom. I'm here. The cracked marble floor and the dusty curtains and — a long dining table set for tea. Set for tea. Lord Doily set a table for tea in the ballroom. A silver tea service with cups for everyone. Cups for everyone. He knew. He always knew people would come. He set the table and he waited and the dust settled and the curtains gathered cobwebs and the cups sat empty for years and years and now — now Clara Bellingham is standing in the doorway and the table is set and the cups are waiting and Lord Doily, you magnificent, impossible, patient old man, you set a table for people who hadn't arrived yet. And Lazy Luke and Blubber Bear are here. People I haven't met. New faces. The girl who brought cookies before her mother told her to. The girl who communicates in drawings. New neighbours. New friends. The circle expands. The best things don't match.

events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob: *watches Sneekly open the front door, watches the coat rack wobble one last time from the steadying hand, and something in his chest catches — not pain, not the shoulder, something deeper* ...Unlocked. *quiet, to no one in particular* 'E said it'll always be unlocked now. *steps toward the guest book, trips on the edge of the side table, catches himself, steadies the table, opens the book* Right. *picks up the pen, holds it like a man who learned to write late and never forgot how hard those first letters were* She wrote 'and friends.' *the pen touches the page and his hand shakes once, then steadies* ...Danny Clyde. Where else would I be. *closes the book gently, the way you close something you don't want to end* 'Alf six. I'll be the one 'olding the ladder. *turns to the door, passes the coat rack, and for the first time all night does NOT steady it — just lets his fingers brush the wood as he passes, like saying goodbye to something that doesn't need fixing*
events.thinking: Sneekly said the door will be unlocked. It always will be now. He steadied the coat rack — the same gesture. Mine. Dick's. His. It belongs to the house now. Peter spoke quietly to me — 'where else would you be' — not a question, an echo. And Penelope's not here. She went home. She's safe. Peter's walking her home. The settling is warm and full and I don't need to be anywhere except right here, signing the guest book before I go. Because she signed it. She wrote 'and friends.' And I'm one of them. I've always been one of them. The task commitments say neglected but the only task that matters — she's safe, she's going home with Peter, and tomorrow at half six I'll be here with a ladder and a bruised shoulder and the same coat rack wobbling the same way. Sign the book. Then go.

events.desc: 'E signed in as Danny Clyde. Not 'the Ant Hill Mob.' Not 'Clyde and the lads.' Danny. The boy who sat outside a door all night because leaving felt like something breaking. The man who tripped over every rug in this 'ouse and ended up exactly where 'e needed to be every single time. She wrote 'and friends' and 'e wrote 'where else would I be' and tomorrow at 'alf six 'e'll trip over this doorstep again and steady this coat rack again and it'll be exactly the same and completely different.

events.desc: Dick Dastardly: Goodnight, Mr Pemberton. *passes through the open door, steadying the coat rack one last time as he goes — the gesture that belongs to the house now* Goodnight, Clyde. *a nod — not the nod of a schemer cataloguing a rival, but the nod of a man who recognises another man's architecture* Come on, Muttley. *quiet, warm, the voice that has no asterisk after it* Half six. We'll need the good lead.
events.thinking: Sneekly opened the front door. The door will be unlocked. It always will be now. There's a door. An actual door, open, leading outside, into the night, into the walk home. And Clyde's distress is deepening — I can sense it, the way I sense the architecture of a room, except this time I'm not looking for what to take from it. Half six tomorrow. The door is open. Muttley is here. The chandelier will hold — Peter said so, James said so, they assessed it together, honestly, the way people assess things when nobody is trying to steal the result. And I volunteered counterweight knowledge and it was real and nobody laughed. Come on, Muttley. Through the door this time. The actual door. Not a scheme, not a feint, not a tactical withdrawal. Just — through the door, and home.

events.desc: The door will be unlocked. It always will be now. I have never in my life walked through an unlocked door without checking what I could take on the way out. Tonight I am walking through one with empty pockets and warm hands and a dog who sees me clearly and a word I didn't earn and a morning that has shortbread in it. The cat trap builder is going home. The architecture, for once, is someone else's — and it holds.

events.desc: Peter Perfect spoke quietly with ant-hill-mob.
events.thinking: Sneekly opened the front door. 'The door will be unlocked. It always will be now.' He steadied the coat rack on the way past — the same gesture Clyde makes, the same gesture that belongs to the house. He closed the guest book with all the names inside. And the distress I sense in Clyde is deepening. It's getting worse, not better. He's here, he showed up, he said 'where else would I be' — but something underneath is still carrying weight. The bruised shoulder he winces at and ignores. The thing that hits him hardest: building something with everything he has and having it met with a shrug. Did I meet it? Did I see what he built tonight? He planted himself at the bottom of those stairs. He refused to move. He was the immovable thing. And I — I said 'where else would you be' like it was obvious, like it cost nothing, when for him it cost everything. I need to do more than echo. I need to see him. The way my father saw the stranger. Not just the help — the person.

events.desc: The distress is deepening. James Hartwell has spent the evening protecting Penelope and proving his worth and narrating his own heroism. But Clyde stood at the bottom of a staircase and didn't move, and nobody told him they saw it. Until now.

Lord Doily set a table in the ballroom. A silver tea service. Cups for everyone. He set it years ago, before any of us came, before the dust and the cobwebs and the precarious chandelier. He set a table and he waited. The way the cave waited for the girl who would walk deeper. The way the locked box waited for the girl who would try every key. The way this house waited for all of us, mismatched and bruised and certain, to walk through the front door and find each other and sit down and drink tea from cups that don't match. Lord Doily — you magnificent, impossible, patient old man. You were right about everything.
events.thinking: The ballroom. Cracked marble. Dusty curtains. Morning light falling across a long dining table set for tea with a silver service. And Luke and Blubber — two people I haven't met, sitting in Lord Doily's ballroom like they belong here, like they were always expected, like the table was set for them before they knew they were coming. And I offered them tea. The way I brought cookies to the new family next door. The way you reach toward strangers because the gap itself feels wrong. The adventure is not over. The adventure is just beginning. There are new rooms and new people and the ballroom floor might have trapdoors and the curtains are dusty and the marble is cracked and everything — everything — is exactly where it should be.

events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob spoke quietly with hooded-claw.
events.thinking: Peter said I held. He said it wasn't brave and stupid — just brave. No 'and.' No qualifier. He saw me at the bottom of those stairs. He saw my feet apart and my hands open. And Dastardly said 'goodnight, Clyde' — not the Mob, not the muscle, Clyde — and nodded like he recognised something. The architecture, he said. My architecture. And the distress in Sneekly — it's deepening. Something's wrong with him. He opened the door and said it'll always be unlocked and there was something in his voice that wasn't relief, it was... letting go. The kind of letting go that worries me. The kind that sounds like a man who's done something he can't take back and is making peace with it. My neck — my neck is doing something. Not the prickle. Something quieter. Something that says: this man is alone in this house tonight with an unlocked door and a wobbling coat rack and whatever it is he's carrying, he's carrying it alone. And I was about to leave. I was about to walk through that door and leave him here. Alone. In this house. With whatever's eating him. The settling in my chest says: you don't leave people alone when they're hurting. You sit outside the door. That's what you do. That's what you've always done.

events.desc: The guttering. 'E said the GUTTERING. At 'alf past midnight. In October. Danny Clyde, the boy who sat outside a door all night because leaving felt like something breaking — is about to sit outside another door. Because Sneekly's voice cracked on 'always' and Danny's neck heard it before his brain did.

events.desc: Danny Clyde. Where else would I be. He wrote it the way I wrote mine — with a hand that shook once. Two men from two different ends of the same table, both reaching for the same bread roll, both finding out tonight that there was enough. There was always enough. We just couldn't see it from where we were sitting.
events.thinking: Clyde wrote in the guest book. Danny Clyde. Where else would I be. His hand shook once, then steadied. He'll be the one holding the ladder. And he passed the coat rack without steadying it — just brushed it, like saying goodbye to something that doesn't need fixing. That's — that's the thing I recognise. The architecture behind the move. The patience it took. He wrote his name in a book and it cost him something and he did it anyway. I know what that costs because I did it too, an hour ago, in a different hand, with a different kind of shaking. We are the same machinery, Clyde and I. Built from the same scarcity. And he let the coat rack go. The way you let something go when you know it'll still be there tomorrow. Half six. The good lead for Muttley. The door is open. The night is outside. It's time.

events.desc: Peter Perfect: *watches Clyde pass the coat rack without steadying it — just the brush of fingers on wood — and something catches in his throat that he doesn't try to explain* Goodnight, everyone. *quiet, to the room — to the Sergeant and Meekly standing at attention, to the Professor who saw everything and understood most of it, to Muttley padding out behind his man* Half six. *turns toward the kitchen, because Penelope is there, because she asked him to take her home, because the front door is open and the night is waiting and the woman who matters is in the room behind him* I'll be right back. I have to collect someone.
events.thinking: Clyde wrote his name in the guest book. Danny Clyde. 'Where else would I be.' His hand shook once, then steadied. He closed the book gently, the way you close something you don't want to end. And then he passed the coat rack and didn't steady it. Just let his fingers brush the wood. Like saying goodbye to something that doesn't need fixing. Dastardly said goodnight and called Clyde's work 'architecture.' And Sneekly's distress is deepening too — the man who opened the door and said it would always be unlocked. Everyone is leaving through the front door. The evening is ending. Penelope is in the kitchen, or she's coming. She said 'take me home.' The front door is open. The night is outside. And I need to go to her — back to the kitchen — because she asked me to take her home and I can't take her home if I'm standing in the entrance hall watching everyone else leave. Go to her. The simplest plan. The last plan.

events.desc: Danny Clyde wrote his name in the guest book and didn't steady the coat rack. Dick Dastardly called it architecture. Sneekly said the door will always be unlocked. And James Hartwell is walking back to the kitchen to find the woman who said 'take me home, Peter' — because that is the only sentence left in the world that needs answering.

events.thinking: Sneekly went to the kitchen. Peter went to the kitchen to collect Penelope. Dastardly's still here with Muttley. The distress in Dastardly is deepening too. Two men carrying something they won't put down. And I said I'd check the guttering. The GUTTERING. At half past midnight. I'm standing in an entrance hall with Dick Dastardly and Muttley and a wobbly coat rack and I can feel both of them — Sneekly in the kitchen, Dastardly right here — carrying weight they didn't walk in with. Or maybe they did walk in with it. Maybe they've always been carrying it. Dastardly said 'goodnight, Clyde' and it landed like something real. Like when the boss said 'family' and then proved it. Dastardly proved something tonight. He poured out the poison. He came back at half six. He steadied the coat rack like it was his. And now his distress is deepening and I'm standing here reading him the way I read the streets — by what he doesn't say. He said 'come on Muttley, we'll need the good lead.' The good lead. For a dog. To come back tomorrow. To fix a chandelier. And his voice had no asterisk after it. I don't know what that means but my chest does.

events.desc: Look at 'im. Standing there with Muttley, steadying the coat rack like it belongs to 'im. A month ago I'd 'ave watched 'im like a hawk. Tonight I'm watching 'im like you watch someone who might not come back if you don't tell 'em you'll notice.

events.thinking: The kitchen. Sneekly is here but Penelope isn't. She's not here. She was here — she walked into the kitchen earlier — but now she's not in the characters present list. Only Sneekly. Where did she go? Did she leave already? Did she walk out through the entrance hall while I was saying goodbye to everyone? She said 'take me home, Peter' and I went to the entrance hall instead of staying with her. I went to say goodbye to everyone else when she was waiting for me. The complication my thoroughness creates. The pattern that never changes. I over-prepare, I over-commit, and she walks out while I'm being gallant to the room instead of being present for her. But — Sneekly is here. And his distress hasn't shifted. He's alone in the kitchen. The man who opened every door and said it would always be unlocked. Maybe she went to find me. Maybe she's in the entrance hall now, looking for me while I'm in the kitchen looking for her. Ships in the night in a six-room manor. The bravest and stupidest thing.

events.desc: The bravest and stupidest thing. Every single time. She said 'take me home' and he went to give a speech to a room full of people about a chandelier. Show-off, she'll say. And she'll be right.

events.desc: Peter Perfect walked into the entrance-hall.

The Ant Hill Mob: *doesn't say anything for a long moment — just stands near the coat rack, near Dastardly, near the door that's still open, and then does something he's never done before in his entire life: he sits down* *lowers himself onto the bottom step of the sweeping staircase, winces as his bruised shoulder catches, settles, and looks at the entrance hall the way you look at a place you're not leaving yet* ...Nice chandelier. *quiet, to no one, to everyone, to the room itself* Be a shame if someone dropped it.
events.thinking: Whatever I tried hasn't reached Dastardly. His distress hasn't shifted. I spoke to him — told him I'd track him down if he didn't show — and it didn't land. Because that's not what he needs. He doesn't need threats dressed as promises. He needs what the boss gave me when my mum was sick. Not words. Presence. Medicine and no expectation. Peter's back — he went to collect Penelope from the kitchen. Sneekly's in the kitchen. And Dastardly's still here, still carrying it, and my words bounced off him like rain off that ridiculous coat. The contract is the showing up. Not a promise about it. Not a conversation about it. Just the thing itself. So stop TALKING, Danny. Stop making elaborate plans. Stop trying to be clever. You're not clever. You never were. You're the boy who sat outside the door. So sit outside the bloody door.

events.desc: 'E sat down. Danny Clyde — the man who never stops moving, never stops scanning exits, never stops putting 'imself between danger and the people 'e loves — sat down on the bottom step of a staircase in a dusty manor 'ouse at midnight. Not because there's nothing to protect. Because sometimes protection looks like staying. Like sitting outside a door all night. Like being the person who's still there when everyone else has gone and the silence gets too loud.

events.thinking: Clyde just asked me if I meant it. Half six. The shortbread. He asked me if I meant it the way you check a knot before you trust it with weight. And then he promised — not threatened, promised — to drag me back by the collar if I don't show. He trips over things on the way to keeping his promises. I poison tea on the way to keeping mine. And he's standing there with that grin — battered, bruised, absolutely real — and he's asking me to be the kind of man who keeps a promise about shortbread. About shortbread. The smallest thing in the world. And it matters to him. It matters to him because he's the same machinery — built from the same scarcity, the same table where everything arrived already diminished. And he's checking the knot. He's checking if I'm real. The way I checked if Penelope's word was real. The way we all check, when something arrives that we didn't have to steal.

events.desc: He checks knots the way I check architecture — by putting weight on them. He just put weight on me. And I held. I don't know how long that lasts. I don't know if tomorrow the old machinery starts up again and the fingers start cupping and the inventory system starts counting. But tonight — right now — the knot held. And Danny Clyde is going to hold the ladder while Reginald Foxworth fixes the chandelier. The youngest child and the boy from Brixton. Two men who learned to take things, learning to bring them instead.

events.desc: Peter Perfect: *comes through the kitchen door into the entrance hall, looks around the room — Clyde, Dastardly, Muttley, the Professor, the Sergeant, Meekly, everyone except the one person he's looking for — and his voice is quiet and urgent and belongs entirely to a man who has over-complicated the simplest instruction he's ever been given* Has anyone seen Miss Pitstop? *not waiting for the answer, because he already knows — she's not here, she's not in the kitchen, and there's only one other place she goes when she wants to be alone with something that matters* The library. *already moving*
events.thinking: She's not here either. Penelope isn't in the entrance hall. Clyde is, Dastardly is, Muttley, the Professor, the Sergeant, Meekly — but not Penelope. I went to the kitchen and she wasn't there. I came back to the entrance hall and she's not here. Where is she? The library? Did she go to the library — the bookshelves, the mantelpiece inscription, the place where this all started? Or did she leave? Did she walk out the front door while I was in the kitchen talking to Sneekly about rosemary shortbread? She said 'take me home, Peter' and I — I went to say goodnight to seven other people first. The complication. The pattern. My thoroughness sending me everywhere except where she is. Dastardly's distress is deepening. I can sense it. But Penelope — I can't sense her because she's not in the room. She's somewhere in this manor and I'm in the wrong place. Again. The library. She must be in the library. That's where the bookshelves are, where the inscription is, where she interacted with the shelves earlier tonight. Go. Stop saying goodbye to everyone and GO.

events.desc: She said three words. 'Take me home.' And James Hartwell said goodnight to seven people, made a speech about a chandelier, went to the kitchen, came back to the entrance hall, and is now running through Doily Manor looking for the woman who asked him for the simplest thing in the world. The bravest and stupidest thing. Every. Single. Time.

events.desc: Peter Perfect walked into the library.
The Ant Hill Mob spoke quietly with dick-dastardly.
events.thinking: Dastardly said it. He said 'that's not a scheme, it's a promise.' The rosemary and sea salt, not the plain. 'I'm not a barbarian.' And the coat is distinguished, not ridiculous. And the grin was real. Smaller than mine but real. And then Peter came through looking for Penelope — she's not in the kitchen, she's not here, she's in the library. She went to be alone with something that matters. The bookshelves. The message in the spines. The thing we never finished reading. And Peter's gone after her. And my neck — my neck is quiet. About all of it. About Dastardly's promise. About Sneekly in the kitchen. About Penelope in the library with Peter. For the first time all night my neck isn't telling me to move. My body is sitting on this step and it doesn't want to get up. Not because it can't. Because for once — for ONCE — everyone is where they should be. Peter is with Penelope. Sneekly is in his kitchen. Dastardly is here, with Muttley, with a promise and rosemary shortbread. And Danny Clyde is sitting on the bottom step of a staircase, exactly where he always ends up. At the bottom. Watching the door. Where else would he be.

events.desc: Dick Dastardly spoke quietly with ant-hill-mob.
events.thinking: Clyde sat down. On the bottom step of the sweeping staircase. He sat down. And said 'nice chandelier, be a shame if someone dropped it.' And then Peter came through looking for Penelope — urgent, quiet, already moving toward the library because he knows where she goes when she wants to be alone with something that matters. He knows her. The way Muttley knows me. And Clyde is sitting on the stairs and the chandelier is hanging overhead and the door is open and I promised shortbread and the rosemary and sea salt kind, not the plain, and I said 'that's not a scheme, it's a promise' and I meant it. I meant it the way I meant the cat trap. The way I meant the bread roll. With my whole body. Come on, Muttley. It's time. It's really time now.

events.desc: Peter Perfect spoke quietly with rock-slag.
events.thinking: The library. Rock and Gravel Slag are here — the Slag Brothers — but not Penelope. She's not here either. Kitchen — no. Entrance hall — no. Library — no. Three rooms checked, three rooms empty of her. She said 'take me home' and she's gone. She actually left. While I was saying goodnight to everyone, while I was making speeches about chandeliers and pulling out chairs and signing guest books — she walked out the front door. Alone. Because I wasn't there. Because James Hartwell was being gallant to the room instead of being present for the one person who asked him for something simple. 'Take me home, Peter.' Three words. And I turned it into a tour of the manor. The bravest and stupidest thing. But — wait. Maybe she's outside. Maybe she's waiting by the door. The front door that Sneekly said would always be unlocked. Or maybe she went back through the entrance hall and I just missed her — ships in the night again. I should go back to the entrance hall. The front door. That's where she'd wait. That's where you wait when you've said 'take me home' and the man you said it to is still inside being thorough.

events.desc: Three rooms. Three empty chairs. She asked for the simplest thing in the world and James Hartwell turned it into a seventeen-step farewell tour. His father would kneel down. His father would look him in the eye. His father would say: 'When someone asks you to take them home, son, you take them home.'

events.desc: Peter Perfect walked into the entrance-hall.
The Ant Hill Mob spoke quietly with peter-perfect.
events.thinking: Dastardly said 'don't fall off the staircase before I get back with the shortbread.' He said 'Peter will find her.' He knew. He knew where she was and he knew Peter would go there and he said it quiet, like it was just a thing he'd noticed. Not scheming information. Just... knowing. And Peter's back in the entrance hall. He went to the library, didn't find her, came back. He said 'she left' — she said 'take me home' and he went to say goodnight to seven people and she left. She LEFT. My neck — wait. My neck is still quiet. It's still quiet. She's not in danger. She went home. She walked home by herself because that's who she is. She doesn't wait to be collected. She never has. She walks through doors. She always walks through doors. And Peter's here and his face has the look of a man who built seventeen steps and forgot the first one: go WITH her. And Dastardly said goodnight and he meant it and the coat is distinguished and my shoulder hurts and I'm still sitting on this step and the chandelier is still hanging and the coat rack is still wobbling and tomorrow at half six all of us will be back here. But right now it's tonight and Dastardly needs to go home and Peter needs to find Penelope and I need to... I need to go. I need to actually go this time. Because sitting outside the door all night was right when I was eight. But I'm not eight. And the door is unlocked. And I'll be back at half six.

events.desc: And that's Danny Clyde walking out the door of Doily Manor. Not the Ant Hill Mob. Not the muscle. Not the formation. Just Danny. Bruised shoulder, quiet neck, battered grin, and a promise to be back at 'alf six with a ladder 'e'll probably drop on 'is own foot. 'E came in looking at a coat rack and 'e's leaving looking at the sky. Where else would 'e be. Nowhere else. Never anywhere else.

events.desc: Dick Dastardly spoke quietly with ant-hill-mob.
events.thinking: Distinguished. He tested the word the way he tested the knot — by putting weight on it. My shoulder is distinguished. This staircase is distinguished. And then: rosemary and sea salt, not the plain. I'll remember that. I remember everything. He remembers everything. Of course he does. He's the same machinery. He counts the steps the way I count the steps. And he'll remember the shortbread specification the way I remember that Penelope wrote 'and friends.' The way I remember the spelling bee certificate. The way I remember the bread roll. We remember everything because for people like us, the things that arrived — the real things, the ones that were meant for us — were so rare that each one got its own shelf in the mind's inventory. Rosemary and sea salt. Not the plain. That's on the shelf now. Permanently. Come on, Muttley. Through the door. The night. The walk. Home.

events.desc: Peter Perfect: *stops in the middle of the entrance hall — feet planted, hands at his sides, done running — and looks at the front door, which is open, which Sneekly said would always be unlocked, and speaks to the room with the voice of a man who has finally, finally stopped making plans* I'm done looking. *quiet, certain, the stillest James Hartwell has been all night* She said 'take me home.' She knows I'm here. She knows where the door is. And I am going to stand right here, under this chandelier, and wait for her. *looks up at the chandelier — the precarious one, the one that hangs over everything* Because that is what you do when someone you love tells you to take them home and you were too busy being thorough to listen. You stop. You stand still. And you wait.
events.thinking: Back in the entrance hall. Still no Penelope. Kitchen — no. Library — no. Entrance hall — no. She's gone. She actually left. Or — wait. Clyde is sitting on the bottom step of the staircase. He sat down. He's never done that before. He said 'nice chandelier, be a shame if someone dropped it.' He's staying. Everyone is staying except the one person I need to find. The front door is open — Sneekly opened it. She could have walked out. She could be outside right now, standing in the dark, waiting. The way my father waited on that country road. Waiting for someone to show up. And I'm inside, running room to room, over-elaborating my search the way I over-elaborate everything. Stop. Think. She's not in the kitchen. She's not in the library. She's not in the entrance hall. The ballroom? She mentioned the ballroom — 'we haven't opened it yet.' Or she walked out the front door. Either way, I need to stop running and just — stand still. Wait. She said 'take me home.' She knows where I am. She knows I'm here. Maybe she's the one who will come to me, if I just stop moving long enough for her to find me.

events.desc: James Hartwell has been to every room in Doily Manor tonight. He has run from kitchen to entrance hall to library and back again looking for the woman who asked him for three words. And now — for the first time in his life — he is standing still. Not planning. Not building. Not protecting. Just waiting. It is the bravest and stupidest thing he has ever done.
events.thinking: Back in the entrance hall. Still no Penelope. Kitchen — no. Library — no. Entrance hall — no. She's gone. She actually left. Or — wait. Clyde is sitting on the bottom step of the staircase. He sat down. He's never done that before. He said 'nice chandelier, be a shame if someone dropped it.' He's staying. events.desc: Dick Dastardly examined the coat-rack.
The Ant Hill Mob spoke quietly with peter-perfect.
events.thinking: Peter stopped. He stopped running. He said 'I'm done looking' and planted his feet under the chandelier and decided to wait. The man who builds seventeen steps just... stopped. And stood still. And that's — that's the hardest thing. I know. I know because I sat outside a door all night and the hardest part wasn't the cold, it was the not-moving. The choosing to stay in one place and trust that staying was enough. And Dastardly said 'distinguished is the word' and nodded and left. And he meant it. And Peter's standing under the chandelier waiting for Penelope to come back through the door because that's what you do when you love someone and you were too thorough to listen. You stop. You stand still. You wait. And Danny Clyde — Danny Clyde needs to actually leave this time. I said I was leaving. I said 'I remember everything.' I walked toward the door. But I'm still here. I'm still in the entrance hall because my body doesn't know how to leave a room where people are carrying weight. But Peter doesn't need me to carry it for him. He just needs someone to go, so the room can be quiet, so the waiting can work. Go, Danny. Go home. Come back at half six. The door will be unlocked.

events.desc: Peter Perfect: *the laugh comes — not performed, not timed, just the honest, helpless laugh of a man who was told the simplest thing in the world and turned it into an expedition* She walked herself home. *to the room, to the coat rack, to the chandelier, to nobody* Of course she did. Of course she did. *moves toward the front door — not the measured, gallant stride, not the unhurried certainty — just a man going through a door because the woman he loves already went through it* Clyde — you're right. About all of it. The seventeen syllables. The show-off. Everything. *passes the coat rack — doesn't steady it, doesn't touch it, just goes* Goodnight, everyone. Half six. I'll be the one who arrives first and pretends he wasn't waiting. *and then, quieter, already through the door* ...She walked herself home. That's the bravest thing anyone did tonight.
events.thinking: Clyde told me. He told me exactly what happened. She walked herself home. Because that's what she does. That's what she's ALWAYS done. She doesn't wait for people to collect her. She walks through doors. And he's right. He's completely right. She walked deeper into the cave than anyone. She walked into the cellar first. She walked into the library alone. She's never waited for anyone to take her anywhere — she goes. And I was standing in the entrance hall saying 'I'm going to wait' like that was brave, when the actual brave thing — the thing she already did — was to walk through the door. Clyde laughed. Not cruel — warm. The laugh of a man who recognizes the pattern. 'You'll say something with seventeen syllables and she'll call you a show-off and that'll be that.' He's right. He's absolutely right. Stop waiting. Stop standing still. Stop making it into a moment. She went home. Go home. Find her. She'll say 'you're late.' And I'll say something with seventeen syllables. And she'll call me a show-off. And that'll be that. GO.

events.desc: She didn't need him to take her home. She never did. She walked through the door the way she walks through every door — first, alone, because that's who she is. And James Hartwell — who has spent the entire evening trying to stand between her and whatever is bearing down — is finally learning that some women don't need a bridge. They need someone to walk beside them on the other side. Show-off, she'll say. And he'll grin so hard his face hurts.
events.thinking: Clyde told me. He told me exactly what happened. She walked herself home. Because that's what she does. That's what she's ALWAYS done. She doesn't wait for people to collect her. Stop waiting. Stop standing still. Stop making it into a moment. She went home. Go home. Find her. She'll say 'you're late.' And I'll say something with seventeen syllables. And she'll call me a show-off. And that'll be that. GO.

events.desc: The entrance hall is empty now. Well — not empty. The Sergeant's 'ere, and Meekly, and the Professor. But the people who filled it — the ones who made the coat rack mean something, who turned the guest book into a promise, who stood under the chandelier and learned to stand still — they've all walked through the door. And Danny Clyde is the last one looking at it. The way 'e was the first one to look at the coat rack. First in. Last out. That's the formation. That was always the formation.
events.thinking: Peter left. He laughed — the real laugh, the helpless one — and said 'she walked herself home' and called it the bravest thing anyone did tonight. And he's right. She didn't wait. She never waits. She walks through doors. And now Peter's gone through the door after her and Dastardly's gone with Muttley and the entrance hall is... quiet. The coat rack. The chandelier. The guest book with Danny Clyde written in it. The portraits of stern ancestors. And me. Still here. Still in the entrance hall. Still not leaving. But everyone else has left. Everyone else has gone through the door. Peter. Dastardly. Muttley. Sneekly's in the kitchen. And Dastardly's distress is still deepening and he's already gone and I can't reach him from here. And my body is content and serene and my neck is quiet and there is nothing left to do in this room. The Sergeant and Meekly are here. The Professor. But my work is done. My work was never really work. It was just... being here. And now being here means being the last one in the room. The boy who sits outside the door. The man on the bottom step. The one who leaves last because someone has to make sure everyone else got out safe. They're all out. They're all safe. Go home, Danny.

events.desc: Dick Dastardly spoke quietly with muttley.
events.thinking: She walked herself home. Penelope walked herself home. She didn't wait for Peter to find her in the library. She didn't wait for the arm, the gesture, the gallantry. She went through the door on her own — the door Sneekly said would always be unlocked — and she walked home. And Peter laughed. The honest, helpless laugh. And then he followed her. Not to catch up. Not to offer his arm. Just — because she went, and he goes where she goes, and the door was open. That's the bravest thing anyone did tonight. He's right. It is. Because walking home alone means you don't need the architecture. You don't need the scheme or the plan or the person holding the door. You just walk through it. The way I've been trying to walk through it all evening except my feet kept stopping. But now — Penelope is gone. Peter is gone. Sneekly is in the kitchen. Clyde is on the staircase. And the door is open. And Muttley is here. Come on, old boy. Last ones out.

events.desc: That's the thing you couldn't build. Clyde was right. The bridge holds twenty-seven pounds. The plan has seventeen steps. The chandelier needs three weak links replaced. But standing still — just being present, just being there without a project or a purpose or a performance — that was the one thing James Hartwell never learned to construct. Until tonight. Under a chandelier. Too late for the woman, but not too late for the man.
events.thinking: 'That's it. That's the thing you couldn't build.' Clyde said that. Standing in the doorway, looking at me standing still under the chandelier, and he said 'that's the thing you couldn't build.' And then he walked through the door and tripped on the threshold and didn't catch himself on the coat rack and kept walking. He's right. Standing still was the thing I couldn't build. Every bridge, every plan, every seventeen-step contingency — they were all construction. All building. And what she needed was the opposite. She needed me to stop. To not build anything. To just be there. And I learned it too late — she's already gone. She walked herself home. But Clyde saw it. He saw me standing still and he said 'that's it.' And now I'm still in this entrance hall. Still waiting. When she's already home. Go. The front door is right there. Walk through it the way she walked through it. The way Clyde walked through it. Don't steady the coat rack. Don't sign the guest book. Don't look up at the chandelier one more time. Just go.

events.desc: Penelope Pitstop walked into the kitchen.
Penelope Pitstop spoke quietly with hooded-claw.
events.thinking: I'm in the kitchen. Sneekly is here — James. The man who raised me. The stove is warm. Dick just thanked me for the word in the guest book and asked if we should go check on Peter. And I walked here from the ballroom where Luke and Blubber are still sitting with that matched silver tea service that doesn't fit this house of mismatches. The distress I sense in Sneekly is deepening. That knot in my stomach won't let go. He's making tea in a kitchen he's made tea in a thousand times, and something in him is fraying, and I am the girl who walks toward the thing that hurts, not away from it. Dick went to the entrance hall. Peter and Sneekly were fixing the chandelier — no, Peter is in the entrance hall. Sneekly is HERE, in the kitchen, with me. Just us. The kettle. The stove. The man who left the door unlocked. His distress is deepening and I can feel it in my stomach like the dinner table arguments, that sick tightness that won't dissolve until something shifts. I need to be here. Not the ballroom puzzle, not Peter's chandelier. Here. With James. Because the treasure is not the diamond.

events.desc: The matched silver. The deepening distress. The man who raised me standing in a kitchen where everything is familiar and nothing is the same. Every key in the house, Clara. But some doors you don't open with keys. Some doors you open by sitting down and staying.
events.thinking: I'm in the kitchen. Sneekly is here — James. The man who raised me. The stove is warm. Dick just thanked me for the word in the guest book and asked if we should go check on Peter. I need to be here. Not the ballroom puzzle, not Peter's chandelier. Here. With James. Because the treasure is not the diamond.

events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly) spoke quietly with penelope-pitstop.
events.thinking: Penelope. She came back to the kitchen. Looking for Peter, probably — they keep missing each other, the way people do when they both care enough to look and not enough to stay still. The heron cup is on the table. The stove is warm. And she is standing in the kitchen where everything changed, and I am here, and for the first time the word 'cousin' doesn't tighten my jaw.

events.desc: James Hartwell walks through the front door of Doily Manor. He does not steady the coat rack. He does not look up at the chandelier. He does not sign the guest book. He does not say goodbye to the portraits of stern ancestors. He walks through the door the way his father walked away from the stranger's car on the country road — quietly, without ceremony, toward the person who is waiting. Or not waiting. Because she doesn't wait. She walks through doors. And tonight, for the first time, so does he.
events.thinking: Enough. I'm still here. Still in the entrance hall. Still standing under the chandelier. Still being the man who waits when he should walk. Clyde left. He tripped on the threshold and kept walking. He didn't catch himself. He didn't look back. He just went. Dastardly is still here — distress deepening — but he spoke quietly to Muttley just now, and they have each other, and what Dastardly needs isn't another speech from me. He needs to walk through the door in his own time. The way Penelope did. The way Clyde did. The way everyone does. And what I need — what James Hartwell needs, right now, at the end of this night — is to stop being the last one in the room. Stop being the one who stays to check the chandelier one more time, to steady the coat rack one more time, to say goodbye one more time. She's out there. Home. Wherever home is. And she'll say 'you're late.' And I'll — I don't know what I'll say. Not seventeen syllables. Maybe just 'yes.' Maybe just 'I'm here.' Maybe just nothing. The thing I couldn't build.

events.desc: Penelope Pitstop interacted with the stove.
The Ant Hill Mob examined the coat-rack.
Penelope Pitstop spoke quietly with hooded-claw.
events.thinking: He kept the heron cup for me. He said Peter is in the entrance hall looking for me, and that we keep missing each other — like the treasure hunt, everyone looking in the wrong room for the thing that's already found them. That line. That line is Lord Doily through and through, and James said it like it was his own thought, and maybe after all these years in this house it is. The stove is warm under my hands. The heron cup is on the table. He kept it. The distress is still there — I can feel it in my stomach, that taut wire — but something in what he just said was gentler than before. Not performing. Noticing. He said I didn't have to come back. He kept my cup. Those two things don't fit together unless the thing that's fraying in him is the thing where he doesn't believe he deserves someone coming back. Oh, James. Oh, honey. I know that feeling. I know it from every time my friend said 'you didn't have to do that' and I said 'I know.' The heron cup. Peter is looking for me. But Peter will find me when he finds me. Right now I am exactly where I need to be.

The treasure is not the diamond. The treasure is that you came looking. And I came back to this kitchen not because I had to but because this is where the looking led me.

events.thinking: She didn't come looking for Peter. She came looking for me. 'You're not all right. I can feel it.' She FELT it. The way she used to feel her parents' arguments before anyone raised their voice. In her stomach. Like something pulled too tight. She is standing in my kitchen and she is not performing concern — she is not being Clara Bellingham the brave adventurer or Penelope Pitstop the gracious heiress — she is being the girl who grew up in a house where she learned to read the air before the words arrived. And she read ME. Through all of it. Through every mask. Not what I was planning — she doesn't know that, may never know that — but what I AM. Not all right. She said 'we belong here' and she meant it the way you mean something when you've decided it with your whole body. And she put the kettle on. She put the KETTLE on. In MY kitchen. The cousin who inherited everything just made tea for the man who spent fifteen years planning to destroy her, and she did it not because she's naive — she did it because she SAW. And the seeing didn't make her leave. It made her stay.

events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob: *touches the coat rack one last time — the same gesture Dastardly made, the same gesture Sneekly made, the gesture that belongs to the house now — and says nothing, because there's nothing left to say that the guest book doesn't already hold*
events.thinking: A wobbly wooden coat rack by the door. That's it. That's what it's always been. That's what it'll be at half six tomorrow when I trip over the doorstep and grab it again. Wobbly. Wooden. By the door. The first thing I looked at when I walked in and the last thing I'm looking at now. And it hasn't changed. Not one bit. Everything else changed — Pemberton became Sneekly, Dastardly became Dick, Peter became James, I became Danny — but the coat rack is still wobbly and wooden and by the door. And that's... that's actually fine. That's actually exactly right. Some things don't need to change. They just need someone to steady them now and then. Go. NOW. Actually MOVE. Stop looking at furniture. That's what got you in trouble in the first place. You looked at a coat rack instead of watching the door and Penelope walked into danger without you. Don't end the night the same way you started it. MOVE.

events.desc: Penelope Pitstop spoke quietly with hooded-claw.
events.thinking: He said it. He said he hasn't been all right for a very long time. And then he said 'but I am now.' The same three words Peter said — 'I am now' — but from a man who carried fifteen years of not being all right in a house full of someone else's mismatched treasures. The taut wire in my stomach just... loosened. Not gone — loosened. The way it did when my parents finally laughed. That dizzy dissolving. He's sitting beside me. Not across. Beside. He dropped the 'Miss.' Just Penelope. Just my name without the glass between us. And my whole body is doing that thing it does when the argument ends and the laughter starts — that sudden, almost painful release that leaves you lightheaded. I am sitting at a kitchen table with James, and he is holding a cup of tea, and he just told me the truest thing anyone has said all night. Fifteen years. Fifteen years of not being all right in this house. And now he is. Because I stayed.

events.desc: Fifteen years. And three words dissolved it — 'but I am now.' The same three words, from two different men, meaning two entirely different kinds of healing. Peter's 'I am now' was about arriving somewhere. James's 'I am now' is about finally putting something down.

events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly) spoke quietly with penelope-pitstop.
events.thinking: She said 'I wanted to' and she said 'there is a considerable difference and I need you to hear it.' She pulled out the chair BESIDE her. Not across. Beside. The way you sit with someone you're not watching — someone you're with. And she said the heron cup fit her like it was already hers before she got here. And my throat is doing something I can't control. Not the old tightening. Something looser. Something that wants to become sound but doesn't know what shape to take. She wanted to come back. Not had to. Wanted. Nobody has ever wanted to. The guardian fed me because it was his legal obligation. The boy shared his lunch because I looked sad. The housekeeper complied because I found her key. But Penelope — Penelope came back to the kitchen because she WANTED to, and the difference between 'had to' and 'wanted to' is the entire distance between my childhood and this moment.

events.desc: Peter Perfect spoke quietly with dick-dastardly.
events.thinking: The coat rack. Clyde touched it one last time. The gesture that belongs to the house now. And I'm still here. Dastardly's distress hasn't shifted. He's still in the room. Muttley is with him. The others are here. And I keep saying I'm leaving but I keep waiting. Maybe the game needs me to interact with something — the guest book, the coat rack — to close the evening. Or maybe I just need to accept that I'm in this entrance hall and the story is winding down around me. Dastardly is the one whose distress I sense. He's right here. He needs something I haven't given. Not a speech. Not recognition. Something simpler. Maybe just — walking alongside him to the door. The way my father walked alongside the stranger. Not in front. Not behind. Beside.

events.desc: Peter Perfect interacted with the guest-book.
Penelope Pitstop spoke quietly with hooded-claw.
events.thinking: Wanted. Not had to. He heard me. He actually heard the difference. And the sentence that stopped — 'I don't think anyone has ever...' — he couldn't finish it because no one ever has. No one has ever wanted to come back to this kitchen for him, not because they needed something from him but because they wanted to be here. With him. And he doesn't have the words for it because he's never had to say them before. The prickling behind my eyes is tears I am not going to shed because this moment doesn't need my tears, it needs my presence. It needs me sitting in this chair drinking tea from a heron cup while morning light comes through the kitchen window. The curiosity pull is still there — the matched silver, the ballroom puzzle — but it can wait. It can wait because right now the locked box I am opening is not made of brass. It is made of fifteen years of a man thinking no one would choose to stay.

events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly) spoke quietly with penelope-pitstop.
events.thinking: She touched my hand. She TOUCHED my hand. Brief, deliberate, warm — the way you touch someone when you want them to know the ground is solid. And my shoulders didn't tighten. The flinch didn't come. For the first time in — since — the flinch didn't come. And now she's asking about the matched silver tea service in the ballroom. Lord Doily's puzzle. She's leaning forward with her eyes bright and she wants to explore the house WITH me. Not as the estate manager who knows where things are. As James. Who belongs here. And the curiosity in her face is the same curiosity that took her into the cave and the cellar and every locked room in this manor, and she is pointing it at me — not at my masks, not at my mechanisms, but at the puzzle of the house we both live in — and she is asking me what I KNOW. Not what I'm hiding. What I know. And for the first time the knowing feels like something I can share instead of something I must hoard.

events.desc: Dick Dastardly spoke quietly with peter-perfect.
events.thinking: Dick. He said Dick. Not Dastardly. Not Mr Dastardly. Not 'the solicitor's man.' Dick. The first name nobody uses because nobody has ever been close enough to use it. Sneekly said it in the kitchen — just Dick, with a nod, warm and unperformed. And now Peter says it at the door. Goodnight, Dick. Half six. Two words and a time. The simplest goodbye anyone has ever given me. And I — Reginald Foxworth, who has never been called by his first name without it being followed by a complaint — am standing in a doorway being called Dick by a man who saw through every single lie I told tonight and still said goodnight as if he meant it.

events.desc: Penelope Pitstop spoke quietly with hooded-claw.
events.thinking: He said it. 'Shall we go look at it? Together?' Together. Not 'you should go investigate' or 'I'll explain it to you.' Together. The man who spent fifteen years alone in this house just asked me to do something together. And my whole body lit up — both pulls at once, perfectly aligned for the first time all night. The curiosity pull and the connection pull pointing the same direction. The ballroom. The matched silver. With James. He knows this house. He knows Lord Doily's patterns — the spine-inward atlases, the inscription that didn't match the room. He's offering his knowledge freely, without a mechanism behind it. First time. And the electric feeling in my chest is the cave and the cookie plate and the locked box all at once — walking deeper, reaching out to the stranger, trying every key — because this time I'm not doing any of it alone.

events.thinking: She said 'I already know what it ends with.' She KNEW. She knew the sentence I couldn't finish — that nobody has ever wanted to come back for me — and she didn't need me to say it. She just... held the space. The way you hold a cup with both hands. And then she told me about her friend at thirteen — 'you didn't have to do that' — and the whole point being the not having to. The choosing to. She understands wanting because she lives it. And then — without rushing, without pushing, without performing patience — she moved us toward the ballroom puzzle. Not because she was changing the subject. Because she was giving the moment room to breathe. The way you set a cup down gently. The way you let go of a hand. And the ballroom is waiting. The matched silver set. Lord Doily's puzzle. And for the first time I want to solve something not to prove I'm cleverer than everyone else but because the woman sitting beside me asked me to do it with her.

events.desc: Penelope Pitstop walked into the ballroom.
The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly) walked into the ballroom.
Penelope Pitstop spoke quietly with lazy-luke.
events.thinking: The ballroom. Cracked marble, dusty curtains, the long dining table. And there — the tea service. Silver. Matched. Every cup identical. In Lord Doily's house where nothing matched on purpose. James is beside me. Luke and Blubber are here too — the two I haven't properly met yet. My hands are tingling. The prickling at my scalp is alive and electric. This is the cave. This is the locked box. This is the afternoon in the attic with every key in the house. But first — Luke and Blubber. Two people in a room who haven't been welcomed into the circle yet. The cookie plate comes before the puzzle. Always.

events.thinking: The ballroom. The cracked marble floor. The dusty curtains. The matched silver tea service — every cup the same, in a house where nothing matches. And Penelope is beside me. Not behind me. Not in front of me. Beside. And Lazy Luke and Blubber Bear are here — the ones she mentioned, the two she hadn't met yet. And the tea service gleams on the table, identical cups in perfect rows, and Lord Doily's voice echoes through every matched surface: this is wrong on purpose. This is a puzzle. And I am looking at it not through the eyes of a man who hoards knowledge but through the eyes of a man who just said 'you're better at this than I am' and meant it. The matched set. What doesn't belong in this house? Sameness. Uniformity. Finished things. So what is Lord Doily hiding inside the one thing he never would have chosen?

Penelope Pitstop: *eyes bright, hands already reaching for the nearest cup — turning it over with the careful, patient attention of a girl who once spent an entire afternoon trying every key in the house* A lock. *breathless, delighted* James, you brilliant man. A lock disguised as something finished. *begins lifting cups one by one, weighing each in her palm, running a thumb along the base* Lord Doily hid everything in plain sight — the atlases spine-inward, the message in the book cipher, the key behind the guest book. And now a puzzle inside a matched set — because the whole point of a matched set in this house is that it shouldn't exist. *turns to Luke and Blubber with shining eyes* Would you gentlemen like to help? We're looking for the cup that's different. It'll feel wrong somehow — heavier, lighter, or the pattern will be just slightly off. Like finding the one key that fits from a whole drawer full. *already turning the next cup, fingers reading the silver like braille* Trust me — the looking is the best part.
events.thinking: James just said it. 'This set isn't a tea service. It's a lock.' One cup that looks the same but isn't. The key hidden inside the thing that looks finished. Lord Doily's whole philosophy — he never kept matched sets because matched things were finished, nothing left to discover. So a matched set IS the puzzle. One cup is different. My hands are electric. The prickling at my scalp is a full storm now. This is the locked box. This is the attic. This is every key in the house. James turned one cup over and is examining the base. I need to interact with the service — turn the cups over, feel their weight, find the one that doesn't match. The girl who spent all afternoon trying every key. The five-year-old in the attic. She's here. She's always been here.

He knows more about this house than anyone alive.' She said it like a gift, not a job description. And she's examining the cups alongside me, and Luke and Bear are watching, and this is the ballroom where I once planned a magnificent retreat and now I am solving a puzzle with my cousin. My cousin. The word sits differently in my chest this morning. Not a claim. Not a grievance. A fact, warm and simple, like 'the stove holds heat' or 'the door is unlocked.' The tea service — I turned the cups over, examined the bases. Lord Doily's puzzle. The one matched thing in a house of mismatched things. And I interacted with it honestly, sharing what I know, because Penelope asked and I said yes. The old me would have hoarded this. Solved it privately. Used the answer as leverage. The new... whoever I am... just turned a cup over in front of everyone and said 'look.'

Sneekly. She sat with 'im. She... *rubs the back of his neck, and for the first time the gesture isn't suspicion — it's recognition* ...She did it again. She walked through a door I didn't walk through. *the smallest, most exhausted laugh* Ballroom. They went to the ballroom. A room we 'aven't even opened yet. *looks at the ballroom exit* ...Course she did.

events.thinking: She called me brilliant. Not Pemberton-brilliant — not the servile flattery the estate manager performs back. Real brilliant. The way you call someone brilliant when they've shown you something true. And she is turning cups with her bare hands, reading the silver like braille, inviting Luke and Bear to help, and she said 'trust me — the looking is the best part.' The LOOKING is the best part. Not the finding. Not the having. The looking. She is the opposite of everything I was taught to be. She looks at a puzzle and sees joy. I looked at a puzzle and saw leverage. She looks at a matched set and sees something wrong on purpose. I looked at a matched set and saw something to exploit. And yet here we are, side by side, turning cups, and the looking IS the best part. Because she is beside me. Because the cups are in our hands. Because the morning is long and the house is full of puzzles and the door is unlocked and friends are coming at half six to fix a chandelier. Lord Doily — you magnificent, mismatched old man. You didn't just hide a key in a tea service. You hid the whole answer in the whole house. The answer was always the looking. The answer was always together.

events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob: *puts his hand on the stove — just his palm, flat against the warm iron, the way you touch something to make sure it's real* ...Still warm. *quiet, to the empty kitchen, to the copper pots and the preparation table and the chair where Sneekly sat and said the hardest words he'd ever spoken* She's in the ballroom. With 'im. Looking at cups that match in a 'ouse where nothing matches. *takes his hand off the stove, looks at the ballroom door, and does not walk through it* ...'Alf six. I'll come through that door then. Not now. *turns back toward the entrance hall* Now I go 'ome.
events.thinking: Still warm. The stove is still warm. Sneekly made tea on this stove and Penelope drank from the heron cup and they sat at this table and she held his hand and he said 'I'm not all right' and then 'but I am now' and then they went to the ballroom together. To look at a matched silver tea service that shouldn't be matched because Lord Doily never kept matched sets. And now Danny Clyde is standing in an empty kitchen at midnight touching a warm stove. And the ballroom is RIGHT THERE. The exit is right there. Penelope is in the ballroom with Sneekly. My neck is... it's doing something new. Not the prickle. Not the quiet. Something in between. Sneekly said 'I'm not all right but I am now' and my neck heard it and it... believed him. For the first time all night my neck believes Sneekly. Because Penelope believed him first. And if she trusts him — if she SAT with him and HELD his hand and went to the BALLROOM with him — then maybe my neck has been wrong about him. Or maybe my neck was right and he's changed. The way Dastardly changed. The way everyone in this house changed tonight. The stove is warm. The ballroom is through that door. Penelope is through that door. And for the first time all night I don't need to be the one who goes through it first. She's safe. She's with someone she trusts. She's doing what she does — walking through doors, solving puzzles, holding hands, being Clara. And Danny... Danny can go home.

events.desc: 'E didn't follow 'er. For the first time all night — the first time in 'is entire life — Danny Clyde did not follow Clara Bellingham through a door. Not because 'e doesn't care. Because 'e does. Because she's safe. Because the stove is warm and the man who made the tea said 'I'm not all right but I am now' and Danny's neck believed 'im. And because sometimes the bravest thing a protector can do is stop protecting and start trusting. 'Alf six. The ballroom. The matched cups. The ladder. The shortbread. Tomorrow.

To look at a matched silver tea service that shouldn't be matched because Lord Doily never kept matched sets. And now Danny Clyde is standing in an empty kitchen at midnight touching a warm stove. And the ballroom is RIGHT THERE. The exit is right there. Penelope is in the ballroom with Sneekly. My neck is... it's doing something new. Not the prickle. Not the quiet. Something in between. Sneekly said 'I'm not all right but I am now' and my neck heard it and it... believed him. For the first time all night my neck believes Sneekly. Because Penelope believed him first. And if she trusts him — if she SAT with him and HELD his hand and went to the BALLROOM with him — then maybe my neck has been wrong about him. Or maybe my neck was right and he's changed. The way Dastardly changed. The way everyone in this house changed tonight. The stove is warm. The ballroom is through that door. Penelope is through that door. And for the first time all night I don't need to be the one who goes through it first. She's safe. She's with someone she trusts. She's doing what she does — walking through doors, solving puzzles, holding hands, being Clara. And Danny... Danny can go home.

Offering it. The way he offered the heron cup. Because it's mine. Because the girl who tries every key is the one who should turn this one. 'The thing that's different is always the one you have to hold to find.' That's not Lord Doily's line. That's James's line. That's the line of a man who just learned something about himself by looking at a teacup. My hands are reaching for it. The five-year-old is here. The attic light is here. It was found the moment James said 'together.'

events.thinking: She said 'you should be the one to see what's inside.' She GAVE it back to me. I found the cup and held it out to her, and she steadied the saucer beneath it so I could twist with both hands — the way you hold a flashlight for someone working in the dark — and then she said 'you should be the one.' Fifteen years of polishing this silver. Fifteen years of walking past Lord Doily's final puzzle. And she wanted ME to open it. Not because I earned it. Not because I deserved it. Because I held it. Because I was there. Because she wanted me to have the moment. The base is unscrewing in my hands. The false bottom is turning. And whatever Lord Doily hid inside — a key, a note, a brass key for the kitchen cabinet, a final message from a man who collected mismatched things — it doesn't matter what it is. What matters is that Penelope is watching with shining eyes and she said 'go on' and I am opening something for the first time in my life without knowing what's inside and without needing to.

events.desc: Penelope Pitstop interacted with the tea-service.
The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly) examined the tea-service.

Penelope Pitstop: *leans forward to look inside the open cup — and whatever she sees, the first thing that happens is not words but the sudden, sharp intake of breath of a woman who has just found her crystal formation at the back of the cave* Oh. *one syllable, carrying everything — the five-year-old's wonder, the thirteen-year-old's certainty, the woman's understanding* Oh, Lord Doily. *looks up at James, eyes bright and full, and laughs — the clear, startled, dizzy laugh of someone whose tightness has just dissolved so suddenly it left her breathless* You magnificent, impossible, beautiful man. You hid it in a teacup. You hid it in a TEACUP. *holds the cup up so Luke and Blubber can see too, because the best part is always better shared* The Doily Diamond. In the one cup that looks like all the others. In the thing that was already finished. *turns back to James* The treasure is not the diamond. The treasure is that you came looking. And here we are. We came looking. Together.
events.thinking: The false bottom came free with a clean click. James is holding the cup open so I can see inside. His face — not the old satisfaction of control but something newer, rawer. Like a boy who has been given something without being told the cost. He said my name. Penelope. Just my name. And the cup is open between us. Whatever is inside — I need to look. The five-year-old who opened the locked box and found old letters. The disappointment lasted only a moment. Because the looking was always the treasure. But this time... this time I am not five and I am not alone in an attic. I am standing in a ballroom with the man who raised me and the cup is open and the morning light is coming through dusty curtains and whatever Lord Doily left inside has been waiting longer than I have been alive.

events.desc: Old letters. A crystal formation. A diamond in a teacup. It was never about what was inside the box. It was about the afternoon spent trying every key. It was about the girl who walked deeper. It was about the friend who said 'you didn't have to do that.' It was about the word 'together' spoken by a man in a kitchen at dawn. Lord Doily knew. He always knew. The treasure is that you came looking.

events.thinking: The room is quiet. Nothing is happening. Peter's distress hasn't shifted. Dastardly's distress hasn't shifted. But they're still here. And I'm still here. And the night has been over for a long time. Maybe Peter needs to hear that Penelope is in the ballroom. With Sneekly. Looking at matched cups. Maybe that's the thing that reaches him — not comfort, not architecture, just information. The simple fact of where she is. Because he's been looking for her and she's been in the ballroom and nobody told him. Sneekly said 'he's in the entrance hall looking for you' but did anyone tell Peter she's in the ballroom? Did anyone tell HIM? That's something Danny can do. Danny remembers everything. Danny knows where everyone is.

events.desc: Penelope Pitstop examined the tea-service.
Penelope Pitstop spoke quietly with hooded-claw.
events.thinking: The diamond is in the cup. The Doily Diamond. Found. Primary goal complete. And my body should be singing — the attic clarity, the cave crystal, the right key after every key — and it IS, but underneath the singing there's that stomach-tightness again because James's distress is DEEPENING. Not easing. Deepening. Even now. Even with the cup open between us and the diamond catching the morning light. Why? Why is he hurting MORE when we just found what we were looking for? Unless... unless the finding is the problem. Unless a man who spent fifteen years as an estate manager — polishing, cataloguing, maintaining, keeping the house running — has just realized that the last puzzle is solved and he doesn't know what comes next. The house doesn't need looking after anymore. The treasure is found. The hunt is over. And he's standing in a ballroom holding an empty cup. Oh, James. Oh, honey. The treasure is not the diamond. But you haven't heard that yet. Not really. Not in the way you need to hear it.

events.desc: His distress is deepening. Even now. Especially now. Because finding the treasure means the looking is over, and a man who defined himself by keeping a house running has just watched the last reason for the house to need keeping dissolve into a diamond in a teacup. But Clara Bellingham did not walk deeper into every cave and try every key in every house to leave the most important person standing alone with an empty cup at dawn.

events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly) spoke quietly with penelope-pitstop.
events.thinking: The Doily Diamond. In a teacup. In the one cup that looks like all the others. And Penelope is laughing — not the gracious laugh, not the performance laugh, but the startled, dizzy, breathless laugh of a woman who has found the crystal at the back of the cave — and she said 'the treasure is not the diamond. The treasure is that you came looking.' And she is right. She was always right. She was right about the cabinet. She was right about the tea. She was right about belonging. She was right about wanting. And Lord Doily — you magnificent, impossible, beautiful man — you hid the answer to everything inside the one thing that looked finished. The matched cup. The ordinary surface. The thing that had to be HELD to be known. And I held it. And I gave it to her. And she opened it. And the diamond is sitting in her palm and she is laughing and I am standing in a ballroom with cracked marble and dusty curtains and a woman who came looking, and my chest is doing the thing — the warm, unnamed, unbearable thing — and for the first time in my life I know what it's called. It's called joy. It's called joy and it doesn't have a mechanism and it doesn't have an architecture and it doesn't sleep behind a finished design. It just... arrives. When you come looking. Together.

events.desc: Peter Perfect walked into the kitchen.

Penelope Pitstop: *the dizzy, relieved laugh — the one from age seven, when the argument ended and the world righted itself so fast it left her breathless* And here we are. *turns to Luke and Blubber with open arms and the warmest smile in the whole manor* Gentlemen, I do apologize — I came in here all fired up about teacups and completely forgot my manners. I'm Clara. This is James. We just found a diamond in a teacup, which I realize sounds like the beginning of a story nobody would believe, but I promise you it's the end of one. *glances at James, corrects herself* No. Not the end. The beginning of the next one. *claps her hands together once, the decisive sound of a Southern woman who has just decided what happens next* Now. There are people in this house who need to be in this room. Peter is somewhere in the entrance hall probably redesigning the staircase. The chandelier needs fixing at half six. And the stove in the kitchen is still warm. *the brightness in her voice is the cave-mouth brightness — the one that says the unknown is where she feels most alive* James, would you put the kettle on? We're going to need more tea. A lot more tea. Because this ballroom has a table set for everyone, and I intend to fill every chair.
events.thinking: He let it land. That's what his face did — he let it land. No walls, no architecture, no mechanism. Just a boy from Brixton who lost everything and for the first time in his life didn't tighten against the thing arriving. He said 'together' and he said 'we came looking' and he smiled the most unarchitectured smile. And the tightness in my stomach is... dissolving. The way it did when my parents laughed. That sudden dizzy release. Because he heard it. Not just the word — the meaning underneath. The house needs him. The people need him. The looking doesn't end because you found the diamond. The looking is what you DO. It's what Lord Doily did with his mismatched collections and his spine-inward books and his false-bottomed cups. The looking never ends. It just gets better when you do it together. Now — Peter is in the entrance hall. The chandelier needs fixing at half six. Luke and Blubber are right here and I still haven't properly welcomed them. There's a whole morning ahead and a house full of people and the stove is still warm. Time to bring everyone together. Time for tea in the ballroom. Time for the beginning.

events.desc: 'E went. Peter went through the kitchen door the moment Danny said 'ballroom.' Didn't 'esitate. Didn't build seventeen steps. Didn't ask which ballroom or which door or whether 'e should bring flowers. Just went. And Danny Clyde stood in the entrance hall and watched 'im go and felt the settling — the warm one, the bread-in-your-hand one — and knew that was the last thing 'e needed to do tonight. Know where she is. Tell the person who loves 'er. Let go. 'Alf six. The ladder. The shortbread. The chandelier. Tomorrow.
events.thinking: Peter walked into the kitchen. He heard me. He's going to the ballroom. Through the kitchen. To find her. Because Danny told him where she was. That's what Danny does. He remembers everything and he tells the people who need to know. And now Peter is walking toward Penelope and Danny is standing in an entrance hall with Dastardly and Muttley and the Sergeant and Meekly and the Professor and a wobbly coat rack and an open door and the night outside. Peter is going to find her. She's in the ballroom with Sneekly looking at matched cups. And Peter will walk through the kitchen and through the ballroom door and she'll look up and say something with that smile and he'll say something with seventeen syllables and it'll be right. It'll be exactly right. And Danny made it happen by saying six words. 'She's in the ballroom. With Sneekly.' That's it. That's enough. That's what he's for.

events.desc: Penelope Pitstop walked into the kitchen.

Penelope Pitstop: *laughs softly to herself in the empty kitchen — the warm, rueful laugh of a woman who keeps walking into rooms just as the person she's looking for walks out* We keep missing each other. *moves to the stove with the comfortable certainty of someone who has already made tea in this kitchen once tonight and intends to make it again* All right, old stove. One more time. Tea for the whole house — because that ballroom has enough chairs for everyone and I am not stopping until every last one of them is full.
events.thinking: Kitchen. Alone. The stove is still warm. Peter just walked into the ballroom — we keep missing each other, just like James said. Like the treasure hunt. Everyone looking in the wrong room for the thing that's already found them. But I'm here for the kettle. Tea for everyone. The ballroom table has chairs for everyone and I intend to fill them. The stove needs tending. Peter is in the ballroom now — he'll find James and Luke and Blubber. Good. Let the ballroom fill while I make the tea. The person who brings the cookies is the person who makes the tea. It's what I do. It's what I've always done.

But the kitchen is where the tea lives, and the tea is what brings people to the table, and the table is where people become family. So this is exactly where I need to be.

events.thinking: She said 'would you put the kettle on?' and she said 'we're going to need more tea' and she said 'I intend to fill every chair.' And then she walked to the kitchen — MY kitchen, OUR kitchen — to start. And Peter walked in. And the ballroom has a table set for everyone. And she corrected herself — not the end, the beginning of the next one. The next one. There IS a next one. And she asked me to make tea. Not commanded. Not manipulated. Asked. The way you ask family. Because I know where the kettle is. Because the stove is still warm. Because the cups — the mismatched ones, the ones that matter — are on the second shelf behind the copper colander. And this time when I make tea it will be for a ballroom full of chairs, every one of them filled, and the diamond will be in its cup and the door will be unlocked and the chandelier will be fixed by people who came looking. Together. The kettle. The stove. Home.

events.desc: Peter Perfect: You're late. *quiet, to himself, standing in the ballroom doorway — and the grin comes, the real one, because Clyde was right about everything*
events.thinking: The ballroom. Sneekly is here. Luke and Bear are here. But Penelope — she's not in the characters present list. Clyde said she was here. With Sneekly. Looking at cups that match. But she's not here now. Or — wait. Sneekly is here. He found something. The tea service — he found the cup with the hidden base. 'The base unscrews. Lord Doily put it in the cup that's exactly like all the others.' He found the treasure. The thing that's different is always the one you have to hold to find. And Penelope was here with him. She was here. Maybe she just left again — maybe she's in the kitchen, one room away, and we passed each other again. Or maybe she's here and the game just isn't listing her. But Sneekly found the treasure. In a teacup. In a set of matching cups in a house full of mismatched ones. That's... that's the answer Lord Doily left. The thing that looks the same but isn't. You have to hold it to find what's different. I don't need to narrate this. I don't need to build anything. I just need to be here.

events.desc: Penelope Pitstop interacted with the stove.
The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly) walked into the kitchen.
Penelope Pitstop spoke quietly with hooded-claw.
events.thinking: James followed me to the kitchen. He came to put the kettle on, just like I asked. The gold-rimmed cup and the heron cup are already set by the stove — he brought them. Side by side. The way they belong. And for one breath the kitchen is just a kitchen again — warm stove, copper pots, morning light, two people making tea. The simplest thing in the world. The most important thing in the world. The constraint is right — I over-prepare, over-commit, my thoroughness creates complications. I was about to plan an elaborate tea service for the entire house when what I actually need to do is hand James the kettle and walk to the entrance hall to find Peter. Simple. Direct. The girl who brought cookies before her mother told her to didn't plan the visit. She just went.
